title: Primetime Roundtable: The lights are shining bright in Atlanta
summary: After looking hopeless in the first two weeks of the season, the Falcons have suddenly become one of the league’s more prolific scoring teams. Getting Michael Penix Jr. back on the field was necessary for the offense to start functioning at a professional level. Since his return, the team has produced two incredibly impressive road […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - OCTOBER 05: Brian Robinson Jr. #15 of the Atlanta Falcons celebrates with Zachariah Branch #17 and Chris Lindstrom #63 after scoring a touchdown against the New Orleans Saints during the second quarter of the game at Caesars Superdome on October 05, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images After looking hopeless in the first two weeks of the season, the Falcons have suddenly become one of the league’s more prolific scoring teams. Getting Michael Penix Jr. back on the field was necessary for the offense to start functioning at a professional level. Since his return, the team has produced two incredibly impressive road wins, led by a thunderous running game and an ultra-aggressive defense that doesn’t commit self-inflicted errors. Kevin Stefanski, Tommy Rees, and Jeff Ulbrich have worked wonders around certain personnel limitations and injury crises outside the quarterback position. These performances have injected optimism into a fan base that has been looking for any sign of sustainable success. Kevin Knight and Aaron Freeman join me to discuss what has gone into their recent resurgence. What has been most impressive about what Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees have done to make the Falcons prolific? Allen Strk: The personnel usage to create more high-percentage looks through the air and varied designs in the running game stands out schematically. It gives Michael Penix Jr. the space to operate in the most comfortable infrastructure imaginable after recovering from his third ACL knee surgery. He is getting the ball out faster and with more conviction into clear passing windows. That improvement led to exceptional efficiency on play-action while still having that explosive element, as shown on his 31-yard touchdown pass to Jahan Dotson. A heavy dose of 12, 22, and 23 personnel has been effective for the ground game, but Stefanski and Rees are utilizing role players effectively to punish opposing fronts. Kyle Pitts, Chris Blair, and Austin Hooper have been used as fullbacks at various points. Nick Muse is playing more often to provide more push in heavier sets. Olamide Zaccheaus and Zachariah Branch are being motioned to the side where the run is directed to create space at the second level. These added nuances to the game plan have helped the Falcons produce a jaw-dropping 60.3% run success rate over the last two weeks. Aaron Freeman: Weaponizing the play-action passing has been the most positive development. The diversity in the run game has also been a welcome addition. Rees and Stefanski are building an offense that marries the run and passing games. It’s been extremely effective in Penix Jr.’s first two starts. It’ll be fun to watch it grow and develop the rest of the way. Kevin Knight: The simplest answer is that coaching from top to bottom has improved. The only notable offensive coaches the Falcons had under Raheem Morris and Zac Robinson were Dwayne Ledford and Kevin Koger. Atlanta kept Koger, then upgraded from Ledford to the legendary Bill Callahan. They also drastically improved their QB coaching with Alex Van Pelt. Tommy Rees also appears to be a significant upgrade over Zac Robinson, who might be one of the worst play-callers in the league based on his early results in Tampa Bay. In terms of what those coaches have done specifically, I think it’s pretty simple: Stefanski and Rees looked at this roster and installed a scheme based on the talent they had available. Such a simple thing, but so very important. It was obvious that Atlanta should’ve been a run-heavy, play-action focused offense with an explosive passing game for years. In just a month, this scheme looks better than whatever abomination Robinson installed previously. How does Jeff Ulbrich move forward with Harold Perkins Jr. after his breakout performance? Allen Strk: Perkins Jr. has seen his playing time rapidly rise over the last two games. Some of it can be attributed to the game script. He played 43 and 52 snaps against Green Bay and New Orleans, compared to only 24 and 26 against Pittsburgh and Carolina. Based on his showing, it could become the norm for the former LSU standout. Perkins Jr. was outstanding last Monday night, showcasing his range, instincts, physicality, and dependability as a tackler. From cleanly breaking up an out route on Juwan Johnson to running in stride with Alvin Kamara to prevent a big play off a wheel route, the sixth-round pick was up for whatever was thrown at him. Kendal Daniels has played well and provides that downhill ferocity to stop the run. What Perkins Jr. brings to the table with his skill set makes it hard to leave him off the field, mainly in passing situations. It seems inevitable that Ulbrich will continue to put as much on Perkins Jr.’s plate as possible, given his dynamic capabilities. Aaron Freeman: With no changes. Perkins is featured exclusively in the team’s nickel subpackage, while Daniels gets all the work in the base and big nickel sets. That delineation suits their skill sets. Perkins’ superior speed makes him more impactful in space or rushing the quarterback on obvious passing downs. In contrast, Daniels’ superior size and instincts make him best suited as a run defender. The Falcons can keep both players in their current roles without needing to change anything. The only real adjustment depends on matchups. If the Falcons face a bigger, more physical tight end, Daniels is probably the better option. But if it’s an athletic player like Johnson, we just saw how effective Perkins can be in those battles. Kevin Knight: Ulbrich seems pretty committed to a rotation at linebacker, but I think Perkins Jr. will continue to dominate the snap share. He was simply too good to ignore against the Saints, putting out some incredible coverage reps alongside a great all-around performance. After starting the season behind Daniels (67.2%) with a 34.3% snap share, the two have swapped places in the lineup. Over the past two games, Perkins has seen his snap share jump to 65.2% and 70.3%, with Daniels moving into the third linebacker spot. My long-term view is that the Falcons view both as starting-quality linebackers. The plan could be for Perkins Jr. and Daniels to take over the starting jobs in 2027. To that end, the team would be wise to make sure both are getting live game reps this season. It’s possible that Daniels moves to backup and special teams status if Perkins keeps playing like this, but for now, I’d expect the rotation to continue. I also don’t think the team is pulling Divine Deablo off the field anytime soon unless his injuries continue to drag him down. He’s a major leader, and his communication is likely critical to how the defense functions. Have any offensive linemen elevated their play in particular in the back-to-back dominant wins? Allen Strk: After being a step behind far too often at the start of the season, Jawaan Taylor has picked it up during this road stretch. He plays with a nasty streak the offensive line lacked last year after Kaleb McGary’s season-ending injury (and eventual retirement). There were moments in both dominant wins that he mauled whoever was in front of him, whether it was an edge defender or a linebacker at the second level. Taylor will need to step up against better competition as a pass protector, but his run-blocking gives the Falcons an enormous lift on the right side, with Chris Lindstrom continuing to perform at an All-Pro level. Aaron Freeman: The Falcons have shown greater down-to-down consistency over the last two weeks by leaning more on the strengths of their various blockers. Lindstrom’s athleticism always shines in the team’s zone-blocking scheme, but he’s also making waves as a puller now that the Falcons are incorporating more gap runs into the mix. But you can’t help but acknowledge that the Packers and Saints are far less formidable on the interior of their defensive lines than the Steelers and Panthers are.…
author: Allen Strk

title: Ravens film study: what does new center Cam Jurgens bring to Baltimore?
summary: The Ravens made a significant move to address their offensive line struggles on Wednesay, acquiring former Pro Bowl offensive lineman Cam Jurgens and a 2027 seventh-round pick from the Philadelphia Eagles in exchange for a 2028 second-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick. While surrendering a future second-round selection is certainly a steep price, this […]
full_text: Sep 21, 2025; Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA; Philadelphia Eagles center Cam Jurgens (51) against the Los Angeles Rams at Lincoln Financial Field. Mandatory Credit: Eric Hartline-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Ravens made a significant move to address their offensive line struggles on Wednesay, acquiring former Pro Bowl offensive lineman Cam Jurgens and a 2027 seventh-round pick from the Philadelphia Eagles in exchange for a 2028 second-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick. While surrendering a future second-round selection is certainly a steep price, this is a move that reflects the urgency surrounding Baltimore’s offensive line situation. Starting-caliber offensive linemen rarely become available through trades, particularly those under the age of 30 with proven success at the NFL level. Jurgens hasn’t been without his struggles recently, partially because he is playing out of position at guard. His recent center tape (all of last year, Week 1 this year) provides plenty of reasons for optimism that he can return to his Pro Bowl form and provide some much-needed stability to Baltimore’s offensive front. Jurgens has spent the last three games starting at guard for Philadelphia as the Eagles have dealt with offensive line injuries of their own, forcing them to shuffle personnel across the interior. His recent performances haven’t necessarily reflected the player who earned Pro Bowl recognition, so his work at center provides a much better indication of what Baltimore could be getting. In Week 1, Jurgens started at center and didn’t surrender a single pressure across 35 pass-blocking snaps. That performance was consistent with his production last season, when he allowed just 11 pressures across 522 pass-blocking snaps while playing exclusively at center. One of the most impressive aspects of Jurgens’ game is his awareness and ability to operate within the larger protection scheme. Jurgens serves as a conduit along the offensive line, consistently recognizing when neighboring linemen need assistance and positioning himself to provide help without compromising his own assignment. New Ravens Center Cam Jurgens reps at center on non play action passes and zone running concepts ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/qCu492PYDQ — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) October 8, 2026 That awareness becomes particularly noticeable against defensive fronts that utilize stunts and twists. Jurgens does an excellent job identifying late-developing loopers, redirecting his momentum and meeting defenders before they can generate pressure on the quarterback. His ability to process movement after the snap and react accordingly is an important trait for an interior offensive lineman, especially in an offense that has struggled with protection consistency. From a technical standpoint, Jurgens is extremely effective once he establishes contact with a defender. He does a good job coordinating his hands and feet to maintain leverage, staying attached throughout the rep and making it difficult for defenders to disengage. His 33.37-inch arms provide additional recovery range, allowing him to reestablish positioning when defenders initially gain an advantage. Combined with his athleticism, that length gives him a larger margin for error when working against quicker interior pass rushers. As a run blocker, Jurgens’ athletic profile makes him a particularly intriguing addition to Declan Doyle’s zone-based rushing attack. Jurgens displays an explosive first step off the line of scrimmage, allowing him to gain advantageous positioning against defensive linemen and execute reach blocks effectively. His ability to generate lateral displacement with his initial punch helps create running lanes, particularly on outside-zone concepts where offensive linemen are tasked with moving defenders horizontally rather than simply driving them backward. What stands out is how comfortable Jurgens looks operating in space. He transitions smoothly from the first level to the second, showing the athleticism and body control necessary to locate linebackers and seal them away from developing rushing lanes. He rarely looks rushed when working in space, displaying the patience to establish proper angles before engaging smaller defenders. That combination of lateral quickness, technical refinement and second-level athleticism should translate well to Baltimore’s rushing attack. Jurgens gives the Ravens an interior offensive lineman capable of executing difficult reach blocks while also providing the movement skills necessary to work within combination blocks and climb to linebackers.
author: Yuri

title: Ravens vs Titans: the Good, the Bad, and the Ugly
summary: In a potential letdown game after a massive win in Rio, the Ravens managed to control the Titans for nearly their entire matchup on Sunday. But, in accordance with franchise tradition, Baltimore’s victory was far from pretty. There was a lot of good, bad, and ugly to go around. The Good Lamar Jackson-Zay Flowers connection: […]
full_text: In a potential letdown game after a massive win in Rio, the Ravens managed to control the Titans for nearly their entire matchup on Sunday. But, in accordance with franchise tradition, Baltimore’s victory was far from pretty. There was a lot of good, bad, and ugly to go around. The Good Lamar Jackson-Zay Flowers connection: There might not be a better quarterback/wide receiver duo on the planet right now. Despite both missing time in the first four weeks, the duo is operating at an otherworldly level. Sunday’s win was a perfect example: Jackson threw for 222 yards in the first half, over 100 of which went to Flowers. That built enough of a lead in the second half for the Ravens to close out the game. Unfortunately, the South Florida natives are going to continue to have mirrored seasons. After Jackson had to work without Flowers in the second half of Week 1 and all of Week 2, Flowers played without Jackson in the second half of Week 4 and likely all of the next game as well. Most rec yards in first half of a game this season Zay Flowers 150 (Week 1) Tetairoa McMillan 147 (Week 4) Davante Adams 145 (Week 2) Christian Watson 131 (Week 1) Zay Flowers 119 (Week 4) pic.twitter.com/3ei0eC5lzs — PFF (@PFF) October 5, 2026 Defensive improvements: The Ravens defense still needs work, and the Titans offense is maybe the worst in football. That being said, I am going to give Jesse Minter’s unit their due after this one. Outside of Tennessee’s first and last drive, this defense did exactly what they needed to. In a game where Lamar Jackson left and the offense put up a big goose egg in the second half, the defense kept the Titans at bay. It wasn’t perfect, and they did let up the late touchdown drive, but they are showing improvement, and that’s what matters. For all the comparisons that Jesse Minter-Mike Macdonald comparisons, it’s important to remember there isn’t a magical button that makes the defense suddenly understand Minter’s vision immediately. Thoughts on Jesse Minter and the Ravens defense: Mike Mac had 2 years as an NFL DC and then became the Seahawks HC. Gave up totals of 20, 20, 42, 29, and 36 in the first 6 weeks. Gave up 31, 26, 30, 27, and 25 in the weeks following. It’s not some magical process. Takes time. — Z.J. (@ZJBeatdown) October 7, 2026 Pass blocking: A big talking point heading into this game was how the interior offensive line oculd struggle against Jeffery Simmons, one of the best defensive linemen in the league. But they beat expectations and allowed just six pressures on Lamar Jackson’s 23 dropbacks and one on Tyler Huntley’s 11 dropbacks, according to Pro Football Focus . Seven pressures across 34 dropbacks (20.5%, a season low) while backups are playing and a rookie guard is out of position is an outstanding effort, especially with Simmons on the other side. It was noticeable that Jackson had a lot of clear pockets to work from on Sunday. Pressure numbers: While the Ravens’ offensive line got after it in pass protection, their pass rush responded kind. While they only converted one sacks, they were in the backfield all day and clearly made Cam Ward uncomfortable, forcing him to move and throw the ball away multiple times. The unit as a whole totaled 18 pressures; Mike Green and Nnamdi Madubuike particularly stepped up in a big way with Trey Hendrickson out for this game. The Bad Second-half offense: I understand that Lamar Jackson was out for the second half of the game. I understand that Jesse Minter specifically said that Tyler Huntley operated in a way that allowed the Ravens – up big already and with the rain coming down – to win. But putting up zero points in the entire second half against the Titans is not something to stand on. The defense did their job by not allowing Tennessee to get momentum, but the offense is going to need a better game plan Sunday night against Atlanta without Jackson. I like Huntley, and I think with a week of preparation Declan Doyle can draw up a way for the Ravens to win another one of his starts. Run blocking: While I noted how well the pass blocking was for the offensive line, they struggled to open lansin the run game. Derrick Henry only averaged 3.2 yards per carry despite getting 23 attempts. Only 25 of Henry’s 73 yards came before contact. 25 yards before contact on 23 attempts is not a stat you want to see if you are the offensive line. They got pushed around up front. They are going to have to be better so they can lean on Henry against Atlanta with no Lamar Jackson sidelined. Sack conversions: While the pass rush was good on Sunday, the Ravens only converted one pressure for an actual sack. It came late in the game from undrafted free agent Ethan Burke. When players like Mike Green and Nnamdi Madubuike are getting five and six pressures in the game, they need to gets hands on the quarterback and impact the play. In fairness to Green, one of his first pressures forced Cam Ward into making an unadvised throw that was rifled in hard to his running back, which bounced off for Trenton Simpson’s interception. But only one sack against this Titans team is a poor effort. The Ugly Penalties: Talk about ugly. I don’t know if there’s anything much uglier than the flag pandemic going on in the NFL this season. The Ravens certainly have their own discipline issues to work out and plenty of pre-snap penalties that prove that. I’m not absolving them of any of that. But I throw that stuff on the back burner after watching the ridiculous show on Kyle Hamilton unsportmanlike conduct and all of the soft holding and pass interference calls. It’s not just a Ravens issue. Twelve teams had double-digit penalties in Week 4. It’s a league-wide problem and it’s getting noticed. The flags are FLYING in the NFL this season 🚩 The NFL has seen the most accepted penalties through Week 4 since play-by-play data became available in 1978. Week 4 alone had 271 accepted penalties, the 2nd most in any week over that span. pic.twitter.com/8JNfqTqzLG — ESPN Insights (@ESPNInsights) October 6, 2026 Injuries: Heading into Sunday’s game, the Ravens already had all three of their centers on injured reserve along with four other would-be contributors. Leading pass rusher Trey Hendrickson was out as well. Then, during the game, Baltimore lost quarterback Lamar Jackson, cornerback Marlon Humphrey, backup guard Andrew Vorhees, and tight end Durham Smythe to injury. Smythe is already confirmed to be out for the season with a torn Achilles and a subsequent placement on IR. The other three didn’t practice on Wednesday but aren’t considered to be IR candidates. The Ravens are looking at their backup quarterback, their fourth option at center, their second backup guard, and a suddenly-thin outiside cornerback corps to play Sunday Night Football. They have since made a trade for center Cam Jurgens that would slide Vega Ioane back to guard but he won’t be ready for Sunday as he works to clear concussion protocol and learn the offense.
author: Zach Canter

title: Has the Ravens defense really been bad?
summary: Jesse Minter and the Ravens defense have taken a lot of heat through four weeks. Minter was supposed to be the savior of this defense, the guy who would end two years of struggles under Zach Orr. Most people expected a dominant unit right away. That hasn’t happened yet, but they haven’t been nearly as […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 04: Linebacker Roquan Smith #0 of the Baltimore Ravens in action against the Tennessee Titans at M&T Bank Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jesse Minter and the Ravens defense have taken a lot of heat through four weeks. Minter was supposed to be the savior of this defense, the guy who would end two years of struggles under Zach Orr. Most people expected a dominant unit right away. That hasn’t happened yet, but they haven’t been nearly as bad as people seem to think. Let’s start with where they rank. In 2024 and 2025, the Ravens were 18th and 30th in penalty-adjusted defensive EPA through four weeks. This year they’re ninth. Those 2024 and 2025 units finished eighth and 22nd, so this defense has historically gotten better as the season goes on, and this year it’s starting from a much better spot. I’m using a penalty-adjusted metric for a reason. Penalties have been a real problem for this team, and they’ve been going almost entirely one way. With penalties included, the Ravens rank 15th in defensive EPA per play. Sunday’s game against the Titans got out of hand: Baltimore was flagged 13 times for 131 yards, compared with 5 for 32 for Tennessee. And that one-sided pattern goes beyond one game. Opposing offenses have been flagged against the Ravens just nine times, tied for the fewest in the league, and Baltimore ranks dead last in EPA gained from those penalties. Short version: the defense is getting no help from the refs. They’ve drawn exactly one offensive holding call through four games, against Dallas, which is again tied for last. The defense hasn’t been clean either, but it’s getting nothing back in return. The offense is in the same spot: it has drawn only four defensive penalties, 31st in the league, while consistently shooting itself in the foot with procedural flags. If opposing offenses were being flagged at even a league-average rate, this defense would jump to 11th in EPA per play. Remove all penalties and it’s 9th. All of this is to say the defense hasn’t been bad; it just needs some penalty luck to swing its way. One holding call or DPI can completely change a drive and turn a three-and-out into a touchdown drive. Fans, players, and coaches have harping on the penalties for weeks because they’re doing so much damage. As a team, the Ravens have lost 329 yards and 40 expected points to penalties, both second-worst in the NFL. Remove the penalties and they’re also 2nd in offensive EPA per play. Without the flags, this team has a top-two offense and a top-10 defense. I said after the Saints game that the Ravens were getting flagged at an unprecedented rate, and that’s turned into a broader NFL story. Teams are getting flagged at the highest rate in a decade, refs are getting suspended, and fans are fed up with how much officials are shaping games. This general pushback against the penalties could lead to a regression to the mean. Add it all up: the penalties, a new head coach, injured players still working their way back and finding their chemistry, and a defense that has historically improved as the year goes on. I have no doubt this will be a top unit over the back half of the season. The defensive line has been a bit of a carousel, but Nnamdi Madubuike and Mike Green have both looked very good – Green in particular looks like he is ready for a sophomore breakout. Trey Hendrickson missed last week after a procedure on his finger and should be back this week or next. The one area that needs immediate improvement is the run defense. The Ravens rank 21st in EPA per rush allowed with penalties removed, and they no longer have time to sort it out. With Lamar Jackson now injured, the defense needs to play up to its potential right away, starting with Bijan Robinson and a red-hot Falcons team.
author: Stephen Bopst

title: Buffalo Bills rooting interests: Who needs to win in Week 5
summary: Well, that wasn’t a fun week. Let’s try again.  The Buffalo Bills suffered their first loss of the season Sunday night, and losing to the New England Patriots made it hurt a little more. Buffalo is still 3-1 and still very much in control of where this season goes, but the loss did change the rooting-interest game a bit.  For […]
full_text: Well, that wasn’t a fun week. Let’s try again. The Buffalo Bills suffered their first loss of the season Sunday night, and losing to the New England Patriots made it hurt a little more. Buffalo is still 3-1 and still very much in control of where this season goes, but the loss did change the rooting-interest game a bit. For starters, the division tiebreaker no longer belongs to Buffalo. Hopefully, that is temporary. The Bills also dropped from the top spot in the AFC, with Kansas City moving into the No. 1 seed, Jacksonville sitting at No. 2, and Buffalo falling all the way to No. 3. None of that is particularly concerning five games into a 17-game season, and all of it is reversible. But we have reached the point where simply rooting against the AFC East isn’t enough. Now we need some help knocking down division leaders and thinning out the teams hanging around the AFC playoff picture. So, the rules are getting a little more complicated. Buffalo wins. The rest of the AFC East loses. AFC division leaders lose, and when two of them meet, we root against the team holding the better seed. Wild-card contenders lose, unless Buffalo needs them to strengthen its schedule — and the AFC East rule always wins that argument. After that, we’ll happily give some wins to the teams hanging around the bottom of the AFC and let them move a little farther away from the top of the draft. And then there’s the NFC, where things are a little simpler. Buffalo opponents can win for strength of schedule — unless, of course, they’re playing the Bills. We’d also like to knock the NFC division leaders down a little when we can, while letting the teams at the bottom stay there and keep those premium draft picks on the other side of the league. Got all that? Good. Let’s find Buffalo some help. _____________________________________________________________________________ AFC EAST Buffalo Bills (3-1) at Los Angeles Rams (2-2) Root for: BILLS We don’t need to overthink this one. There’s only ever one right answer here, but in case you need a reason, here you go: Buffalo has to take care of its own business before any of the help elsewhere really matters. The Bills get the Monday night stage this week, and a win gets them right back on track after last week’s loss. Go Bills! Las Vegas Raiders (3-1) at New England Patriots (2-2) Root for: RAIDERS Remember when we said the AFC East rule trumps everything else? Here is our first test. Buffalo plays Las Vegas next week, so a Raiders win would give the Bills a little strength-of-schedule boost. More importantly, though, New England just handed Buffalo its first loss and owns the head-to-head tiebreaker. We don’t need the Patriots stacking wins while they have that in their pocket, so this one gives us double the benefit: Go Raiders. Cleveland Browns (3-1) at New York Jets (1-3) Root for: BROWNS This one breaks another rule. Cleveland is sitting at the top of the AFC North, which would normally make the Browns exactly the kind of team we want knocked down. But the Jets are the Jets, they live in the AFC East, and the division rule comes first. We’ll deal with Cleveland later. For now, give New York another loss — although at this rate, it won’t be long before the Jets aren’t a factor (I know, I know, but for now we have to let the math do its work), and we will be trying to get them out of draft position. But not quite yet. Cincinnati Bengals (2-2) at Miami Dolphins (0-4) Root for: BENGALS Cincinnati is hanging around the AFC playoff picture, while Miami is still looking for its first win. Normally that would make the Dolphins useful — give a basement team a win, hurt a potential wild-card contender, and call it a day. Nope. Miami is still in the AFC East, and we’re not volunteering to help anybody in the division. Let the Dolphins stay winless for another week. _____________________________________________________________________________ REST OF THE AFC Philadelphia Eagles (2-2) at Jacksonville Jaguars (3-1) Root for: EAGLES Here’s the big one. Jacksonville has jumped Buffalo in the AFC standings and currently owns the No. 2 seed, so knocking the Jaguars back down is exactly the kind of help we’re looking for now. This one doesn’t require any complicated tiebreaker math or competing rules. We need Jacksonville to lose. Fly Eagles, Fly. Baltimore Ravens (3-1) at Atlanta Falcons (3-1) Root for: FALCONS Baltimore isn’t leading the AFC North right now, but the Ravens are sitting in a wild-card spot at 3-1 and are very much part of the AFC race. Buffalo will get its own shot at Baltimore later this season, but for now we can let an NFC team do some work for us. A Falcons win puts another loss on an AFC contender without giving anything to another AFC team. Yes, there’s the whole strength-of-schedule thing since Buffalo plays Baltimore later, but at some point we have to stop helping good AFC teams win games just because they’re on the Bills’ schedule. Indianapolis Colts (2-2) at Pittsburgh Steelers (2-2) Root for: STEELERS Now we get into the games where somebody in the AFC has to win. Neither team currently holds a playoff spot, but Indianapolis is in the AFC South chasing Jacksonville, while Pittsburgh is trying to keep pace in the North. Buffalo already beat Pittsburgh, so if one of these teams has to move to 3-2, we might as well make it the one that helps the Bills’ strength of victory. Denver Broncos (2-2) at Los Angeles Chargers (0-4) Root for: BRONCOS Normally we’d be all aboard the 0-4 Chargers finally winning one and moving themselves away from the top of the draft. But Denver is on Buffalo’s schedule, which gives us a reason to keep building the Broncos’ record before the Bills see them later this season. Strength of schedule wins this argument. Go Broncos. Houston Texans (0-4) at Tennessee Titans (0-4) Root for: TEXANS We have been begging Houston to do something for weeks, so how about starting here? The Bills already have a win over the Texans, which means every Houston win from here makes that victory a little more valuable for strength of victory. The fact that it would also pull the Texans away from the top of the draft is just a bonus. Come on, Houston. Surely you can beat somebody. _____________________________________________________________________________ NFC Detroit Lions (2-2) at Arizona Cardinals (1-3) Root for: LIONS Buffalo already has a win over Detroit, so every Lions win from here makes that victory a little more valuable. That’s enough to make this an easy choice. The Cardinals can keep doing their thing at the bottom of the NFC while Detroit gives Buffalo a little strength-of-victory help. Chicago Bears (3-1) at Green Bay Packers (2-2) Root for: BEARS Chicago is on Buffalo’s schedule later this season, so we’re sticking with the Bears here. Sure, they’re 3-1 and hanging around near the top of the NFC North, but that doesn’t matter nearly as much to Buffalo as a stronger schedule could when the AFC playoff tiebreakers start coming into play. We’ll worry about where Chicago sits in the NFC another time. For now, Bear Down. San Francisco 49ers (4-0) at Seattle Seahawks (3-1) Root for: SEAHAWKS This is exactly what our new NFC rules were made for. San Francisco is undefeated and sitting atop the NFC West, so let’s knock the 49ers down a little. Seattle isn’t exactly a basement dweller at 3-1, but somebody has to win this thing. Give the division leader a loss and tighten up the NFC West. Minnesota Vikings (4-0) at New Orleans Saints (1-3) Root for: SAINTS Here’s where two of our NFC rules run into each other. We’d be perfectly happy leaving New Orleans near the bottom and keeping premium draft picks in the NFC, but Minnesota is 4-0 and leading the NFC North. Knocking down the division leader wins out. Give the Vikings their first loss, and we’ll worry about the Saints’ draft position another week. BONUS HINT: Keeping NFC division leaders’ records below their AFC counterparts also helps keep the better draft picks…

title: Buffalo Bills will get Dome Josh Allen vs. Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football in Week 5
summary: Josh Allen is a superstar in any weather. And starting right around November, at home, he plays in plenty of windy, snowy games in Orchard Park. For as much as Allen has embraced the elements as Buffalo’s starting quarterback and played a myriad of outstanding games when the weather has been far from ideal, the […]
full_text: Josh Allen is a superstar in any weather. And starting right around November, at home, he plays in plenty of windy, snowy games in Orchard Park. For as much as Allen has embraced the elements as Buffalo’s starting quarterback and played a myriad of outstanding games when the weather has been far from ideal, the best Josh Allen is Dome Josh Allen. Here are Allen’s career stats in his nine games when playing in a dome: Completion rate: 68.8% Yards per attempt: 8.81 TD & INT: 19 & 6 Passer rating: 110.1 Rushing yards & rushing TDs per game: 43 & 1.33 To put that 110.1 rating into perspective, to date, Allen’s best season-long rate came in 2020, and it was 107.4. It was 101.4 when he won MVP in 2024 and 102.2 a season ago. And of course, SoFi Stadium is a dome, where the Bills will take on the Rams on Monday Night Football in Week 5. We all remember Allen’s outrageous performance against the Rams back in 2024, when he went 22-of-37 for 342 yards with three passing touchdowns, no interceptions, and toted the rock 10 times for 82 yards and three more scores. Pro Football Reference makes a distinction between dome and retractable roof stadium, the latter of which would include Houston’s Reliant Stadium. Allen did some rough outings in that building but did go bonkers on the Texans defense inside in Week 1. Yet in a classic dome, Allen has been spectacular both as a passer and a runner.

We have a lot to watch this week as the Bills prepare to head west for their Monday night showdown with the Los Angeles Rams. Here’s what we know after day one of practice. Thursday injury report pic.twitter.com/eKp7Jz02Zy — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) October 8, 2026 NOT PRACTICING: WR DJ Moore – shoulder DT Ed Oliver – knee NCB Dee Alford *DB Te’Cory Couch *Couch is on the practice sqaud so frequently not listed on the daily injury reports. However, he was not seen during the portion of practice open to media according to multiple sources. LIMITED PRACTICE: CB Christian Benford – ankle FULL PRACTICE: ILB Terrel Bernard – knee OLB Bradley Chubb – thumb ILB Joe Andreessen – knee WR Keon Coleman – ankle RB Ray Davis – hamstring S Damar Hamlin – rib OG Ar’maj Reed-Adams – eblow DT T.J. Sanders – illness LB Dorian Williams – hip WHAT WE‘RE WATCHING: Benford practicing is going to be a big positive this week. Yes, he’s not been stellar, but he’s better than whatever that was Buffalo was doing on Sunday. If he’s unable to run, however, the Bills did sign A.J. Woods to their practice squad this week, giving them another young option at cornerback. Likewise, if Alford can’t go, we could see Geno Stone called up to help that very confused looking back seven. On offense, the question will always be can Moore go. The 29-year-old wide receiver thinks he’s Ironman, and he never misses games – like seriously, never. And Joe Brady told us today that if Moore says he can go, he will be active. But if not – will we get to see rookie Skyler Bell wear a game day jersey this week?

title: Dallas Cowboys vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers, ‘TNF’ Week 5 fan discussion
summary: It’s already Week 5 of the 2026 NFL season, and yet again we have another NFC battle in primetime. Tonight, the 2-2 Dallas Cowboys take on the 0-4 Tampa Bay Buccaneers inside of Jerry’s World. Admittedly, this isn’t an extremely exciting matchup on paper. First of all, it sure feels like NFC teams are getting […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 8: Jalon Daniels #10 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers warms up prior to an NFL game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on October 8, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s already Week 5 of the 2026 NFL season, and yet again we have another NFC battle in primetime. Tonight, the 2-2 Dallas Cowboys take on the 0-4 Tampa Bay Buccaneers inside of Jerry’s World. Admittedly, this isn’t an extremely exciting matchup on paper. First of all, it sure feels like NFC teams are getting a large percentage of primetime exposure to start the season. Second, the Buccaneers are dreadful right now, and the Cowboys are their typical selves. Dallas can light the scoreboard up with the best of them, and quarterback Dak Prescott is playing well right now, but their middling 21st-century ways continues with a .500 record. Will Tampa Bay finally pick up a win, and on the road, or will Dallas get itself above .500 in Week 5? It’s not going to be easy for the Bucs, which former Bills quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick mentioned last Thursday in previewing this matchup. Tonight, rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels gets the start with Baker Mayfield still recovering from a gruesome hyper-extended thumb on his throwing hand. It’s already proven tough enough for Tampa Bay with Mayfield this season, so asking an undrafted rookie quarterback to make magic happen seems unwise. Daniels becomes the first undrafted rookie quarterback to start a game in Week 4 or earlier since the AFL/NFL merger in 1970. Daunting. Without a doubt, it’s been an awful start for the Buccaneers. Being shorthanded as they are, it might prove difficult to take advantage of a putrid Dallas defense in primetime. No NFL teams has ever made the playoffs after starting 0-5, so you have to expect Tampa Bay to approach Week 5 like an elimination game. With that, here’s your open thread for Thursday Night Football . As always, be kind to one another — and in all things… Go Bills!

title: Josh Allen provides update on whether or not a knee injury is hindering his running
summary: Josh Allen has hardly been himself the past two weeks as a runner, but the Buffalo Bills quarterback is not blaming a sudden lack of scrambling production on an injury. He had 13 carries for 22 yards rushing combined against the Chargers and Patriots, which included a five-carry, four-yard effort in Week 4’s loss. But […]
full_text: Josh Allen has hardly been himself the past two weeks as a runner, but the Buffalo Bills quarterback is not blaming a sudden lack of scrambling production on an injury. He had 13 carries for 22 yards rushing combined against the Chargers and Patriots, which included a five-carry, four-yard effort in Week 4’s loss. But it’s not just the lacking production that’s caught everyone’s attention. In both the Chargers and Patriots games, it appeared as though Allen passed up clear scrambling opportunities, something Allen hardly does. After the Week 3 win over Los Angeles, speculation swirled that Allen injured his knee in the fourth quarter. After Thursday’s practice in preparation for the Rams on Monday Night Football in Week 5, Allen said the following regarding said speculation: “There is no truth to that. Feeling great.” — Josh Allen responding to the idea that he’s not running as much because of a knee injury. — Jay Skurski (@JaySkurski) October 8, 2026 A pretty strong statement from Allen. And now, we have to take him at his word. Of course, we’ll all continue to be monitoring whether or not he runs as frequently and is as effective as normal. In 2024 against the Rams, Allen ran 10 times for 82 yards with three touchdowns. In the first two games of the this season, Allen toted the rock 20 times for 92 yards with four scores.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Exploring Los Angeles Rams tendencies ahead of Week 5’s primetime game against Buffalo Bills
summary: The Rams have long been Super Bowl contenders. Heck, it’s felt like they’ve had that label for the entire duration of the Sean McVay era that began in 2017. And they’ve of course hoisted the Lombardi Trophy once in that time frame. Let’s dive into those Los Angeles’ tendencies before the Bills trip to SoFi […]
full_text: The Rams have long been Super Bowl contenders. Heck, it’s felt like they’ve had that label for the entire duration of the Sean McVay era that began in 2017. And they’ve of course hoisted the Lombardi Trophy once in that time frame. Let’s dive into those Los Angeles’ tendencies before the Bills trip to SoFi Stadium for Monday Night Football in Week 5. Rams offense Matthew Stafford vs. pressure Entering this game, Stafford owns the NFL’s third-worst rating at while under pressure (among qualifiers) at 29.1 His completion percentage under pressure is sixth-lowest at 37.0%. Now, Drake Maye did enter Week 4’s game against the Bills with a 50.7 rating under pressure in the first three weeks then managed a 102.6 rating while pressured in Orchard Park. However, the disparity between’s Stafford clean-pocket play vs. his under-pressure play is as sizable. His accuracy percentage — completion rate discounting spikes, throwaways, and instances when a quarterback is hit as he throws — is 34 percentage points worse under pressure than it is when he’s kept clean, the largest disparity among all qualifying quarterbacks entering Week 5. 13 personnel I’ve written “13 personnel” more in the first month of this Bills season than I probably have in the past five years covering the NFL. Add to the counter here. Because the Rams are the NFL’s top 13 personnel team. Through four games, they’ve utilized the three tight end look the highest rate in league (30.8%). But that comes with a caveat. After an injury to second-year tight end Terrance Ferguson — now on IR — the Rams have shifted away from it. In Week 3, when Ferguson got hurt, Los Angeles used 13 personnel on 31 plays. Last week against the Eagles, it was deployed on one play. Kyren Williams as a receiver Williams is fresh off a 13-target, 10-reception performance in the Rams win over the Eagles in Philadelphia in Week 4. That effort got him to 21 catches on the season, he’s more than halfway to his regular-season career high in catches at 36. For as good as Williams is knifing between the tackles in Sean McVay’s zone-blocking based system, he’s become an important security blanket and screen option for Stafford this season. Play Action Josh Allen enters this game with the NFL’s second-highest play-action rate among qualifying quarterbacks at 39.4%. The Rams barely use it. Among those 39 qualifying passers, Stafford’ play-action rate of 22.5% ranks 31st. Rams defense Safeties and Trent McDuffie McDuffie was the Rams second enormous offseason acquisition, and he’s played like an All-Pro through the first month of the season. The former first-round pick the Bills know quite well has yet to miss a tackle and has allowed just five receptions for 74 yards on a whopping 18 targets in his coverage area. McDuffie also has an interception and has been credited with seven pass breakups to date. The Rams safety duo of Quentin Lake and Kamren Curl are as good as any in the NFL. Lake too has an interception and five pass breakups while Curl has just one missed tackle on 215 snaps through four games. They’re both sizable safeties at over 6’0” and 200 pounds. Emergence of new No. 1 pass rusher Gone is Jared Verse. Myles Garrett remains on IR. Byron Young has emerged for the Rams as the team’s top outside pass rusher. The 2023 third-round pick from Tennessee is 6’2” and 250 pounds but wins with surprising speed-to-power conversion and a nonstop motor. He brings a hefty 20.1% pressure rate into this game. Cover 1 The Rams are running Cover 1, a man concept, at the fourth-highest rate in the NFL through Week 4, at 27.0%, per Football Insights. Of course that’s not a ridiculously high percentage, but relative to the rest of the league’s coverage tendency, it is. The coverage they’ve used at the second-highest rate is Cover 4 — zone — at 23.4%

title: Bills news: Assessing Buffalo’s offense through 4 weeks
summary: For the first two weeks of the season, it appeared that Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills offense would once again be one of the most potent in the NFL. The Bills hung 36 points on the Houston Texans—widely considered to have one of the stingiest defenses in the league—in Week 1, and followed up […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 27: Tarheeb Still #4 of the Los Angeles Chargers punches the ball loose from Dalton Kincaid #86 of the Buffalo Bills during the second half at Highmark Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the first two weeks of the season, it appeared that Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills offense would once again be one of the most potent in the NFL. The Bills hung 36 points on the Houston Texans—widely considered to have one of the stingiest defenses in the league—in Week 1, and followed up with a 41-point output in a Week 2 win over the Detroit Lions. But since then, Buffalo’s offense hasn’t appeared quite right, and that starts with Allen, who has thrown three interceptions with two fumbles (one lost) over the last two weeks. The Bills held on to beat the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3 despite committing five turnovers, but turnovers and an offense that mustered zero or one first down on seven of 11 possessions doomed Buffalo in a Week 4 home loss to the New England Patriots. New live chat feature during the games Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . After four weeks of the season, today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by assessing the state of Buffalo’s offense following a 3-1 start, including how defenses have succeeded in containing talented tight end Dalton Kincaid, and why head coach Joe Brady says solving the issues on offense will take improved efforts from everybody, not just Allen. “There’s a standard by which we play, and we’re either playing to that standard or not,” Brady said. “It obviously wasn’t good enough [against New England], and we didn’t find a way to go 1-0.” Check out the assessments below and then let us know your thoughts in the comments section. Have teams figured out how to contain TE Dalton Kincaid? In wins over the Texans and Lions, Kincaid hauled in 12 of 14 targets for 245 yards and a touchdown, sporting a 4.69 yards per route run (YPRR) figure that trailed only Jaxson Smith-Njigba of the Seattle Seahawks, and a 29.2% targets per route run figure that was 12th highest in the NFL. Since then, Kincaid has been getting challenged by opposing defenses, amassing only three receptions on five targets for 45 yards with a lost fumble. His YPRR plummeted to 1.13, and his target rate declined to 12.5%, tied for 160th out of 209 qualifying players. Against the Chargers and Patriots, the defenses played physical with Kincaid and provided help over the top, neutralizing Buffalo’s 2023 first-round pick. The one good development from Buffalo’s receivers through the first four weeks? Keon Coleman, who broke out with six catches on seven targets for 116 yards with a touchdown against New England. But for Buffalo’s offense to be on its game, the Bills need to figure out a way to get Kincaid more involved. title: Kaleb Elarms-Orr is quietly earning more playing time on Buffalo Bills defense
summary: Kaleb Elarms-Orr was the talk of Buffalo Bills training camp and preseason. It’s time to check in on the rookie linebacker after he played 16 snaps against the Patriots, the most to date in his NFL career. The currently shaky state of the team’s inside linebacker position warrants this KEO evaluation too. Elarms-Orr played eight […]
full_text: Kaleb Elarms-Orr was the talk of Buffalo Bills training camp and preseason. It’s time to check in on the rookie linebacker after he played 16 snaps against the Patriots, the most to date in his NFL career. The currently shaky state of the team’s inside linebacker position warrants this KEO evaluation too. Elarms-Orr played eight snaps in Week 1’s win over the Texans, 12 against the Lions, and nine against the Chargers. KEO’s 15.5% defensive snap rate pales in comparison to inside linebacker starters Dorian Williams and Terrel Bernard who’ve appeared on 67.1% and 96.1% of Buffalo’s defensive snaps through four games. But I have an inkling Elarms-Orr is going to continue to become a larger part of Buffalo’s inside linebacker unit as the season progresses. Partly because he’s playing quality football. Partly because the team’s other inside linebackers aren’t thriving in Jim Leonhard’s scheme right now. On those limited snaps, KEO has nine tackles without a miss. He was credited with four receptions allowed in his coverage area for 61 yards in the first three contests of the 2026 campaign but no receiving production on nine coverage snaps against the Patriots. He’s identifying plays and getting to the football in a flash all while smoothly covering plenty of ground in coverage to close throwing lanes. Let me show you. Watch how explosively KEO filled his lane on this tackle for loss on Rhamondre Stevenson on a critical third down late in the third quarter: pic.twitter.com/4dPJTaVG6y — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 7, 2026 Read his key. And hit the accelerators. No hesitation. Impact tackle. That’s textbook. But it wasn’t the only standout play from KEO against the run in Week 4. On this play, notice his twitchiness attacking the line of scrimmage and how assertively he stacked and shed the left guard to help slow Stevenson on this short gain: pic.twitter.com/WXhAekcC8o — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 7, 2026 I’ve scouted hundreds of linebacker prospects over the years, and the vast majority of them really struggle getting off blocks early as professionals, regardless of the round in which they were drafted. Elarms-Orr made it look easy on that play. Very authoritative. But if you’ve followed me for any period of time you know how much I harp on the importance of coverage for the modern-day linebacker. And against the Patriots, KEO showed veteran-like presence in that regard too. Watch here how, after mugging the A-gap alongside Bernard before the snap, he smoothly and swiftly floated down the seam and initially checked the three pass-catcher side before getting his eyes back to Drake Maye while continuing to get vertical depth: pic.twitter.com/6pczelJhZJ — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 7, 2026 KEO’s smooth sink clogged the throwing window to Romeo Doubs down the middle which caused a second pat of the football by Maye and thereby gave Greg Rousseau an extra split second to get a hit on the quarterback and force an incompletion. Outstanding. Back to one more subtly awesome run-defense rep against the Patriots. On this play, KEO didn’t just initiate first contact with the tight end at the second level…as he bench pressed the blocker, he first peaked to the outside to steer the running back away from the outside running lane before working back to the inside to help with the tackle: pic.twitter.com/NYnvbHwpmb — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 7, 2026 That’s veteran-level awareness, processing, and effectiveness beating the blocker in space on an inside run. Something else I noticed, from a more general and schematic standpoint, about KEO’s outing against the Patriots — he’s was the team’s main dime linebacker. That means, when Jim Leonhard used one linebacker and six defensive backs on the field KEO was typically that linebacker against the Patriots. And through four games, dime is the second-most utilized personnel package by the Bills defense at 27.1%, which is being used a little less than one percentage point higher than base, per Fantasy Points data. I’ll admit — it’s been reasonably easy to overlook Elarms-Orr in his first four NFL games. But I believe he’s about to see the field more frequently and start making a variety of plays on this Bills defense.

title: Storylines to follow for the rest of the season: Bryce Young contract extension, and more!
summary: Hello CSR! Normally, my column is reserved for the storylines to watch for the upcoming game. However, this is the Panthers much needed bye week, as they get a week off to recover from the recent games and potentially get back some key pieces for the rest of the regular season. The Panthers are 2-2 […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - JANUARY 10: Taylor Moton #72 of the Carolina Panthers walks off the field during warm-ups prior to the NFC Wild Card Playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams at Bank of America Stadium on January 10, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello CSR! Normally, my column is reserved for the storylines to watch for the upcoming game. However, this is the Panthers much needed bye week, as they get a week off to recover from the recent games and potentially get back some key pieces for the rest of the regular season. The Panthers are 2-2 and control their own destiny as they sit atop the NFC South. So, what storylines do we want to follow for the rest of the season? Let’s find out! Offense: What happens if Bryce Young keeps up this incredible pace? The most talked about topic of the off-season was definitely Bryce Young. I got questions every week in the mailbag about moving on from Bryce, giving Haynes King the starting job, trading for a potential successor, or signing some free agent that could shift the franchise back to winning ways. Well, after a 2-2 start and Bryce Young leading the NFL in most of the basic and Next-Gen statistical passing categories, all of a sudden Bryce Young’s performance on paper makes him look like a top QB in the NFL. This is not something I had on my bingo card going into the 2026 season, but here we are. Obviously, there is a chance that Bryce Young comes back down to Earth against some of the better defenses on their schedule after the bye week. The offense should have quite a test against a good Philadelphia Eagles defense following their bye week. But, if by some miracle, Bryce Young continues on this upper tier QB trajectory, what do the Panthers do with his contract? He’s currently on the 5th year option of his rookie deal, so he’s under contract at least until the end of the 2027 season. But, if he continues to traffic in the upper echelon of quarterbacks in passing yards, touchdown, yards per attempt, and all those fun Next-Gen stats that nerds like Jon use to fill their spreadsheets, what do the Panthers do? Well, they probably sign Bryce Young to a pretty hefty extension. I’d estimate around $60 million a year in average contract salary with a pretty hefty guaranteed amount. That would put him in the top 3 of QBs in average annual salary, but every new “franchise quarterback” contract tends to reset the market. And if Bryce Young continues on this trajectory, it might actually be smart to just go ahead and get him signed in the off-season rather than wait until he’s approaching free agency status and potentially looking at getting the franchise tag. As the salary cap goes up and as time goes on, more young QBs will get extensions and make Bryce Young more expensive. The Panthers might have SOME leverage and negotiate Bryce Young down to maybe $55 million a year like some of his contemporaries who are currently signed to big deals, but I have doubts they can make that work if he continues to play at this level. So while I am very happy to see Bryce Young doing so well throughout 4 games, that contract situation could very well dictate the next 5+ years of this franchise’s fortunes. Defense: Princely Umanmielen could take center stage I didn’t even realize until writing this article that Princely Umanmielen leads the Panthers in sacks with 3 throughout 4 games. While they spent major salary capital on Jaelan Phillips in free agency, I think we all knew someone would need to step up on the opposite side for this defense to really take off. Phillips is currently nursing an injury, though he may be back and ready to go versus his former team, the Philadelphia Eagles in week 6. But this is a major opportunity for the Panthers 2025 3rd round pick to really cement a role in the Panthers front seven, and they have ramped up his snap usage quite a bit. He already has as many pressures in 2026 as he did in all of 2025 per Pro Football Reference. He’s slotted in as a major pass rushing piece, and honestly the biggest help for this battered secondary is going to be a stronger pass rush. Princely Umanmielen could control that and really cement himself as a difference maker for this defense going forward. This is his time to show us what he can do. Bonus Storyline: Offensive Tackles Monroe Freeling got dinged up a little bit in the Panthers win over the Lions on Sunday. Conveniently, the Panthers freed up some roster spots as RB Trevor Etienne, OT Taylor Moton, and DL Tershawn Wharton are working their way through injuries. The offensive tackles in Freeling and Rasheed Walker have held up, but Moton returning as soon as possible from blood clot treatment could be huge for this offensive line. The question that will arise once he returns though is what this line will look like if they add him back to the starting lineup. Freeling, their high first round pick this season, has been practicing as a right tackle since the Moton news came up in the offseason. Walker took over at left tackle and hasn’t looked back. If Moton is ready to play, do you take Freeling out of the lineup completely? Do you shift him to left tackle, a position he hasn’t really been practicing for since being drafted? Or do you let Moton ride the bench and give him some time to get into game shape and see how the OL health looks throughout the season? It’ll be interesting to see how the coaches navigate this. What storylines are you watching for the rest of the season? Comment down below!

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Will Echoles
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: OXFORD, MISSISSIPPI - SEPTEMBER 27: Will Echoles #52 of the Mississippi Rebels reacts against the Louisiana State Tigers at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium on September 27, 2025 in Oxford, Mississippi. (Photo by Randy J. Williams/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Ole Miss Rebels defensive lineman Will Echoles. Bio Echoles (6’3”, 310 lbs.) was a consensus four star recruit from Mississippi, playing both sides of the ball. He enrolled early at Ole Miss and even suited up as a true freshman despite the Ole Miss defensive line having four future NFL players at the time. He still saw the field in eight games and limited snaps. Echoles took over the starting role as a true sophomore, playing in 15 games for the Rebels. He accumulated seven sacks, six passes defended, and 35 defensive stops. So far in 2026, he’s racked up 12 tackles, three for loss, and half a sack. Strengths/Weaknesses Echoles has the size and strength to anchor the point of attack against the run. The offensive line is rarely able to move the line of scrimmage against him. On top of that, he’s shown the ability to split gaps and make stops in the backfield. That block beating ability also shows up in the pass rush, which is surprisingly good for an interior lineman. Echoles does an excellent job of using leverage to collapse the pocket and get his hands in the passing lanes to knock down passes. While Echoles is great in a phone booth, it’s his ability in space that leaves something to be desired. His range is average at best, and he struggles to wrap up, missing ten tackles last season. His durability is great over the course of the game, but he does tend to tire after long drives leading to high pad levels. Projection If Echoles continues to grow this season, he’ll no doubt be a hot commodity in the NFL Draft. He’s got the level of disruption teams love to have on the first couple of downs and enough of a pass rush to make him a true three down lineman. Where he goes in the Draft will depend largely on how well he improves his tackling ability. It’s one thing to disrupt a running play to limit the gain; it’s another thing entirely to blow up a run and secure the TFL. The Panthers invested in the defensive line the last few years with mixed results. Derrick Brown is still one of the best tackles in the league, but free agent signings Turk Wharton and Bobby Brown III have had injury issues. They do have some decent depth with guys like Aaron Hall and Cam Jackson, but a player like Echoles could really change the Panthers front. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Will Echoles is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!

title: Should the Chicago Bears Trade for a Defensive Player?
summary: The Chicago Bears have opened the season with a shocking degree of balance. Instead of looking like a struggling defense being carried by an overpowered offense, Dennis Allen’s unit has held its own. Nonetheless, the Bears continue to be mentioned among teams that might make a move before the November 10th trade deadline—especially when it […]
full_text: The Chicago Bears have opened the season with a shocking degree of balance. Instead of looking like a struggling defense being carried by an overpowered offense, Dennis Allen’s unit has held its own. Nonetheless, the Bears continue to be mentioned among teams that might make a move before the November 10th trade deadline—especially when it comes to improving a maligned defensive line. Of course, a trade at the deadline would come in the middle of the bye week for Chicago, which is unusually convenient. However, as teams make surprise moves in response to the season, Ryan Poles could easily decide to act more quickly than that as well. Therefore, we asked ourselves a few questions about potential trade targets, including who we want Chicago to trade for, who we want them to stay away from, and whether or not anything would actually shock us at this point. Up first is our wish list. Who do you want Chicago to go after in the trade market and at what maximum cost? Lester Wiltfong: Khalil Mack would be a lot of fun, and I think a fourth-round pick (plus a day-three sweetener) might be enough to get it done. Mack has a no-trade clause in his contract, so going to a city he knows, and that is also a contender, makes sense for both parties. Sure, he’s 35, but he’s still got it. Bryan Orenchuk: I would love for them to bring in Jeffrey Simmons but I wouldn’t give up more than a 3rd rounder for him. Khalil Mack for a day 3 pick might make the most sense, though. And his return would be epic. Erik Duerrwaechter : I truly want to see the Bears go after a game-wrecking DL, if one is available. While the saying, “no cost is too great,” for securing elite DL these days, I’d rather keep my first round pick for 2027 if possible. Only players of the same caliber as Jeffery Simmons would warrant such a deal. Swinging big on young players like Byron Young, Moro Ojomo, or Tuli Tuipulotu would be excellent too. If it’s Khalil Mack, then that’s a “yes” for me if it’s a day three pick. Josh Sweat is a good player that I’d be in the market for if the price doesn’t exceed a 2027 third round pick and a conditional 2028 pick. Donald Gooch : The poetic beauty of it demands Khalil Mack. First, he’s still got it. Not the absolute game-breaker he was five years ago, but instantly the best defensive lineman on the Bears. Second, I think he can be had for a 4th or 5th round pick – and that’s as far as I would go in terms of cost. Return of the Mack. Make it happen. Mongo Peanut : I want them to go after Jeffrey Simmons. I understand he is costly. I understand he is not super young. But he is possibly the most important and rare asset on a defense – a game-wrecking pass-rusher up the middle. He opens up everything for Dennis Allen, who I am concerned is going to have his blitzing tendencies bite him at some point. Josh Sunderbruch : Chicago needs to improve its run defense, and Khalil Mack has had an average depth of tackle of 1.3 yards this season, only a slight increase from his 1.1 yards in 2025. For frame of reference, Maxx Crosby is at 1.3 yards for his career. Add in that Mack still has a pressure rate above 13%, and I think it’s obvious that he should come back to Chicago for another playoff push. I would love for Chicago to send a third-rounder and get a late Day 3 back, as this would motivate the Chargers to close the deal but also keep Chicago with the same number of overall selections. Overall, it looks like there’s consensus around a few names among the contributors. Now it’s your turn–if Chicago is making calls about improving its defensive line, who do you want them to target and how much do you think they should offer?

full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - SEPTEMBER 20: Xavier McKinney #29 of the Green Bay Packers and Zaire Franklin #44 defend against Adonai Mitchell #15 of the New York Jets during the first half of the game at MetLife Stadium on September 20, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. So here we are, with the Bears on the road in Green Bay as favorites with their backup QB starting. A combination of sloppy play and injuries on the Packers and the utter dominance of the Ben Johnson/Dennis Allen coaching insulates the Bears from any disadvantage that Lambeau and Bagent might present. Still, Tyson needs to approach this game very carefully. You have to assume that Ben Johnson’s game plan will be run-heavy given their success to start the season, coupled with the injury to standout Packer linebacker Edgerrin Cooper. This means that Bagent’s role is likely to be that of game manager, keeping the offense on schedule, with a few well-timed downfield shots to the keep the defense honest. It’s those downfield shots that have me most nervous. Against the Jets, Bagent was fairly efficient with his deep passing game, going 7/10 with passes that traveled more than 10 yards downfield. Here is the pass chart for #Bears QB Tyson Bagent via NFL NextGen: pic.twitter.com/IOO9bQ1PiR — Zack Pearson (@Zack_Pearson) October 4, 2026 But one of those three misses was a doozy, where he threw behind Colston Loveland on a crosser, gifting Minkah Fitzpatrick an INT, the first interception for the Jets in 20 games. Unfortunately for Bagent, the Packers have a very similar type of player to Fitzpatrick in Xavier McKinney — a ballhawking safety that likes to roam over the middle of the field. In fact, McKinney has already secured an interception that is eerily similar to the one Fitzpatrick had against the Bears. Michael Penix Jr. throws a pick on his first drive back 😬 Xavier McKinney comes up with his 20th interception of his career 🔥 (via @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/XhuxsvqeMA — Yahoo Sports (@YahooSports) September 25, 2026 While McKinney had a down year last season, only securing two interceptions, he is one of the lone players on a depleted team that can make big impact plays for the Packers. Bagent would be wise to be extra careful when throwing downfield so that McKinney cannot give the Packers’ offense extra chances.

title: Tyson Bagent Week 4 QB Grade: Jets @ Bears Film Breakdown
summary: Well, Ben Johnson got us again. After spending the entire week refusing to publicly name his starting quarterback, Johnson decided to take things one step further Sunday afternoon. Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent both trotted onto the field for Chicago’s first offensive snap, with Bagent split out wide while Keenum took the snap, handed the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Case Keenum #11 of the Chicago Bears throws during the first quarter of the NFL game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Well, Ben Johnson got us again. After spending the entire week refusing to publicly name his starting quarterback, Johnson decided to take things one step further Sunday afternoon. Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent both trotted onto the field for Chicago’s first offensive snap, with Bagent split out wide while Keenum took the snap, handed the ball off and promptly headed to the sideline. So, technically, both quarterbacks started. Very funny, Ben. From that point forward, though, this was Tyson Bagent’s offense. With Caleb Williams missing his second consecutive game due to the hamstring injury suffered against Minnesota, Bagent stepped back into the lineup after clearing concussion protocol and was tasked with following up Case Keenum’s fantastic performance against Philadelphia. The result? Another Bears win, and somehow an even more dominant offensive performance. Chicago defeated New York 23-12, but the final score doesn’t come remotely close to explaining what happened at Soldier Field. The Bears outgained the Jets 492-157, picked up 34 first downs compared to New York’s seven and possessed the football for an absurd 42:45. Chicago ran 89 offensive plays. The Jets ran 32. According to Football Perspective, that 89-to-32 split was the second-most lopsided play differential in NFL history , trailing only Pittsburgh’s 90-to-28 advantage over the expansion Browns in 1999. It gets better. Chicago actually finished with more first downs than New York had offensive plays, something SumerSports noted hadn’t happened in an NFL game since 2016 . The Bears’ 34 first downs were also their most in a game since at least 1941, while their +335 advantage in total yardage was Chicago’s largest since a +343 performance against the St. Louis Cardinals in 1979. Oh, and Tory Taylor never had to punt. It was one of those afternoons where it felt like the Bears had the football for about three hours while the Jets occasionally stopped by to run a few plays. A lot of that credit belongs to the running game. Kyle Monangai absolutely wore New York down, carrying the ball 30 times for 146 yards and two touchdowns, while Chicago finished with 232 yards on the ground. That allowed Johnson to keep Bagent in favorable situations throughout the afternoon and control the game without asking his backup quarterback to carry the offense. But Bagent held up his end of the bargain. He completed 25 of 34 attempts for a career-high 268 yards, finishing with no touchdowns, one interception and an 84.0 passer rating. Those numbers aren’t going to jump off the page, especially after what Keenum did against Philadelphia, but I thought Bagent looked noticeably more comfortable operating this offense than the quarterback I charted back in 2023. If you’ve followed my work for a while, you know I haven’t exactly been shy about my concerns with Bagent. The arm talent is limited. That’s not suddenly going to change. There are throws Williams can make within this offense that Bagent simply cannot, and we’ve seen how that can restrict the field when defenses begin squeezing the underneath areas. But what has changed is how comfortable he looks operating within those limitations. Bagent has always gotten the ball out quickly and avoided sacks well, but against New York there was more confidence in what he was seeing. He played within structure, got through the concepts more consistently (but did have a few plays he perhaps moved through those concepts a bit too quickly, overlooking open receivers down field) and generally gave his playmakers opportunities to do the work after the catch. When the pocket was clean, he was about as efficient as you could ask for. Next Gen Stats had Bagent completing 21 of 23 passes from a clean pocket for 202 yards, performing 17.3 percentage points above expectation. Under pressure, however, things changed dramatically. He completed just four of 11 attempts for 66 yards with the interception. That split does a pretty good job of illustrating both sides of Bagent’s afternoon. When Chicago kept him comfortable and the offense stayed on schedule, he distributed the football efficiently and helped sustain drive after drive. When New York forced him off his spot or sped up the picture, some of the limitations and questionable decisions began to surface. And the afternoon certainly wasn’t flawless. The official box score lists one interception, but there were a few other throws where Bagent flirted with danger, including turnovers that were erased by Jets penalties. The interception that did count came on a pass behind Colston Loveland over the middle, giving Minkah Fitzpatrick New York’s first interception since the final game of the 2024 season. So we’re not walking away from this pretending Bagent suddenly turned into a different caliber of quarterback. What we can say is that he looked like a more developed version of the player we saw three years ago. That’s exactly what you want from a backup quarterback. The Bears didn’t need Bagent to play hero ball. They needed him to run the offense, stay on schedule, avoid sacks and allow the talent around him to take over. For most of Sunday afternoon, that’s exactly what he did. And for the second consecutive week, Ben Johnson showed just how adaptable this offense can be without Caleb Williams. Keenum beat Philadelphia by operating like the veteran point guard we talked about last week, consistently anticipating windows and getting the football where the design told him to go. Bagent brought a little more mobility and a quicker trigger against New York, while Chicago leaned even harder on its rushing attack and controlled the football for nearly three quarters of the game. Different quarterbacks. Different approaches. Same result. The Bears are 3-1, and three different quarterbacks have now led them to victories through the first four weeks of the season, something no NFL team had accomplished that early since the 1997 Jacksonville Jaguars.
