title: Cowboys vs Bucs: 2 players to buy, 2 to sell
summary: The Dallas Cowboys head into Thursday night’s matchup with Tampa Bay at 2-2 after CeeDee Lamb put together one of the best games in Cowboys history against Houston. Now, the Cowboys face a Buccaneers team that is 0-4 but has a defense that ranks fourth in the NFL in total yards allowed. There are plenty […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Tim Heitman-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Dallas Cowboys head into Thursday night’s matchup with Tampa Bay at 2-2 after CeeDee Lamb put together one of the best games in Cowboys history against Houston. Now, the Cowboys face a Buccaneers team that is 0-4 but has a defense that ranks fourth in the NFL in total yards allowed. There are plenty of reasons to like what Dallas can do on Thursday night, particularly with Baker Mayfield sidelined and Tampa Bay preparing to start rookie Jalon Daniels for the second time in his career. But there are also a couple of Cowboys who deserve a closer look after the first month of the season. Here are this week’s buys and sells. Buy: WR CeeDee Lamb At this point, why would you bet against him? Lamb is coming off a ridiculous performance against Houston in which he caught 17 passes for 189 yards and the game-winning touchdown, helping Dallas overcome a 10-point halftime deficit to beat the Texans 34-30. It was not just another big game from Lamb. It was the kind of performance where the Cowboys knew exactly where they wanted to go with the football, Houston knew where the ball was going, and the Texans still couldn’t stop it. Lamb has now caught 37 passes for 498 yards and four touchdowns through four games, leading the NFL in both receptions and receiving yards. He is averaging 13.5 yards per reception while accounting for a massive portion of Dak Prescott’s production. Against Houston, Prescott targeted Lamb on 21 of the 45 routes he ran, the highest target rate for any receiver running 45 or fewer routes in the Next Gen Stats era. Brian Schottenheimer also moved Lamb around the formation, allowing him to create mismatches both outside and from the slot. That is the formula Dallas should continue using. The Buccaneers have allowed three straight opponents to finish with 285 yards or fewer, and their defense ranks fourth in the NFL in total yards allowed. This isn’t necessarily a matchup where Lamb is going to catch 17 passes again, but Tampa is also going to be without starting safety Antoine Winfield Jr., who suffered a rib fracture against Green Bay. If Lamb is already playing at this level, Dallas shouldn’t be looking for reasons to get him less involved. It should be looking for different ways to get him the football and force Tampa to adjust. After four weeks, CeeDee Lamb isn’t simply having a hot stretch. He’s been a driving force in what has been, up to this point, a very efficient and capable offense. Sell: TE Jake Ferguson Holy moly what is going on with Fergie? His blocking has become increasingly difficult to overlook. Ferguson caught three of four targets for 11 yards against Houston (granted one was a crucial fourth-down catch), but the bigger concern was what he did, or failed to do, as a blocker. He spent much of the afternoon chipping against Houston’s edge rushers, and there were multiple moments where his technique and effort left Dallas’ offense in difficult positions. That has become a larger issue because Ferguson isn’t being asked to be a traditional pass-catching tight end who can occasionally contribute as a blocker. Dallas relies on him to do both. The Cowboys have a quarterback in Prescott who is playing at a high level, a receiver in Lamb who is virtually impossible to contain right now, and a running back in Javonte Williams who has already shown he can be a major part of the offense. If Dallas is going to get the most out of all three, the blocking from its tight ends has to be reliable. Instead, Ferguson has had too many snaps where he either misses the assignment entirely or makes contact without doing enough to actually finish the block. Meanwhile, the Buccaneers are going to use multiple methods to create pressure, and their defense has held three consecutive opponents to 285 yards or fewer. Tampa’s pass rush could be a problem for Dallas, and the Cowboys cannot afford to make it easier by allowing preventable pressure through missed blocks. Ferguson is still an important part of this offense, and he has shown he can make plays as a receiver. But the Cowboys need more consistency from him as a complete tight end, particularly with the defense likely to make Prescott and the passing game work for every yard. Ferguson is a sell. Buy: Cowboys defensive secondary This is probably the most optimistic buy of the week, but the circumstances are finally lining up for Dallas’ secondary to make some plays. Through four games, the Cowboys have yet to record an interception, and their defense has allowed the third-most yards in the NFL. That is obviously not a recipe for success, particularly when the pass rush has struggled to generate consistent pressure and sacks. But Thursday presents a much more favorable situation. Baker Mayfield, and his innate ability to extend plays, is out with his thumb injury, meaning Tampa will turn to rookie Jalon Daniels for his second career start. Daniels threw for 148 yards and a touchdown against Green Bay last week, but he also threw two interceptions in the first half. That is where Dallas’ secondary finally has an opportunity to make some plays. The Cowboys have added Joey Porter Jr., who is expected to play in his second game with Dallas after being acquired from Pittsburgh. Porter isn’t going to magically solve every problem in the secondary, but, as we saw on Sunday, his presence gives Dallas another legitimate outside corner who can play aggressively without necessarily requiring constant safety help. Tampa’s passing game has not exactly been lighting up the scoreboard. The Buccaneers rank 28th in passing offense at 172.3 yards per game, while their offense ranks 28th overall at 278.3 yards per game. Emeka Egbuka and Chris Godwin remain legitimate weapons, but the Bucs are asking a rookie quarterback to operate that offense against a Dallas defense that desperately needs to create its first interception. Dallas has been waiting four games for its first interception. Thursday feels like as good an opportunity as any to finally get one. Sell: LB DeMarvion Overshown This is a different kind of sell this week, because we know that DeMarvion Overshown isn’t playing due to injury. This is more about questioning whether his current role is the best fit for what Dallas needs at linebacker. Jaishawn Barham has emerged as one of Dallas’ more consistent linebackers during the first month of the season, and he currently leads the Cowboys with 25 tackles alongside Dee Winters. Overshown has a unique skill set, particularly as a player who can attack downhill, rush the passer and move around the formation. The problem is that the Cowboys need stability at the second level of their defense, and Overshown’s continued availability questions make that difficult to count on. There is also a legitimate question about whether his leaner build is ideal for consistently playing inside against NFL-sized offensive linemen and downhill running games. When you’re repeatedly taking on blocks in the middle of an NFL defense, those extra pounds can matter and Overshown just might not be cut out for interior LB play. The bigger question for Dallas is whether Barham has simply done enough to make the decision more complicated. If the rookie continues playing at a high level while Overshown struggles to stay healthy, the Cowboys may have to consider whether Barham has earned a larger role even when everyone is available.
author: Jorge Guajardo

title: Sean Payton explains why he’s taking back Broncos play-calling
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! What’s old is new again. By now, you’ve heard that Sean Payton is taking back play-calling duties for the Denver Broncos offense. Through the first four weeks, the Broncos have been inept offensively. That’s not all on the new offensive coordinator, Davis Webb, who was calling plays in the first four […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - JANUARY 04: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos and Head coach Sean Payton of the Denver Broncos speak in the second quarter against the Los Angeles Chargers at Empower Field At Mile High on January 04, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by C. Morgan Engel/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! What’s old is new again. By now, you’ve heard that Sean Payton is taking back play-calling duties for the Denver Broncos offense. Through the first four weeks, the Broncos have been inept offensively. That’s not all on the new offensive coordinator, Davis Webb, who was calling plays in the first four games. As Payton said to the media on Thursday after practice, it’s a collective. In the end, the Broncos offense has not been good enough, and Payton felt the time was right for the change. Denver heads on the road to face the hapless and winless Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday. As Payton said on Thursday: “We’ll make a change offensively. I’ll call the plays. I understand the questions at the start of the week. I want to say this first, and I said it to Davis the other day, talking to him. I’ve done this long enough where I know when I have a future head coach, and he’s going to be one. All the things that it’s hard to find will happen. In fact, the same thing to some degree — a little bit different — happened to myself early in my career. I met with the offense. “As the head coach, no different than evaluating your right tackle, your slot receiver, your running backs, something to change it up. Ultimately, I used that word the ‘collective’ yesterday. It’s the group. So when I met with the offense, it’s about buttoning up all of the little things that keep you from sustaining drives. Davis is all-in with the game plan, just like we’ve been operating. He’ll be down on the field with me.” When Payton was asked why he made the change now rather than waiting, he said there were too many to list. “We know we have to improve our balance in running the football,” he said to the media. “There’s a handful of things. Then the hard thing when you are not the head coach is certainly there are things you want to feel like are cleared, where when you’re calling them as the head coach, you’re in your mind prepared to say, ‘I don’t have to run it by anyone.’ So it’s changing things up and really trying to reduce some of the calories to get back to getting some things really well. That’s going to be the focus.” If it’s any solace to Webb, Payton had the play-calling duties taken away from him in 2002 when he was with the New York Giants. So Payton is using that experience now in Denver. “We’ll do what’s best for the team." HC Sean Payton to reassume play-calling responsibilities ahead of #DENvsLAC » https://t.co/hpkLHNtgWd pic.twitter.com/F9XQefRqLl — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) October 8, 2026 “It was tough,” Payton said when asked how he handled getting the play-calling taken from him. “Davis, he’s going to respond well. It was different. I’d just lost my mother during the bye week. We got imbalanced a little bit. I just remember the professional setback, if you will. We had gone to the Super Bowl in (2000) so this was a couple years into it. It wasn’t until a couple years later that you’re like, ‘Man, you really didn’t mourn the loss of your mom because you were so out of whack with your career.’ And the team did better. “Very quickly, it’s still about the team, and we went to the playoffs. There are certain things that I learned that maybe I needed to. Then shortly thereafter, I’m in Dallas, and then three years later, I get that opportunity (in New Orleans). He’s been fantastic. A much different situation, if you will.” As for this Sunday, Payton will be the voice in Bo Nix’s helmet. Payton also said he and the Broncos are focused on this week. As the head coach, Payton felt the time was right to make the move for the team. He saw something that needed correcting, and this was the course of action to fix it. “Everyone’s a little disappointed because you feel like you let one of your teammates down,” Payton said when asked if Nix had any reaction. “That’s the human part of it. That’s our game a little bit in this league. I’m going to go back to what I said earlier relative to (Webb’s) talent. It’s rare. He’s gifted. It’s all ahead of him.” Broncos links

title: Sean Payton takes over play-calling duties on offense for the Broncos
summary: In the NFL, experience matters — especially at the coaching level. Few offensive minds have more experience calling plays in the NFL than Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton. Which is why it came as a surprise that he gave up that job after promoting Davis Webb to offensive coordinator. Unfortunately, Webb has faced a […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 04: Head coach Sean Payton of the Denver Broncos with his game-plan in his arm looks on prior to the start of the game against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the NFL, experience matters — especially at the coaching level. Few offensive minds have more experience calling plays in the NFL than Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton. Which is why it came as a surprise that he gave up that job after promoting Davis Webb to offensive coordinator. Unfortunately, Webb has faced a gauntlet of strong defenses with defensive coordinators with far more experience than he at calling their plays. The result has been a very inconsistent and ineffective offense through four games. With pressure mounting outside of the building, it appears Payton chose to protect his offensive protégé rather than expose him to even more negative press. BREAKING: Sean Payton will call the Broncos offensive plays. pic.twitter.com/ck0UUsfrdo — Zac Stevens (@ZacStevens) October 8, 2026 As someone who has covered the NFL for a while himself, these kinds of changes often accompany the coordinator being demoted as taking the heat and the blame for the issues on offense. And more often than not the change doesn’t result in any marked improvement. However, Payton chose a different route and talked Webb up and was frank about the negatives around taking play calling away. I think we’ll see Davis Webb return to calling plays at some point either here or elsewhere, but in 2026 with a contention window open, it makes sense to return duties to the experienced hand and try to get Bo Nix and the offense back in sync winning games. Broncos daily recap Sean Payton will be more heavily involved in the play-calling vs. the Chargers There have been multiple confirmation reports that Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton will become more active in playcalling over offensive coordinator Davis Webb. Broncos vs. Chargers: 3 Things to Watch for in Week 5 Here are three storylines I’ll be watching closely when the Denver Broncos battle the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday. How the Denver Broncos can beat the Los Angeles Chargers Here are three things the Denver Broncos have to accomplish to defeat the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 5. Potent quotables Sean Payton Opening statement “I’ll go quick. So the coordinators will go tomorrow. We’ll make a change offensively. I’ll call the plays. I understand the questions at the start of the week. I want to say this first, and I said it to [Offensive Coordinator] Davis [Webb] the other day talking to him. I’ve done this long enough where I know when I have a future head coach, and he’s going to be one. All the things that it’s hard to find will happen. In fact, the same thing to some degree—a little bit different—happened to myself early in my career. I met with the offense. As the head coach, no different than evaluating your right tackle, your slot receiver, your running backs, something to change it up. Ultimately, I used that word the ‘collective’ yesterday. It’s the group. So when I met with the offense, it’s about buttoning up all of the little things that keep you from sustaining drives. Davis is all-in with the gameplan, just like we’ve been operating. He’ll be down on the field with me. So I’ll take any questions.” On if the change was more about the play calling communication on gameday or the preparation during the week “I think it’s probably… There’d be too many things just to list. We know we have to improve our balance in running the football. There’s a handful of things. Then the hard thing when you are not the head coach is certainly there are things you want to feel like are cleared, where when you’re calling them as the head coach, you’re in your mind prepared to say, ‘I don’t have to run it by anyone.’ So it’s changing things up and really trying to reduce some of the calories to get back to getting some things really well. That’s going to be the focus.” On when he made this decision “Monday we met and met with the players. I met with [Offensive Coordinator] Davis [Webb]. He’s been fantastic. Like I said, he’s super talented. All of us, everyone’s disappointed in the unit itself. We’re 2-2, but we feel like there’s more there. He was fantastic in my meeting with him, and the approach all week has been fantastic.” On his initial decision to give Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb play calling responsibilities because of the prevalence of talented young play callers around the league “I think I’m still one of them. That was a good storyline for you guys. Because I honestly felt like it was going to help us. I wouldn’t have done it if I didn’t think… That’s how unique I think he is. It was because I honestly thought standing back as the head coach it would help us.” On if he thinks Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb was calling the plays at times that he wanted “Let’s be clear: it’s the Broncos’ offense. So naturally there are some things… When you’re empowering someone, you want him to come up with things that maybe you otherwise hadn’t. It’s our offense, and we want to improve.” On if this was a harder decision than giving Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb play calling in the beginning “Yes. Yes, absolutely.” On how he handled when former Giants Head Coach Jim Fassel took over play calling in 2002 “It was 2002. It was tough. [Offensive Coordinator] Davis [Webb], he’s going to respond well. It was different. I’d just lost my mother during the bye week. We got imbalanced a little bit. I just remember the professional setback, if you will. We had gone to the Super Bowl in [2000] so this was a couple years into it. It wasn’t until a couple years later that you’re like, ‘Man, you really didn’t mourn the loss of your mom because you were so out of whack with your career.’ And the team did better. Very quickly, it’s still about the team, and we went to the playoffs. There are certain things that I learned that maybe I needed to. Then shortly there after, I’m in Dallas and then three years later, I get that opportunity [in New Orleans]. He’s been fantastic. A much different situation, if you will.” On if they will adjust terminology at all “Well I just said it to him, to the assistants. What these guys have learned, I can adjust and learn. Sometimes it might be something where I want to call it this. They’ll learn it. The things that have been tweaked relative to certain formations or calls, that’s the easy part.” On if he will be talking to QB Bo Nix on gameday “I’ll be in [QB] Bo [Nix]’s head. Otherwise you lose like four seconds.” On working through the mechanics of getting the play call in “The mechanics will be fast. It’ll be fast. Part of it is just having that balance of proper sleep and all those things. The mechanics will be quick.” On if they will adjust anything else about their meetings or schedule “Not really. Maybe just some of what we’re doing in practice, how we’re doing it. There were a few things, but for the most part, it’s the little things that every one of us has to look closely at.” On if he thinks it was a sequencing issue on gameday or a feel issue “I don’t know specifically. There’s just a… I think my instincts have just maybe from experience, having a chance to see kind of where we’re at and then maybe where we need to go. I think that’s really my instincts.” On if watching someone else call plays gave him a different perspective on self-scouting the offense “Sometimes, yes. Let’s just say the average is 67 selections in a game. It’s impossible to think that we would all be in the same… It’s easy to say, ‘The short yardage call is going to be this out of the gate.’ You could take 32 play callers, and the sequencing would be completely somewhat different.” On what makes this situation different than the one he was in during the 2002 season “That was such a media circus and such a… I’m…

title: Sean Payton will be more heavily involved in the play-calling vs. the Chargers
summary: Here we go. The smoke began to circulate last night when former Broncos wide receiver and now radio personality Brandon Stokley tweeted out that he is hearing that “Sean Payton is going to be taking over play calling this week”. Then, this morning, Pro Football Talk’s Mike Florio is also reporting that Payton will be […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - SEPTEMBER 27: Head coach Sean Payton of the Denver Broncos looks on before a game against the Los Angeles Rams at Empower Field at Mile High on September 27, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here we go. The smoke began to circulate last night when former Broncos wide receiver and now radio personality Brandon Stokley tweeted out that he is hearing that “Sean Payton is going to be taking over play calling this week” . Then, this morning, Pro Football Talk’s Mike Florio is also reporting that Payton will be calling plays on Sunday, not Davis Webb. Well now, the national reporters have picked up this story, and it appears to be true. According to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo, Denver Broncos Head Coach Sean Payton will be more heavily involved in the offensive play-calling this week. #Broncos coach Sean Payton will be more heavily involved in offensive play-calling this week, sources told me and @MikeGarafolo . The process will remain collaborative, with OC Davis Webb continuing to be a major voice on game day & during the week. But Payton will have say. pic.twitter.com/H7YBs1k4vt — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) October 8, 2026 Rapoport adds that the process will remain collaborative, with offensive coordinator Davis Webb continuing to be a major voice on game days, but Payton will have a larger say in the process. Payton met with the media on Wednesday and was asked if a four-game sample size was enough to evaluate a play caller. He told reporters that “our focus needs to be more on the specifics and the detail of each play regardless,” but did add, “certainly this isn’t championship football”. “I think our focus needs to be more on the specifics and the detail of each play regardless. I think [Offensive Coordinator] Davis [Webb] is very fast and quick and understands what we’re doing. So I appreciate the question, but I think that the most important job I have is really evaluating the why’s. I think collectively we all after a game… After a four-game sample size… All right, certainly this isn’t championship football or what we see, how quickly can we correct those things?” This switch had to happen, and it makes sense for Payton to take the reins once again. Let’s face it, the offense has been bad. Every part of the offense has taken a step back from last season. Nix has been inconsistent and hasn’t looked like the quarterback we saw vs. the Bills last season. The run game is nonexistent again, and JK Dobbins is either hurt or washed. Courtland Sutton went from being a 1,000-yard receiver catching nearly 10 touchdowns to having 9 catches for 86 yards and 0 touchdowns through 4 games. Remember Jaylen Waddle and how he was going to transform the offense? Well, now, outside of one game vs. the Jaguars, he has not been featured and feels like an afterthought in the offense. The Broncos could not afford to let this Davis Webb play-calling experiment continue much longer with these results. They are likely in a short Super Bowl window right now and are off to a poor start. They need to make changes, get things rolling again, and look like the offense that clicked against the Packers and Bills late last season. They play the 0-4 Chargers this Sunday, who are banged up and struggling on all sides of the ball. They cannot afford to struggle or lose against this team, with the Seahawks coming to town on a short week next Thursday. Hopefully, this move gets the offense rolling in the right direction, and we see a better offensive output moving forward,

title: Broncos vs. Chargers: 3 Things to Watch for in Week 5
summary: The Denver Broncos trek back to California again in Week 5 to battle their division rival Los Angeles Chargers. At 0-4, the Chargers have had a disastrous start to the season. Meanwhile, the Broncos are 2-2 and are still working on playing their first complete game of the season in all three phases. Here are […]
full_text: DENVER , CO - AUGUST 21: Nik Bonitto (15) of the Denver Broncos stands with teammates during the first quarter against the Green Bay Packers at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver, Colorado on Friday, August 21, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images The Denver Broncos trek back to California again in Week 5 to battle their division rival Los Angeles Chargers. At 0-4, the Chargers have had a disastrous start to the season. Meanwhile, the Broncos are 2-2 and are still working on playing their first complete game of the season in all three phases. Here are three storylines I’ll be watching closely on Sunday. Can the Bo Nix to Courtland Sutton connection be revived? To put it mildly, the Broncos have been underwhelming on offense to start the season. Neither the running game or passing attack looks formidable or consistent. That’s got to change fast. Perhaps one of the most troublesome issues has been the lack of impact from wide receiver Courtland Sutton. After their loss to the San Francisco 49ers, Head Coach Sean Payton emphasized how important it was to get Sutton going. With Pat Byrant out for the foreseeable future with an ankle injury, the Broncos desperately need their longtime ‘X’ receiver to produce more than he has thus far. On 22 targets, the ninth-year pro has just nine catches for 86 yards. That’s an abysmal 41-percent catch-rate when targeted—by far the lowest of his career. We have seen the Nix-to-Sutton connection look sluggish early on the past two seasons, but this is definitely the worst. Will there actually be an emphasis on establishing the run? There are a lot of things Broncos Country can rightfully criticize first-year Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb for. While Payton and the players have expressed confidence in Webb’s abilities, the offense is currently one of the worst in the National Football League. In my opinion, his feel for sequencing seems to be a drastic drop off compared to Payton. Moreover, his overreliance on passing has put a lot of weight on the arm of Bo Nix. Last week against the 49ers, the Broncos waited until late in the game to try and get their running game going. That’s too long in my opinion. Both Payton and Webb have vowed to be more dedicated to the run game. Whether or not that happens on Sunday remains to be seen. The Chargers are a bottom ten run stopping defense and are allowing over 120 yards per game on the ground. This matchup seems like the right time to try and feed J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey early and often. Nik Bonitto has been quiet start to the season. Can he get back on track versus the Chargers? The past two seasons, edge rusher Nik Bonitto has been a rising star for Denver’s defense. Bonitto has posted back-to-back years of double-digit sacks with two Pro Bowl honors and one All-Pro accolade. Unfortunately, the fifth-year pro has started off slow in 2026. Through four games, Bonitto has only one sack, four hurries, eight quarterback hits, and 11 pressures. There has been a significant drop off in his hurry, sack, and pressure percentages compared to last season. I can’t help but think the absence of Jonathon Cooper opposite of him, as well as the departure of John Franklin-Myers, has played some role in his production decline. However, the Chargers have an offensive line that has already allowed twelve sacks on the season. Pro Bowl offensive tackle Rashawn Slater will be out of Sunday’s matchup due to a high ankle sprain. Along with some other injuries up front for the Chargers, that may provide Bonitto and his defensive front seven teammates with an opportunity to get back to being a feared pass rush.

title: How the Denver Broncos can beat the Los Angeles Chargers
summary: For their Week 5 matchup, the Denver Broncos head on the road to battle the winless Los Angeles Chargers. At 2-2, the Broncos are looking to rebound after last Sunday’s loss to the San Francisco 49ers. Here are three things Denver must do in order to achieve their third victory of the season. The defense […]
full_text: Sep 20, 2026; Denver, Colorado, USA; Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix (10) is hugged by offensive tackle Garett Bolles (72) defeating the Jacksonville Jaguars at Empower Field at Mile High. Mandatory Credit: Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect For their Week 5 matchup, the Denver Broncos head on the road to battle the winless Los Angeles Chargers. At 2-2, the Broncos are looking to rebound after last Sunday’s loss to the San Francisco 49ers. Here are three things Denver must do in order to achieve their third victory of the season. The defense has to make Justin Herbert look bad At 0-4, it’s been a disaster for the Chargers thus far. Their offense has looked terrible with Offensive Coordinator Mike McDaniel calling the shots. Los Angeles has failed to score more than fourteen points in three of four games. Moreover, their passing game is one of the worst in the National Football League. It’s been a disappointing start for quarterback Justin Herbert. The seventh-year signal caller is completing less than 60-percent of his passes. Herbert has just four touchdowns and six interceptions. He is also averaging the lowest number of passing yards per game in his career. This will be an important matchup for Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph and his players. With Patrick Surtain II and potentially Riley Moss out for this contest, they will need Jahdae Barron and Kris Abrams-Draine to step up in a big way when they are on the field. They can’t let this game be the one where Herbert and the Chargers’ offense get back on track. It’s time for Denver’s offense to start pulling its weight The Chargers aren’t the only team whose offense has been a dud to begin the 2026 season. The Broncos are right there with them. Denver sports one of the lowest scoring units in the NFL, a bad run game, and a woefully inconsistent aerial attack. After their loss to the 49ers and earlier in the week, Head Coach Sean Payton said time is of the essence for things to get moving in the right direction. Your mileage may vary, but going up against a winless Chargers squad seems like the perfect time to finally get things right. The pre-snap penalties have to stop, the run game needs to be committed to early on, and quarterback Bo Nix needs to stick in the pocket and deliver throws with accuracy and consistency. The Chargers have experienced a significant drop-off on defense compared to last season going from a top 10 unit to a bottom 10 unit in ‘26. Will this game finally be the one where Denver’s offense shows signs of life? I certainly hope so. The Broncos need better play from their trench players Entering the season, most fans would have pointed to the offensive and defensive lines as being some of the top strengths of the team. Based on what we have seen thus far, I don’t think that’s necessarily the case. Though I’m not ready to hit the panic button quite yet on either group. The Chargers have a beat-up offensive line that has already surrendered twelve sacks on the season. They could be without their starting left tackle and left guard this weekend. With that in mind, finding a way rattle Herbert and force him into some bad decisions will be an important part of the equation for the Broncos to win on Sunday. On the offensive side of the ball, the Broncos front five need to come up big. Protecting Bo Nix will be key, but paving better running lanes for their running backs will also be mission critical. If Denver wants to get their offense going, they need to have one of the highest paid offensive lines in the league perform well.

title: NFL picks and predictions: Broncos vs. Chargers and the rest of Week 5
summary: Welcome back to the fifth installment of Hart’s Picks for the 2026 NFL regular season. A big thanks once again to Bixbys Hooman in the comments for riding along with me this year to see who picks the best. For Week 4—if my math is right this time—I was 8-8—only predicting the Rams, Bears, Packers, […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 4: Fred Warner #54 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates on the field after an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Levi's Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to the fifth installment of Hart’s Picks for the 2026 NFL regular season. A big thanks once again to Bixbys Hooman in the comments for riding along with me this year to see who picks the best. For Week 4 —if my math is right this time—I was 8-8—only predicting the Rams, Bears, Packers, Ravens, Vikings, Seahawks, Chiefs, and Falcons correctly. Let’s see how well I do in Week 5. Keep in mind, there are only fifteen games with the Carolina Panthers and Kansas City Chiefs on their BYE. Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Dallas Cowboys — Thursday Night Football The Buccaneers are 0-4 to start the season. They’ll be without Baker Mayfield again on Thursday Night Football against the Cowboys. Dallas is struggling on defense, but I’m pretty sure Dak Prescott and their offense will be able to score a lot more points than Tampa Bay with Jalon Daniels. I’m going with the home team. Winner: Cowboys Philadelphia Eagles at Jacksonville Jaguars — Sunday (Morning Game) This Week 5 matchup for the morning game will be played in London. After two straight losses, the Eagles are trying to find a way to get back on track. Though they may be without Saquan Barkley and Tank Bigsby. If so, that means Will Shipley is their starting running back. I don’t think that will bode well for them. Jalen Hurts isn’t playing well and Lane Johnson just retired. Meanwhile, the Jaguars are playing good football, and I expect them to take care of business at home. Winner: Jaguars Indianapolis Colts at Pittsburgh Steelers — Sunday (Early Game) The Colts and Steelers are both 2-2 to start the season. Pittsburgh has struggled to put points on the board and Indianapolis has a few issues on defense. I don’t think any team has a clear advantage in this matchup. My gut is telling me to go with the Steelers here—so I’ll do that and take the home team. Winner: Steelers Cleveland Browns at New York Jets — Sunday (Early Game) Can you believe it? The Browns have reeled off three victories in a row. On the flip side, the Jets have lost three in a row after starting off the season with a victory. Cleveland does have some injuries on their offensive line that give me some concerns. Nevertheless, Deshaun Watson is playing decent, and rookie wide receiver Denzel Boston seems to make a big play every week. I’ll take the Browns here. Winner: Browns Cincinnati Bengals at Miami Dolphins — Sunday (Early Game) The Dolphins aren’t doing much on offense and their defense is one of the worst in the NFL. I don’t think Joe Burrow and his playmakers will have a problem scoring points against Miami. Easily one of the easiest picks for me in the Week 5 slate of games. Winner: Bengals Minnesota Vikings at New Orleans Saints — Sunday (Early Game) Surprise! The Vikings are 4-0 to start the season. Their offense has been hit or miss, but Brian Flores may be coaching the best defense in the NFL thus far. Given that, I think they will find a way to make it five in a row on the road against New Orleans. Winner: Vikings New York Giants at Washington Commanders — Sunday (Early Game) Somehow, even with all their injuries, the Giants are the top team in the NFC East. A lot of folks seem to be picking the Commanders in this one, but that defense is terrible and has allowed at least thirty points or more the past three contests. It’s hard to pick them with that in mind. I’ll be taking the G-Men. Winner: Giants Las Vegas Raiders at New England Patriots — Sunday (Early Game) After three quarters, it sure looked like the Raiders had the Kansas City Chiefs beat. However, Patrick Mahomes and Kenneth Walker II were able to work some fourth quarter magic and score 20 points to remain unbeaten. Meanwhile, the Patriots were able to edge the Buffalo Bills in a thriller. I didn’t expect that. Drake Maye performed quite a bit better against the Bills but needs to stop turning the ball over. All things considered, I’ll take New England at home. Winner: Patriots Houston Texans at Tennessee Titans — Sunday (Early Game) Oof. These two AFC South teams are winless to start the season. I honestly can’t believe Houston’s four-game skid to start the year. I thought they’d be doing much better than that. But somebody has got to win this one, right? Who will that be? I’m betting on the Texans. Winner: Texans Chicago Bears at Green Bay Packers — Sunday (Early Game) This is a classic NFC North matchup. Virtually nothing has gone right for Green Bay this year. They have some major issues on both sides of the ball. The Bears will be starting Tyson Bagent at quarterback who performed decently against the Jets last week. I’ve been impressed with Kyle Monangai. He has really stood out to me the past few weeks for the Bears. I’ll be taking Chicago on the road because they have a much better defense and can run the ball well. Winners: Bears Denver Broncos at Los Angeles Chargers — Sunday (Afternoon Game) The Broncos are coming off a tough loss to the San Francisco 49ers while the Chargers keep spiraling downward and are winless to begin their 2026 season. Both teams are struggling mightily on offense, but I have confidence in Denver’s ability to bounce back and earn their third win of the season. Winner: Broncos Detroit Lions at Arizona Cardinals — Sunday (Afternoon Game) The Lions defense is an absolute mess right now. You can say the same for the Cardinals who also have allowed over 110 points through four games. That being said, I feel confident in Detroit’s ability to outscore Arizona on the road and earn their third win of the season. Winner: Lions San Francisco 49ers at Seattle Seahawks — Sunday (Afternoon Game) This NFC West affair will determine who has the early lead in the division after Week 5. Both are really good teams that are scoring well and have solid defenses. The Seahawks may have the homefield advantage, but I’m a big fan of how Brock Purdy has been playing to start the season. I’ll roll the dice here and take the 49ers as road victors. Winner: 49ers Baltimore Ravens at Atlanta Falcons — Sunday Night Football The Falcons have earned back-to-back victories after starting out the season 0-2. Their recipe for success? Running the ball well and being the best run stopping defense in the NFL. The Ravens’ defense doesn’t look too great, but they can run the ball with authority with future Hall of Famer Derrick Henry. Winner: Ravens Buffalo Bills at Los Angeles Rams — Monday Night Football This game might be my favorite of the week. The Bills are coming off a loss to the Patriots, and the Rams were able to edge out the Eagles. Both teams have a few key injuries, but I like the Rams as the home favorites in this one. The Bills defense has struggled to keep their opponents at bay, but with Davante Adams and Puka Nucua will be back in the fold for the Rams’ offense. Winner: Rams

title: Courtland Sutton confident Broncos will find their way on offense

Yet being a .500 ball club given their tough slate of opponents isn’t a terrible spot. Moving forward, the Broncos have a lot to work on. That […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - SEPTEMBER 27: Courtland Sutton #14 of the Denver Broncos warms up prior to the game against the Los Angeles Rams at Empower Field at Mile High on September 27, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country. Entering Week 5 of the NFL regular season, the Denver Broncos are 2-2. It’s certainly not where they hoped to be four games in. Yet being a .500 ball club given their tough slate of opponents isn’t a terrible spot. Moving forward, the Broncos have a lot to work on. That much is certain. It’s safe to say they haven’t played a complete game in all three phases thus far. They’ve struggled stopping the run on defense. After back-to-back franchise record setting seasons sacking opposing quarterbacks, Denver’s fearsome front seven haven’t been as potent rushing the passer. On special teams, the only bright spot has been Jeremy Crashaw and decent coverage units. Unfortunately, there have been several missed field goals, a big turnover that proved to be a backbreaker against the San Francisco 49ers, and few kick or punt returns that have given them quality field position. However, the lack of production and consistency on offense may be the most worrisome development to date. Prior to the season, many fans believed Nix and Denver’s offense was poised for a breakout campaign. The team added Jaylen Waddle to upgrade their wide receiver corps, drafted Jonah Coleman to bolster their rushing attack, and brought back their entire offensive line that ranked as one of the best in 2025. Those were all adequate reasons for fans to be bullish on their potential. Alas, the Broncos have started off slow—much like in years past. That has led to rightful criticism and concerns on how things will shake out as the season continues. Nevertheless, longtime wide receiver Courtland Sutton remains confident Denver has the players and coaching staff to get things back on track. “It is all right in front of us. We still have the utmost faith in our players and our abilities that we have and the coaches to put us in the right position. It’s just maximizing those opportunities when they do arise,” stated Sutton. Sutton placed the onus on himself and the rest of his teammates on offense to get things right. They know the talent is there; they just have to focus on the details and minimize the self-inflicted wounds and mistakes that have got them in an early-season rut. “From a player perspective, we can always do more. There are things here and there that we may not be fully dialed in on. There is a little bit of attention to detail that we need to tighten up as players. As a collective, we need to find a way to maximize the opportunities when they do pop and minimize the lack of attention to detail that may transpire over the course of a full game,” added Sutton. The opportunity to put their best foot forward presents itself on Sunday when the Broncos head to Los Angeles to take on the winless Chargers. There is no doubt that they have a lot of talent offensively. The question is can they finally live up to it? We are fixing to find out shortly. As always, thank you for reading. title: What is the ceiling for the Lions’ OL when Cade Mays returns to the field?
summary: When the Detroit Lions hired Dan Campbell as their head coach and Brad Holmes as the general manager back in 2021, one thing was very clear from the beginning—they wanted to establish an identity with their offensive line. They immediately backed up those words when they made All-Pro tackle Penei Sewell the seventh overall pick […]
full_text: When the Detroit Lions hired Dan Campbell as their head coach and Brad Holmes as the general manager back in 2021, one thing was very clear from the beginning—they wanted to establish an identity with their offensive line. They immediately backed up those words when they made All-Pro tackle Penei Sewell the seventh overall pick in the 2021 NFL Draft. Football is both complicated and simple. If you want to win, you have to be able to control the line of scrimmage. After a down year in 2025 where the offensive line was one of the factors that led to a disappointing 9-8 finish, it was time for a change of the guard. Left tackle Taylor Decker was released by the team along with interior offensive lineman Graham Glasgow. On top of those moves, All-Pro center Frank Ragnow had tried and failed to make a comeback out of retirement. It was time for the organization to lean into the youth, and that is exactly what they did. Now, after spending the first few years as the young guy in the room, Sewell is the most tenured player along the offensive line as well as one of the oldest at nearly 26 years of age. To his right is third-year left guard Christian Mahogany, center Juice Scruggs, second-year right guard Tate Ratledge, and rookie right tackle Blake Miller. And while Scruggs has played well, newly-signed center Cade Mays recovers from a broken wrist suffered in training camp, it’s hard not to wonder what this unit may look like around Week 10 of the 2026 season. That brings us to today’s question of the day. What is the ceiling for the Lions’ offensive line once Mays returns to action? My answer: I think this unit could quickly become a top-five unit in all of football with time on task. Sewell will only get better as he settles back in on the left side; Mahogany has had good moments and bad, but I like the power aspect he brings to the table next to Sewell. On top of that, Scruggs may get the chance to push for that job once Mays returns to center. Ratledge is playing like one of the better guards in the league, and Miller has been steadily improving save for a few mental mistakes here and there. As the season marches on, it’s important to remember that this is a bit of a transitional year for the offensive line. With that said, it’s also an exciting time. If they can continue to grow in their roles and begin to gel as a unit, the Lions’ offense could really begin to hit their stride. What about you? What do you think the ceiling is for the offensive line in 2026? Let us know in the comments below.

title: 5 takeaways from Kelvin Sheppard’s presser: Lions DC stands by scheme, blitzes
summary: Normally during a game week, I like to provide takeaways from all three Detroit Lions coordinator media sessions on Thursday. But with the pressure mounting on Kelvin Sheppard, I thought it made sense to focus solely on his press conference from Week 5—and to be honest, Sheppard offers more interesting answers anyways. So here are […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 02: Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard of the Detroit Lions reacts during the second half of a game against the Minnesota Vikings at Ford Field on November 02, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images Normally during a game week, I like to provide takeaways from all three Detroit Lions coordinator media sessions on Thursday. But with the pressure mounting on Kelvin Sheppard, I thought it made sense to focus solely on his press conference from Week 5—and to be honest, Sheppard offers more interesting answers anyways. So here are five takeaways from Sheppard’s Thursday media session head of the Arizona Cardinals game. He knows lip service is worthless Normally, Kelvin Sheppard opens his press conference recapping the previous games, highlights strenghths and pinpoints the mistakes, vowing to clean everything up. This week, after another disappointing performance, Sheppard said he knows the promises to fix the problem don’t carry any weight until there are actual results on the field. “Until it starts to show on Sunday, until the evidence starts to show up at the game, it’s lip service,” Sheppard said. “What we do here, bridging it to the game, it sounds good, but it’s lip service. So, what I will say is we did not play well enough defensively to help this team win that football game Sunday night at Carolina. There were a lot of things in there that we absolutely didn’t like. That we turned on the tape as a unit on Monday, hashed out, talked about, and the same thing I told them, it’s lip service. So there has to be real change. It has to be real evidence of change.” They’re letting the defensive line down The only silver lining in Detroit’s defensive performance this year has been the play of the defensive line. The Lions rank in the top-10 of just about every pass rushing metric you can think of, and Sheppard believes they are playing very stout run defense up the middle of the line, as well. “The way that Tyleik Williams and Alim McNeill is playing B-to-B gap, teams rarely run the ball there and we have identified that now,” Sheppard said. “And then having a disruptive edge in Aidan Hutchinson and now complementary pieces opposite him with (Derrick Moore) DMo and (DJ) Wonnum. We have to feed off of them.” Unfortunately, they haven’t as of yet. Despite the pressure and decent interior run defense, the Lions back seven has had too many mental errors and lackluster play. “I told them and I told the D-line, ‘It’s a disservice what we’ve been doing to you all,’” Sheppard said. “I truly feel like this is the best D-line we’ve had in my six-year tenure here since I got here in 2021. And we haven’t been complementing it well enough on the back end to see the benefits of it and be outright beneficiaries is what they should be with what the D-line is doing, especially Sunday night. They assaulted the pocket all night.” Sheppard is standing by his scheme, his blitzes Despite the early game struggles, Sheppard made it clear he is standing by the core beliefs of the current defensive system. More over, he is sure that things will only get worse if they abandon their beliefs and start back at square one. “We have a certain way we say we’re going to play,” Sheppard said. “Now, do you tweak things here and there? Alright, you’re seeing different concepts. They’re attacking you differently. They’re doing—yeah, that’s football. But to just outright bring in a new playbook every week because the last one didn’t go right. That, to me, leads to ultimate dysfunction and the dam completely breaking.” Sheppard was also asked about the team’s ineffective blitzes. Last Sunday, Carolina quarterback Bryce Young completed 9-of-11 passes for 95 yards and a touchdown (per NFL Pro) against the blitz. However, Sheppard maintains they were the right calls in the right situations. “Those calls were the right calls. Those calls were the right calls, and I’ll leave it at that.” When asked a follow up about the disconnect between the right call and the lack of execution, Sheppard denied providing details. “Those are private conversations that we have that I’m going to keep in-house. Those calls were the right calls.” Fixing the trust issues As coach Dan Campbell has talked about in recent weeks, the Lions suffer from a problem of not being in the right place at the right time, and that has led to teammates overcompensating for each other and a lack of trust. So how do you fix that? “I told the guys this, ‘We’ve got to make sure the guys you don’t trust aren’t out there or you guys get it corrected and you get it corrected in a hurry,’” Sheppard said. “Because we don’t want to start doing that and guys feeling like they have got to carry the weight for another guy out there.” He’s insulted by the suggestion the offense needs to carry the defense This week, coach Dan Campbell has several times talked about how the offense needs to be better, and some have taken that as a suggestion that he holds them to a higher standard than the defense. Despite averaging 29.8 points per game (fifth-most), Campbell expects even more out of the unit. Is that because he knows the team needs to carry the 32nd-ranked defense? Behind the scenes, that may be true, but Sheppard was insulted by the insinuation. “We have a three-phase team here and I firmly believe that. And I’m going to stand strong in that belief,” Sheppard said. “I think that’s ultra disrespectful to my unit to say somebody has to carry us. We’re going to do our one-third here. Hell or high water. Point blank period.”

title: Before the Roar: Previewing Detroit Lions vs. Arizona Cardinals
summary: You often hear people around the NFL describe the regular season as a marathon and not a sprint. That is good news for the Detroit Lions because after a bumpy Week 4 loss in Carolina, they are back on the road this week to visit the Arizona Cardinals for a Week 5 matchup. To preview […]
full_text: You often hear people around the NFL describe the regular season as a marathon and not a sprint. That is good news for the Detroit Lions because after a bumpy Week 4 loss in Carolina, they are back on the road this week to visit the Arizona Cardinals for a Week 5 matchup. To preview Sunday’s game, my good friend Meko Scott and I are back with a new episode of “Before the Roar.” We start with a quick overview of the Cardinals’ 2026 season so far and how they got to a 1-3 record. From there, we jump into what makes the Arizona offense go, and, to nobody’s surprise, much of our conversation centered on their All-Pro tight end Trey McBride. The Lions have struggled defending tight ends through four weeks of the season, so having a plan to at least slow down the focal point of the Cardinals’ offense has to be the first order of business for Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard and his staff. On the other side of the football, we discuss how good Arizona’s run defense has been through one month, and how nose tackle Roy Lopez can affect an offense’s game plan without stuffing the stat sheet. We also touch on safety Budda Baker’s impact, and whether the Lions should try to pass early to set up the run. You can watch the entire episode on the Pride of Detroit YouTube channel right here . title: Kelvin Sheppard: Lions S Brian Branch looks ready to play now
summary: After watching Brian Branch practice just one time following his 10-month rehab from an Achilles tear, Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard couldn’t hold in his excitement. “How many positions can he play and how fast?” Sheppard joked with the media on Thursday. And while that was a joke, Sheppard insisted that Detroit’s Pro Bowl […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 27: Brian Branch #32 of the Detroit Lions runs onto the field prior to an NFL football game against the Green Bay Packers at Ford Field on November 27, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images After watching Brian Branch practice just one time following his 10-month rehab from an Achilles tear, Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard couldn’t hold in his excitement. “How many positions can he play and how fast?” Sheppard joked with the media on Thursday. And while that was a joke, Sheppard insisted that Detroit’s Pro Bowl safety looked so locked in and ready on Wednesday that he believes Branch could play a game on Thursday, if cleared. “If we were playing tonight, it would be realistic,” Sheppard said. “Like, this dude—it’s like he hadn’t been out. I’m serious. It literally looks like he hasn’t been out. It’s unbelievable. So, it’s just a matter of I’m going to lean on (Director of Player Health) Brett Fisher, (Head Trainer) Mike Sundeen, and our medical staff here. They’ve always done a tremendous job, and whatever they tell me. If that’s 20 plays, if that’s 30, if it’s 50—I want it to be 60—but whatever they tell me, I’m going to lock that, and we’re going to roll.” It would be pretty unorthodox for the Lions to put Branch into the starting lineup after just three practices, since he hasn’t been on the field since early December. And even Sheppard admitted they need to make sure they don’t put Branch in a tough position. “We also gotta do right by that player,” Sheppard said. “So just make sure we pick and choose how much, how soon, where, what’s best for him right now, and just kinda take that approach to him.” The Lions have taken a somewhat conservative approach with Branch throughout his rehab, ensuring that he was fully ready before they even put him back on the practice field. While Branch has been eager to get out there, he said Wednesday that he appreciates them keeping both his short- and long-term health in mind. That said, he feels like only a few things stand between him and playing time on Sundays. “Just catching my wind. That’s the only hurdle, I feel like,” Branch said. “Catching my wind and contact with each other. Just getting more contact with each other. Yeah, more one-on-ones.” When Branch is back, he can have a significant impact on the Lions’ bottom-ranked defense. Not only will his presence help out a safety group that has struggled through four weeks, but Detroit believes his playmaking and discipline can have a trickle-down effect. “He’s an instinctive, aware player and he’s a violent player,” coach Dan Campbell said this week. “And so, he’s got a knack for the football and his production, even if it’s not what it was in the immediate as he grows back to that will have an impact, I believe. And then with that, then it helps the guys around him. It makes the guys next to him better because this guy will be where he’s supposed to be. He’ll be able to make some plays and alleviate a little stress, and whether it’s the other safety, the corner, Jack (Campbell), some of those things.” It still seems like a long shot that the Lions would opt to play Branch on Sunday against the Cardinals, but it’s clear that Sheppard wants him as soon as possible. “I’m ready for him to go all 70-80 (snaps). However many we play. Saints game, that was 90? Let’s go 90, BB. As much of Brian Branch as I can get right now, I want it.”
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Lions vs. Cardinals 5 Qs preview: Does Arizona do ANYTHING well?
summary: One more game remains for the Detroit Lions before they’re off for a week—and it’s an important game in deciding the vibes as Detroit heads into their Week 6 bye. We had the pleasure of connecting with Seth Cox, the Managing Editor for Revenge of the Birds, to give us some insight into this Arizona […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - SEPTEMBER 22: Aidan Hutchinson #97 of the Detroit Lions looks on against the Arizona Cardinals during the fourth quarter at State Farm Stadium on September 22, 2024 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images One more game remains for the Detroit Lions before they’re off for a week—and it’s an important game in deciding the vibes as Detroit heads into their Week 6 bye. We had the pleasure of connecting with Seth Cox, the Managing Editor for Revenge of the Birds , to give us some insight into this Arizona Cardinals team ahead of this week’s matchup. We learned about the offense’s check-down struggles under Jacoby Brissett, the early-season hullabaloo surrounding the fatigue facing Arizona’s top pick Jeremiyah Love, and a passive defensive scheme that’s struggling to generate pressure—plus much more. 1. Per Next Gen Stats, Jacoby Brissett completed just six of 18 pass attempts for 55 yards, two touchdowns, and two interceptions against the Giants’ blitzes, facing pressure on 52.4% of his dropbacks. What about the Giants’ blitz packages caused problems for Brissett and the offense? How does losing Paris Johnson Jr. for the season complicate things for Arizona’s offensive line? The Arizona Cardinals offensive line stinks, the quarterback sat out all offseason of a new system after going 1-11 and the Cardinals caved and gave him $10 million more and then this has been the result. An offense that looks like it’s afraid to or just unwilling to push the ball down the field right now. The thing is, the offensive line was bad last year and the problem was all the running backs were hurt. Now this year, they got rid of the “problems” in Drew Petzing and Kyler Murray, and the passing attack is literally just check downs. It’s actually not even enjoyable to watch for the first four weeks. 2. Arizona took a bold and brave swing by drafting running back Jeremiyah Love with the third overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. He’s dealing with a new ankle injury that head coach Mike LaFleur said is separate from the injury he suffered back in August. “It’s more of just the whole thing,” Love said after last week’s game. “It’s been a long year for me. Like, [my] body sometimes is down. Somebody [is] sometimes tired. So, like, it’s just managing those things. Like, coaches know that. Like, this is probably gonna be the longest year of my life.” How have fans reacted to Love’s postgame comments, what have you made of his rookie season so far–and what about the run game as a whole? There’s always the “it is taken out of context” remarks, but through the first four weeks he does seem genuinely dejected and not like he’s having fun. Of course being in a losing situation with a team that doesn’t seem to have a big plan week to week on how much they are using that huge investment does make sense on why it has been tough through the first month of the season. 3. The Cardinals defense looks like it’s struggling a bit to pressure the quarterback, ranking 29th in pressure rate (30.3%) and 30th in passing EPA per play allowed (+0.29). In what ways have opponents been successful against the Cardinals pass defense? Can you rush the passer? No. Can you cover? No. Does your defensive coordinator employ blitzing to manufacture pressures? No. Well, then you see the results. Their schemes are super passive, and they have one super talented guy in Walter Nolen, a guy who is good when he’s on in Josh Sweat, but seems to be completely checked out right now. There’s not a whole lot to it. They stink. 4. Arizona’s run defense looks like it’s pretty solid: 15th in yards per carry, 14th in stuff rate (17.0%) and second in rushing EPA per play allowed (-0.24). Who has been key in the Cardinals ability to stop the run this season? It’s fine in the sense that the numbers look okay, but the reality is that a lot of those good numbers come from the fact that they are down so much and teams just are running and they know it’s coming. When games are competitive though, you are seeing good things out of Roy Lopez, Nolen, Zaven Collins and then Mack Wilson doing good work. Of course there is always Budda Baker as well, who remains one of the best run support safeties in the NFL, and Andrew Wingard has done well (although he is out this week it seems like). 5. The Cardinals opened as 4.5-point underdogs heading into Week 5 against the Lions, and that line has remained steady so far over at FanDuel Sportsbook. What’s one thing you want to see, what’s one thing you need to see, and one thing you’re sure you’ll see happen in this matchup between the Lions and Cardinals on Sunday afternoon? I’d love to see the Arizona Cardinals push the ball down the field. Against what has been a poor Lions pass defense, you’d love to see that come into play, but you do have a very good pass rush through four weeks so that’s something to worry about starting two backups (left tackle and right guard) and Elijah Wilkinson. So, I’d also like to see them use their third overall pick like that type of investment (of course if his ankle really is messed up then I retract this statement) and really force the Lions to load up and stop Jeremiyah Love. What I expect to happen is that the Detroit Lions score 30+ points, and the Arizona Cardinals do well enough to keep it close before the Lions pull away and have their best game of the season. Good luck and good health to the Lions in this one.

full_text: Aug 28, 2026; Green Bay, Wisconsin, USA; Arizona Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur during the game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field. Mandatory Credit: Jeff Hanisch-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Detroit Lions (2-2) and Arizona Cardinals (1-3) will square off in a Week 5 battle in the desert. The Cardinals are in the early stages of a coaching change, now led by Mount Pleasant, Michigan-native Mike LaFleur—the brother of Packers coach Matt LaFleur—and are still searching for their identity. Let’s take a closer look at the Cardinals’ coaching staff, the scheme they run, and scouting notes from their most recently viewed games. Cardinal s head coach: Mike LaFleur NFL coaching seasons: 13th season (Browns, Falcons, 49ers, Jets, Rams, Cardinals) Head coaching seasons : First (Cardinals) Offensive coordinator : Rams (2023-25), Jets (2021-22) Passing game coordinator : 49ers (2017-20) Influences: Kyle Shanahan, Sean McVay, Matt LaFleur (Brother) Coached under: Shanahan, McVay, Mike Pettine, Dan Quinn, Robert Saleh Play caller : Yes Dan Campbell on LaFleur: “These guys are playing hard. Coach LaFleur’s doing a really good job with them. They’ve been in all these games. I know the Seattle game got a little bit out of whack there, but these guys play hard. And they’re in all these games, man. They can score points on offense. They have got weapons.” Offensive coordinato r: Nathaniel Hackett NFL coaching seasons : 18th season (Bucs, Bills, Jaguars, Packers, Broncos, Jets, Cardinals) Offensive coordinator seasons : 11th season (Bills, Jaguars, Packers, Jets, Cardinals) Head coaching seasons : Broncos (2022) Previous coaching positions : QB coach, TE coach, offensive quality control, defensive analyst Influences: Matt LaFleur, Doug Marone, Jon Gruden Coached under: LaFleur, Marone, Gruden, Dick Jauron, Gus Bradley, Greg Olsen, Robert Saleh Offensive scheme Passing game : West Coast Shanahan offense Running scheme : Outside-zone/GAP orientated Scouting notes : There are clear signs of Shanahan and McVay’s system in play in Arizona, like leaning on an outside-zone rushing attack and leaning into 13 personnel, but… There are also some stark variances, such as Shanahan/McVay schemes leaning heavily on play-action, but the Cardinals have used it sparingly: 17.8% (27th in the NFL) 11 personnel is the most prevalent at 61.7% usage 12 personnel is moderate at 14.8% 13 personnel heavy usage has carried over from the Rams: 20% Run/pass split is roughly 38/62% Jacoby Brissett has struggled and ranks in the lower third, or at the bottom, of most QB categories. Passing yards per play: 5.4 (32nd), Explosive pass plays (32nd) Brissett EPA: drop back (36th), vs. man coverage (36th), vs. zone (23rd), on play-action (32nd), in red zone (28th), vs. pressure (29th), per SumerSports Offensive line isn’t helping much, allowing pressure in 2.51 seconds (28th) OL struggling to pick up blitz, very late to adjust; Brissett EPA vs. Blitz (40th), per SumerSports Making matters worse, starting LT Paris Johnson just landed on season-ending injured reserve Brissett’s mobility has kept him upright, and he has only been sacked seven times (10th fewest) The rushing attack deploys an outside-zone blocking scheme and gap-blocking scheme, each about a third of the time, splitting the final third between inside zone, pullers, and draws. They don’t use many, if any, counters or traps Run game is solid (EPA per rush -0.05, 14th); they lack explosives (32nd) and don’t get much initial push from their offensive line (0.73 yards before contact, 29th), forcing the RBs to do most of the work RB Jeremiyah Love and Tyler Allgeier could be a problem for the Lions, but… If the Lions can take away the run, the Cardinals will abandon it Dan Campbell on Cardinals tight end Trey McBride: “When you’re a big physical guy that can run and separate and make tough catches and have some run after catch. I mean that’s hard because you’re big and physical. And so, you can separate from a safety. And then linebackers, a lot of times they can run away from them or their catch radius, things of that nature. So, they’re going to give this guy (McBride) the ball because he can make plays with the ball in his hand and he’s tough. He’s going to get his targets and we’re going to have our hands full.” Defensive coordinator: Nick Rallis NFL coaching seasons : 9th season (Vikings, Eagles, Cardinals) Defensive coordinator seasons : 4th (Cardinals, 2023-present, retained from previous regime) Previous roles : LB coach, assistant LB coach, and defensive quality control Influences: Jonathan Gannon, Mike Zimmer Coached under: Gannon, Zimmer, Nick Sirianni Staff ties to Detroit : Teryl Austin (Senior Defensive Assistant) Defensive scheme Base : 3-4 Base Coverage : Fangio zone principles, two-high split-zone safeties Scouting notes : Diverse scheme, but they lack a defining identity on defense Spent the majority of their time in their 3-4 Base defense: 52.4% Supplement that with a 2-4 nickel: 44.5% Heavy zone coverage: 81.3% In 2025, highest usage of Cover-4 (30%) in the NFL; in 2026, it’s been scaled back to 20% New favorite coverage scheme: Cover-6 at 27.6% (most in the NFL — up from just 5.5% in 2025) Note: The difference between Cover-4 and Cover-6 isn’t that big; in Cover-4, they drop four DBs deep with two (or three) underneath, while Cover-6 inverts that, dropping three DBs deep with three (or four) underneath. Other zone coverages used: Cover-2 (14%), Cover-3 (21%) Man coverages used: Cover-0 (2.4%), Cover-1 (5.8%), Cover-2 man (2.4%) 29th in defensive DVOA, 29th in points allowed (29.3) Strong numbers defend the run: DVOA (10th), EPA per rush (-0.24, 2nd), yards before contact allowed (0.77, 4th) Disastrous numbers defending the pass: DVOA (31st), 9.1 yards allowed per pass (32nd), 0.29 EPA per pass (30th), Explosive plays allowed (32nd), 37 pressures forced (32nd) Zone is very loose, especially between the LBs and safeties Willing to allow completions underneath because they’re solid tacklers Slot defenders are very instinctual: S/NB Budda Baker and NB Garrett Williams made impact plays in the game I watched Dan Campbell on the Cardinals’ defense: “In this defense, man, it gives you different looks. They have got length. (safety) Budda Baker is problematic. (LB Mack) Wilson, man, he kind of runs the show over there. And we know Roy Lopez, man. He’s a lunch pail guy, going to give it everything you got and make you earn it, among others over there.”

title: Discussion: How much will Brian Branch’s return help the Lions defense?
summary: With Brian Branch’s 21-day evaluation clock officially started on Wednesday, it’s only a matter of time before the Detroit Lions’ Pro Bowl safety is back in the lineup. That’s obviously not likely to happen this week against the Arizona Cardinals, but it seems almost certain that Branch will return for Detroit’s first game out of […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - DECEMBER 05: Brian Branch #32 of the Detroit Lions runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the Green Bay Packers at Ford Field on December 5, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images With Brian Branch’s 21-day evaluation clock officially started on Wednesday , it’s only a matter of time before the Detroit Lions’ Pro Bowl safety is back in the lineup. That’s obviously not likely to happen this week against the Arizona Cardinals, but it seems almost certain that Branch will return for Detroit’s first game out of the bye week: Week 7’s home game against the Green Bay Packers. On Wednesday, coach Dan Campbell talked about the kind of impact that Branch could have on the team. “He’s an instinctive, aware player and he’s a violent player,” Campbell said. “And so, he’s got a knack for the football and his production, even if it’s not what it was in the immediate as he grows back to that, will have an impact, I believe. And then with that, then it helps the guys around him. It makes the guys next to him better because this guy will be where he’s supposed to be. He’ll be able to make some plays and alleviate a little stress and whether it’s the other safety, the corner, Jack (Campbell), some of those things.” The Lions defense is in a pretty big hole, though. How much difference can one guy make? Today’s Question of the Day is: How much will the Lions defense improve with Branch’s return? My answer: Obviously, that’s a hard thing to quantify. Could they go from the 32nd ranked defense to the 20s? That seems a bit optimistic. Could they turn down the points per game allowed from nearly 32 to maybe the mid-to-high 20s? That seems a little more doable. As Campbell pointed out, Branch’s return is not just about upgrading the safety position, it’s about making everyone around him better. As the Lions coach continually points out, players are currently in the wrong place at the wrong time too often. That has led to one of the biggest problems a cohesive defense runs into: a lack of trust. Players are covering for one another, and that only leads more people out of position. As Anthony Balaj pointed out in his Lions defense film study vs. the Panthers , Detroit’s zone lapses were often the result of slow or undisciplined play from the safety group. Branch’s ridiculous instincts and knowledge of the scheme should be a very direct solution to those problems. And if he’s playing better assignment-sound football, the linebacking crew will look better, the cornerbacks will have an extra weapon at their disposal, and it could free up the other safety position to have a cleaner fit with personnel—whether that means more Christian Izien in the slot or Chuck Clark in a look less vulnerable that single-high. However, we can’t ignore that expectations for Branch should be lowered for at least the first month that he’s back. He’s coming off a major injury, hasn’t had any live reps in 10 months, and will need time to kick off some rust. And like we saw with Alim McNeill, there’s certainly a chance we don’t see the Branch we’re accustomed to seeing until 2027. But even Branch at 70-80% of what we’ve seen him at is likely an upgrade over what Detroit currently has at the safety position, so I wouldn’t be surprised to see a noticeable difference the minute he takes the field. Do you think Branch will make a noticeable difference or is the defense beyond saving at this point? Share your answers in the comment section at the bottom of this page. Join the conversation! title: Packers sign Pierre Strong Jr. to active roster
summary: The Green Bay Packers announced on Thursday that they have signed running back Pierre Strong Jr. to the active roster, giving them a fourth option if the team can’t play Chris Brooks on Sunday against the Chicago Bears. Brooks left Week 4 with an ankle injury and hasn’t practiced with the team since. In his […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers announced on Thursday that they have signed running back Pierre Strong Jr. to the active roster, giving them a fourth option if the team can’t play Chris Brooks on Sunday against the Chicago Bears. Brooks left Week 4 with an ankle injury and hasn’t practiced with the team since. In his pre-practice press conference, head coach Matt LaFleur said Green Bay would give Brooks another day before testing how he feels, but signing Strong sure seems to point in the direction of Brooks missing Week 5. Strong was previously on the Packers’ practice squad, which signed running back Damon Bankston earlier this week. Strong hasn’t played in a regular-season game for Green Bay in his two years with the club, but he was activated last year due to injuries. Strong will likely back up MarShawn Lloyd and Kaleb Johnson in the running back unit, as well as potentially replacing Brooks on special teams. For reference, Brooks has played 29 snaps on special teams, just a few snaps less than kicker Trey Smack, while Johnson has played three (on kickoffs) and Lloyd has played none this season. The Packers’ 53-man roster and practice squad are now full, following their most recent set of transactions, which included signing linebacker Jack Dingle to the practice squad .
