title: Packers Injury Report: Jager Burton returns on Thursday
summary: Green Bay Packers offensive lineman Jager Burton, who, according to head coach Matt LaFleur, is dealing with back spasms, went from a non-participant in Wednesday’s practice to a limited participant in Thursday’s practice. Burton is the only player whose status changed today. Players who remain as non-participants are left guard Aaron Banks (knee/toe), running back […]
full_text: (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Green Bay Packers offensive lineman Jager Burton, who, according to head coach Matt LaFleur, is dealing with back spasms, went from a non-participant in Wednesday’s practice to a limited participant in Thursday’s practice. Burton is the only player whose status changed today. Players who remain as non-participants are left guard Aaron Banks (knee/toe), running back Chris Brooks (ankle) and offensive lineman Jacob Monk (quadricep). LaFleur told the press on Thursday that the team was going to give Brooks another day of rest before seeing how his ankle holds up. Brooks went down against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and was previously the team’s number one back in terms of snap counts. If the Packers are down Brooks, they’ll only have two players at the position on the 53-man roster, which probably means that Green Bay will need to call up Pierre Strong Jr. from the practice squad against the Chicago Bears. Limited participants in practice today were right tackle Anthony Belton (knee), defensive lineman Anthony Campbell (ankle), edge defender Lukas Van Ness (shoulder) and defensive lineman Devonte Wyatt (ankle). LaFleur said that there are no concerns about Belton being a limited participant this week, as the current expectation remains that he will be starting as a bookend on Sunday. We’re not allowed to film, but Micah Parsons doing some fairly strenuous running on the side at practice with some sort of wrap/brace on his left knee. LaFleur said Parsons made progress last week but wasn’t ready to practice. — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) October 8, 2026 In Micah Parsons news, The Athletic’s Matt Schneidman noted that the All-Pro edge defender was running at practice today, even though he hasn’t had his 21-day practice window open up. Currently, Parsons remains on the physically unable to perform list. Only change for the Packers is Burton goes from DNP to limited. Talked to Burton after practice and he said he’s never had any back issues before. Said he was able to do the individual drills without any issues. https://t.co/BWhGgyBtJK pic.twitter.com/f17EwT5met — Rob Demovsky (@RobDemovsky) October 8, 2026 The Bears had significant changes on their injury report, as offensive lineman Jonah Jackson (ankle), running back D’Andre Swift (hip/knee), offensive lineman Joe Thuney (pectoral) and offensive lineman Darnell Wright (ankle) were all elevated from non-participants on Wednesday to limited participants on Thursday. With that being said, linebacker Keyshaun Elliott seemed to take a backslide with his quadricep injury, as he went from limited to a non-participant. Beyond Elliott, the only other non-participants in Chicago’s practice today were quarterback Caleb Williams (hamstring) and running back Kyle Monangai (thumb/toe). The Bears’ running back room and offensive line is a little banged up right now, so it’ll be interesting to see how they hold up against Green Bay in Week 5.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Baby steps for Packers run game
summary: The Packers’ offensive line woes this year are well documented, and they tend to lead the public discourse about the team. Rightfully so.  Dive just beyond the surface, though, and the true ouroboros becomes more clear.  A unique combination of intense pass rushing teams, green linemen, and a startlining lack of schematic understanding has made […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 4: Defensive end Elijah Roberts #95 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and offensive tackle Anthony Belton #71 of the Green Bay Packers chirping at each other in the third quarter at Raymond James Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Packers’ offensive line woes this year are well documented, and they tend to lead the public discourse about the team. Rightfully so. Dive just beyond the surface, though, and the true ouroboros becomes more clear. A unique combination of intense pass rushing teams, green linemen, and a startlining lack of schematic understanding has made it open season on Jordan Love, who has been hit over 30 times this year. Despite that, he’s managed to throw 8 TDs (tied for third in the league). The passing game would come easier if the running game were respectable, though. And while it’s easy to blame Marshawn Lloyd’s poor visibility and Kaleb Johnson’s plodding nature, the offensive line hasn’t been up to the task in the run blocking game either. Both of those issues combined mean opposing defenses are free to continue to send the house against Love all while having precisely zero respect for the running game. Everything stalls. The snake head eats itself. Reinforcements are on the way, however. Last week’s game saw Laken Tomlinson and Travis Glover inserted into the lineup, and the instant improvement was obvious. A line that had been league worst by a country mile seemed to quickly join the “among the worst in the league” group. That small gain benefited the running game, even producing a (gasp) explosive run — a 31-yard Kaleb Johnson jaunt. This week should see the installation of Kevin Zeitler at guard (a bonafide decent lineman!). Ideally this helps bolster a simple “big guys moving forward” approach that can benefit Kaleb Johnson. Pepper in Marshawn Lloyd as a pass-catching threat and, hey, maybe you have a backfield that defenses have to pay at least a little more attention to. That might even free up the passing offense to breathe just a little bit, with speedsters like Christian Watson and Matthew Golden able to turn an inch of separation into a yard given the right conditions. All of this is not to say the Packers are on their way to defeating the Chicago Bears this Sunday and truly turning their season around. Instead, I’d set expectations this way: a slightly below league average offensive line now feels at least possible. And if achieved, that would certainly allow the offense to function a bit more as intended — both on the ground and in the air. More offensive production means longer drives and more points. Both of those things benefit the defense, who have been victimized by the worst offensive time of possession in football this season. All of this hinges first on the changes at offensive line proving out. Last week was a baby step forward. Can the Packers take another toddle this Sunday? Here’s hoping! title: Houston Texans: How to watch, who to blame
summary: Houston Texans head coach Demeco Ryans announces he’s taking over defensive play calling. Offensive coordinator Nick Calley continues to make elementary “hat on hat” comments as his brand of the Erhardt-Perkins offense struggles. Primarily due to telegraphed formations, confused offensive linemen and Madden 95 level play calling. Mediocrity doesn’t win championships. Players are saying the […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: Head Coach DeMeco Ryans of the Houston Texans looks on during the second half of the game against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images Houston Texans head coach Demeco Ryans announces he’s taking over defensive play calling . Offensive coordinator Nick Calley continues to make elementary “hat on hat” comments as his brand of the Erhardt-Perkins offense struggles. Primarily due to telegraphed formations, confused offensive linemen and Madden 95 level play calling. Mediocrity doesn’t win championships . Players are saying the losses are on them. Ex-Texans continue to excel with other teams. Other teams with less talented rosters are winning. A vocal minority of fans are calling for general manager Nick Caserio’s resignation. Another contingent of fans are calling for an entirely clean slate from owner to ball boys. So, who is to blame for the worst flop of the Texans’ 25 year existence? Who do we pin the pain on for going from Super Bowl contender to current #1 draft picker? Houston Texans general manager It’s easy to blame Nick Caserio for all this, since he is mostly responsible for assembling the roster and hiring head coach Demeco Ryans. At the end of the day, the GM is the top of the franchise food chain, the one ultimately responsible for everything that happens regarding the actual football team. Caserio hired Ryans, had a say in hiring his buddy and former college kegger companion, Caley. He also signed off on elevating Cole Popovich to offensive line coach. He’s also the guy that pulled the trigger on drafting Will Anderson Jr., C.J. Stroud and several other star players. In the off-season, he shaped a roster based on the needs of offensive and defensive schemes he signed off on. In the end, it’s easy to blame him. And, some of that blame is very valid. Nepotism doesn’t win pro football games Caserio bringing in his buddy Caley is likely his worst misstep so far. But, Caserio was brought in by his other buddy Bill O’Brien, so maybe that apple didn’t fall far from the tree. Either way, sending Caley to Boston College for some slightly used harbor tea sounds like a great idea at this point. Houston Texans head coach NEW: DeMeco Ryans said changes will be made this week. And as they should. Because the Texans' loss to the Cowboys made one thing clear: This team just isn't good. On a season that continues to spiral. https://t.co/WeiRarQXUE via @houstonchron — Jonathan M Alexander (@jonmalexander) October 5, 2026 Speaking of nepotism, it’s really hard to root against Demeco Ryans in just about anything. His impact on this team, as both a player and a head coach have been mostly positive. He’s smart, passionate, charismatic and simply the sort of guy you want to see win. But liking the head coach doesn’t always equate to Lombardi Trophies. Not sure a lot of people loved Bill Belichick, but his ring collection speaks for itself. More than Caserio, Ryans should have say in which coaches stay and go. Who is hired, who is fired, promoted and demoted. This means he has to take some, if not all, of the blame in the coaching performances. Ultimately he should take all of it, as it’s his job to coach the coaches, as well as the players. Houston Texans offensive coordinator A lot of us saw the writing on the wall with Nick Caley early last season. While many teams bring in first time OCs and take off, Houston did and had more of the same. Caley’s play calling is sus, he’s frequently out-football-knowledge’d by local football analysts, and brings a smugness to his press conferences that seems diametrically opposed to the Demeco Ryans brand of coaching mentioned above. Quarterback C.J. Stroud has alluded to communication issues with Caley so often that Jerry Shuplinski was elevated to QB Coach in the off-season to act as a go-between. Unlike Caserio and Ryans, it’s nearly impossible to plant a flag on a landmark achievement in Caley’s H-Town career. Often, it seems, the offense succeeds in spite of, not due to, Caley’s efforts. Houston Texans defensive coordinator When Matt Burke first took over as the Houston Texans DC, it seemed like the unit took an exponential step forward, going from good to great. For those outside the building, it’s not easy to quantify just what went down in that transition phase. Did Ryans act as training wheels for Burke, proving 2 heads are better than 1? The combination of both men working in sync leading to a lights out D? And, maybe this off-season Ryans took a step back, figuring Burke’s “got this” and didn’t need his head coach to stay all up in it? With little to illustrate how Burke went from “Matt who?” to “hot head coaching candidate”, the collapse this season definitely points to a lack of vitamin ‘Meco. Houston Texans players From a casual fan perspective, whichever player failed to make whatever play they deem key to winning/losing a game, is an easy target. Miss a game winning field goal? Blame the kicker. Throw an ill-fated interception? Blame the quarterback. Give up a key touchdown? Blame the defense. Unfortunately, it’s not that simple. However, the players do need to do their jobs to the best of their ability on and off the field. Believing their own hype/reading their own press, is a currently trending reason for why the Texans defense has fallen from grace. Anyone who has watched the NFL for any amount of years has likely heard stories of entire rosters stricken with the flu. Locker rooms tanked by negative-minded players with big personalities that use their leadership to drag everyone down. Key members of the roster failing to buy in to the coaching, leading the players who look up to them to do the same. Or simply guys thinking they’ve arrived and no longer striving to get there day in and day out. Who is to blame? In the end, it’s hard to definitively point at 1 person and conclusively say the 0-4 start is their fault, solely. However, you can look at the facets listed above and narrow it down with logical conclusions. Winning and losing comes down to 2 things: the roster and how the roster is leveraged to win games. Roster Management : Not really an issue. This team is as talented as the Buffalo Bills, Minnesota Vikings, San Francisco 49ers, Kansas City Chiefs and just about any other 3+ win team right now. In some cases, more so. Getting the most out of said roster shows some disconnects, however. Grade: Pass Head Coaching : Ultimately, leveraging the roster is up to the coaching staff. And leveraging the coaching staff is up to the head coach. Both facets are failing this franchise right now. Grade: Fail Offensive coordinator : Despite Caley’s charter school offensive strategy, C.J. Stroud is balling out and the Texans have been in a position to win each game this season. Unfortunately, the run game is still abysmal, the offensive line is still offensive and Caley continues to convey it’s simply a matter of brute force. Grade: Fail Defensive coordinator : Burke is living the wrong end of the rags to riches to rags story this season. With Ryans relieving him of defensive play-calling duties, it’s clear the belief inside NRG is that Burke isn’t getting it done in all phases of his job. Grade: Fail …. pic.twitter.com/43LeNpoqDo — Harley Dugan (@TheLead_HOU) October 4, 2026 Player performance : Here’s where it gets bewildering. C.J. Stroud is having the season of his life. He’s currently 6th in passing yards with 1141, carrying a 95.9 passer rating and only he, along with Jared Goff are the only passers with over 1000 air yards to throw zero interceptions this season. Will Anderson Jr. is on another tear, tied with T.J. Watt for 3rd place in total sacks (4.5), 11 QB hits and 7 tackles for loss. Despite the 2 team leaders rising up, mental mistakes, dropped passes, missed tackles and blown assignments seem to mar every game. Grade: C- Other teams have also…
author: Mike Bullock

title: Groupthink: Is this the most disappointing season in Texans History?
summary: It’s an all-time rant session by the Battle Red Blog after the Texans fall to 0-4 and effectively are out of the playoffs for the first time in four seasons. The Super Bowl hopes are all but lost in easily one of the most devastating, late game loses to the Dallas Cowboys. One month in […]
full_text: It’s an all-time rant session by the Battle Red Blog after the Texans fall to 0-4 and effectively are out of the playoffs for the first time in four seasons. The Super Bowl hopes are all but lost in easily one of the most devastating, late game loses to the Dallas Cowboys. One month in and the entire season is essentially null and void. The vibes are low right now and the team is in a bad position. With that being said, I asked the writers of the blog one simple question: Is this the most disappointing season in Texans History? VBallRetired: I’m going to say the last Kubiak year (2013) but this is close. It’s hard to watch the defense go from first to this in one season. I’m waiting to see the end result before a final verdict, but this team just fails to make that one play in every game. It’s maddening really. Stroud has been good and that’s the criminal part of it. L4Blitzer: Not sure if the sis worse than 2010 or 2013, but it may yet end up similar to those. If it isn’t one thing, it’s another. Something about the fourth stain a Texans coach is here… Anyway, now that all of the postseason goals are effectively off the table, it will be interesting to see where the team goes from here. Patrick H.: I want to start with a question: what would you be able to do if you had 25 years to do it? Because think about it for a moment. I don’t know you long any over you have been Texans fans, but I was one from the get-go. I have watched almost every game this team has played for 25 years. That’s three hours a day, for 16 or 17 days a year, for 25 years. That’s 1,215 hours (roughly), spent watching Houston Texans football that I could’ve spent learning something new or building a bard or something way more complex than that. And we’ve spent it watching these frauds lose more often than they win. Think of what we could’ve done with 25 years and -1,200 hours that we’ve sunk into this team. I could have been fluent in Japanese! It’s exhausting, depressing, and infuriating. A perfect encapsulation of what it is to be a Texans fan. This is not the worst team or most wailful team to watch. Those honors still go to the Culley and Smith years. This is probably the most dissapointed I’ve ever been in the Texans. It’s the most disappointed I’ve ever been as a Texans fan. And it’s the first time I’ve started questioning just what the hell I’m doing with my life. VBallRetired: Hadn’t thought of that, but it’s true. I’m looking at 2013 and the benchmark. We were preseason Super Bowl favorites and it all went to crap. It was the total disintegration that makes that season the top choice, but that was the pick six Festival of Suck. This season seems to be a scatterplot of unpredictibleness. The only predictable part is where we have an opportunity to win at the end and are just not able to get it done. Mike Bullock: Yes, but they got to sell a lot of white out merch on the coat tail of all that offseason hype. I’m not a Caserio hater and love DeMeco Ryans, but this is absolutely unacceptable after last season and the “improvements” earlier this year. And “tank for Manning”? Why? So he can embrace the suck of the Cal McNair product? Time to find another hobby… Joe Critz: Not sure if it’s the most disappointing loss in franchise history quite yet, but man it’s pretty close. This last offseason was the first time I can remember hearing so many analysts, podcasters, talking heads, and random friends that like football calling for the Texans to make the Super Bowl, and there haven’t been enough injuries to the roster to justify such a wildly ugly start. The last three years of success have granted us, as Texans fans, the freedom to place reasonably high exceptions on our favorite team. Nick Caserio’s success rebuilding the defense through the draft from 2022-2025 (and his less notable success rebuilding the offense in the same manner) meant that we could trust the entire roster would be capable of a championship. There were no massive losses from last year’s 12-5 roster, and you could argue that the team actually improved, but it sure doesn’t look that way on the field. Without Nico Collins on the field, the offense became one-dimensional and, in stretches, arguably as ugly as the 2022 or 2024 years, which is unacceptable at this point in the Ryans/Stroud era. ON defense, they’re incredibly reliant on the ir pass rush to get home, and the backup linebackers and starting cornerbacks couldn’t close out the game when the moment arrived. Something that we’ve heard before this season too. I don’t know what the cure is on defense and that makes all of this even worse because it means I don’t know how the Texans will stop the bleeding. They obviously have impressive spurts both on offense and defense, but will it ever be enough to beat a good team? Will it even be enough to beat a bad team? A lot of how I feel comes down to this: after all of these years, are the Texans really so bad that even the return of their star receiver and best offensive lineman isn’t enough to get a single victory? After all of these years after the Bill O’Brien/Jack Easterby/David Culley period, the Texans’ roster is still this unpredictable, mistake-prone, and sloppy? Where has all of the development that was promised after 2023 gone? If it has me questioning everything about the process that DeMeco Ryans and Nick Caserio have promised, then this loss has to be at least one of the most disappointing in recent Texans history. VBallRetired: In three of four games, one play at any point in the game changes the outcome. That’s what makes this so cruel. Joe Critz: Yeah, but like, they’re supposed to be beyond winning close games. Wining close was how they got it done in 2023, 2024, and 2025. Texans can’t count on that luck forever. They have to build their team to the point where winning big becomes a reality Ala the 49ers or another franchise. They can’t win big all the time, but they should be able to sometimes if they want fans to believe the development is really happening. VBallRetired: They are coached to play close, one-possession games. Joe Critz: My whole optimism for 2023 was “oh wow, if C.J. Stroud is this good in year one, imagine how good he will be in year three, four, or five”? At some point, I gave up that exciting development from happening. To VBallRetired’s point, I get this to a degree, but I believe the offense isn’t coached to win close. Stroud has said time and time again his biggest strength is throwing the deep ball, which means the offense is probably looking to do that and score point off of it on most drives. I know they want to be complimentary with their suffocating defense and let their defense control the game, but in the real moment-t0-moment action of the game, I think the offense tries to be more aggressive than just “play one-possession games”. I think their attempts to go for it on fourth down – and failures to convert- are evidence of that. Kenneth L.: Coming into this late, but I couldn’t agree more with Joe’s initial sentiment about the roster. That is, this is almost the same exact defense and team that went 12-5. We were sold that they improved their biggest weaknesses from last year. They added immediate impact players in the draft and had the depth to make a run. Turns out, the veterans are broken, the rookies can’t make the roster (Marlin Klein), and the offense hasn’t evolved. This 0-4 start illustrates a lack of evolution. It’s the same thing, from coach to coach, season to season, player to player. The ‘Texans way’ is in the water and instilled in the franchise. The logos of this team is to play gritty games and win on the margins. The lack of schematic and strategic evolution from 2025 to 2026 is evident in the losses and poor efficiency on critical downs. Houston’s opponents scouted them and made adjustments while Houston stuck to its laurels. The Cowboys and Colts, two teams who are no better than the Texans, beat. them on critical plays by knowing what Houston…

Thursday's practice report for #INDvsPIT pic.twitter.com/seXUTJxpF6 — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 8, 2026 Wide receiver Keenan Allen (groin) was limited at practice today. Allen has been dealing with a groin injury the past couple of weeks and it caused him to miss the game against the Commanders. A team looking to boost its passing attack can’t afford one of its veterans to miss another game. Center Tanor Bortolini (ankle) was limited at practice today. Bortolini missed practice yesterday so him managing to practice today is a positive step for him. Bortolini is still looking uncertain to be available for Sunda.y. Linebacker Jaylon Carlies (ribs) continued to miss practice today. Carlies looks set to miss Sundays game with a rib injury. If he is unable to play expect Bryce Boettcher to start in his place. Linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither (knee) was a full participant at practice today. Davis-Gaither returned to practice having missed it the day before. He looks set to be available Sunday and continue to start at the MIKE. Wide receiver Ashton Dulin (hamstring) and defensive end Arden Key (hamstring) both missed practice today. Both look set to miss Sundays game. Key will miss his first of many to come and Dulin will miss his third already for the year. Tight end Will Mallory (thumb) was a full participant at practice again today. Mallory looks to be trending in the right direction to be activated off injured reserve and it may come this week. Cornerback Charvarius Ward (groin) was limited again today at practice. Ward looks to be still dealing with a groin injury this week even though he played through it last Sunday. Expect him to do the same this week too.

title: 5 Questions with Bleeding Green Nation: Do the Lane Johnson-less Eagles stand a chance?
summary: As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 5, we exchanged questions with Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation to learn more about the opposing side. Question 1: Future Hall of Fame right tackle Lane Johnson announced his retirement on Tuesday. Did the news catch you off guard? What will the […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Lane Johnson #65 of the Philadelphia Eagles walks off the field against the Washington Commanders following an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 5, we exchanged questions with Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation to learn more about the opposing side. Question 1: Future Hall of Fame right tackle Lane Johnson announced his retirement on Tuesday. Did the news catch you off guard? What will the on-field fallout look like? It didn’t catch me off guard. It caught me off tackle! (Boooooooooooooo.) But, no, I can’t say it was a *total* surprise. Johnson has given weight to retiring in the past, including back in the offseason and then seemingly again in training camp as he spent an excused absence away from the team. Upon returning, he talked about his changing values and how 2026 was probably going to be his last season. It was surprising to see Johnson scratched for Week 4 with very little advance notice. But then there were murmurs that he could indeed retire. And he did. Which is a really big deal because he’s an awesome player and the Eagles have always been significantly worse when he’s been unavailable. I wrote about the Eagles’ offensive line outlook more in-depth at BGN, so, I’ll shamelessly plug that here . Of course, the Eagles have also traded Cam Jurgens since then. He wasn’t playing very well at left guard, which wasn’t a surprise since he had literally never played that position before. The Eagles moved him to that spot in desperation after having to put Landon Dickerson, who looked cooked in the season opener, after Week 1. The Eagles’ starting offensive line against the Jags could look like this: LT Jordan Mailata LG Willie Lampkin C Drew Kendall RG Tyler Steen RT Markel Bell I can’t say with 100% certainty that this will be the configuration. There’s some talk that they could move Kendall to left guard and put the smaller Lampkin at center. But it would be weird to move Kendall to guard since most of his experience has come at center and the Eagles could’ve kept Jurgens at center and put Kendall at guard previously. But, who knows. Also, Kendall apparently missed Wednesday’s practice, so his situation is something to continue to monitor. Mailata and Steen are definitely locked in at their spots. The rookie Bell is probably going to start at right tackle … but there’s a non-zero chance that veteran swing tackle (and former Jag!) Fred Johnson could factor in. Fred Johnson and Micah Morris are currently the only two backup blockers on the roster. The Eagles will probably look to call up some of their practice squad offensive linemen (John Ojukwu, Jake Majors, Kiran Amegadjie). Get ready for game day with SB Nation’s new app! SB Nation’s NEW game chat feature in the app is perfect for keeping the latest Jaguars updates and conversations at your fingertips. With a couple of clicks you can visit Dawgs By Nature and learn everything you need to know about this week’s opponent! Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Question 2: Through four weeks, Philadelphia’s offense has averaged 269.8 yards per game (29th) and 18.8 points per game (26th). Is it time to have a serious conversation about Jalen Hurts, or has he truly been dealt a poor hand of playcallers throughout his career? It’s beyond time to have a serious conversation with the entire offensive operation. Head coach, quarterback, offensive coordinator, the players. This isn’t just about one person. You don’t go 0/17 on third down over the last six quarters without collective failure. My criticism goes first and foremost to Nick Sirianni, who had to give up play-calling several games into his head coaching tenure back in 2021 because he was so bad at it. And while the Super Bowl-winning head coach has a track record of winning, it’s more than fair to question the extent to which he’s been driving this team’s success. I’d make the case that he’s greatly benefited from Howie Roseman’s personnel prowess and Vic Fangio’s mastermind defensive savvy. With the Eagles needing Sirianni to have answers on offense, the head coach hasn’t been able to provide any. That much has been apparent since the start of the 2025 season. This isn’t to absolve Hurts by any means. He deserves criticism as well. It’s pretty hard to win when your quarterback only has 68 net passing yards, which was the case in Week 4. But Hurts also played pretty well in the first two games of this season and even the first half of Week 3. The offense as a whole wasn’t functioning properly but Hurts was bailing that unit out by making big plays on third down. Not a great way to sustain success. So, if the offense only looked good at times this season because the QB played well in high-leverage situations, I can’t say it’s all his fault that it’s bad. Question 3: On the other side of the ball, Philadelphia’s defense has allowed 344.0 yards per game (21st) and 23.3 points per game (16th). What’s holding that unit back from being among the league’s best? Yeah, the defense has been a disappointment. Given the presence of Fangio and the talent on that side of the ball, expectations were very high. There was thought they’d be one of the best defense in the NFL, if not the very best. Clearly hasn’t been the case. A big reason why? The Eagles aren’t nearly as strong up front as we expected them to be. The highly-paid defensive line isn’t generating pressure at a high rate. Jalen Carter is playing with a cast on his hand that is neutering his ability to play at the top of his game. Elsewhere, Jihaad Campbell has been a downgrade from Nakobe Dean. Cooper DeJean had an uncharacteristically bad game in Week 1; he doesn’t seem to be totally healthy. The Eagles’ safety situation is a weak point. Tackling has been an issue. I think there’s hope for this unit yet. This isn’t the first time a Fangio defense had a slow start to a season. I think some of these players can and will play better. The Eagles also won’t have to go up against Ben Johnson, who seems to have Fangio’s number, every week. Will they be an awesome defense? Maybe not. But do they have the ability to make games winnable? Yes, although it’s hard to believe the offense will live up to their end of the bargain. Question 4: Who is an under-the-radar player Jaguars fans should know about before Sunday? Darius Cooper. With five receptions resulting in three touchdowns this season, he’s less under-the-radar than he used to be. But I’m guessing most Jags fans don’t know much about him. The skinny is that he was a star at Division I FCS Tarleton State, leading all college football wide receivers at every level (D1 FBS, D1 FCS, D2, D3) in total receiving yards and yards per route run before signing with the Eagles after not being selected in the 2025 NFL Draft. Cooper caught my eye in training camp practices, which led to me hyping him up prior to last year’s preseason games, where he also shined. Cooper didn’t play much as a rookie and he entered this season as a “dirty work” role guy who was mostly limited to special teams duty. But my calls for Cooper to have a bigger role were answered. He caught a game-winning touchdown pass in Week 2 and then took advantage of increased playing time with DeVonta Smith out in Week 4. Cooper actually played more snaps than 2026 first-round pick Makai Lemon against the Rams. Put simply, good things happen when Hurts throws the ball to Cooper. He can get open, he can make tough catches, he can block, he can contribute on special teams. He’s a nice player and he would’ve been more celebrated coming out of Week 4 had the Eagles not blown a 10-point fourth quarter lead to LA. Thank you for allowing me to…

title: Looking ahead to the rest of the Chiefs’ schedule after the bye
summary: It feels good to be back on top. Kansas City Chiefs fans got used to being the class of the AFC with quarterback Patrick Mahomes at the helm. Last season feels like an anomaly as the team starts this year 4-0 and sits atop the conference’s standings as the only undefeated team. That will hold […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images It feels good to be back on top. Kansas City Chiefs fans got used to being the class of the AFC with quarterback Patrick Mahomes at the helm. Last season feels like an anomaly as the team starts this year 4-0 and sits atop the conference’s standings as the only undefeated team. That will hold through the Week 5 bye, but the Chiefs can’t get comfortable with the hot start. A much tougher schedule awaits on the other side of the bye, starting with two AFC West matchups over three weeks, sandwiching a road trip to take on the defending champions. Week 6: vs. Los Angeles Chargers Week 7: at Seattle Seahawks Week 8: at Denver Broncos The Chiefs have an early lead in the AFC West, but imagine the cushion Kansas City could build by beating the Chargers and Broncos over the next month. Those will be the critical matchups here, while a road primetime game against Seattle is less crucial. It would be hard to be upset with a loss there if it is accompanied by victories against the division rivals in Weeks 6 and 8. Week 9: vs New York Jets Week 10: at Atlanta Falcons Week 11: vs. Arizona Cardinals This feels like the first three-game stretch of the second half of the season, even if the schedule no longer allows for a clean midway point. Four of the team’s division games would be behind them, and this stretch could test the Chiefs’ ability to stay locked in for the noon slate against desperate teams; the team’s least impressive performance this year was arguably the noon kickoff against the Miami Dolphins in Week 3. Week 12: at Buffalo Bill s Week 13: at Los Angeles Rams Week 14: at Cincinnati Bengals A Thanksgiving night game against the Bills is just the start of a stretch of playoff-preview-type matchups. This feels like the beginning of the “playoff push.” You can see certain aspects of the team, especially defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s unit, start to take shape for the remainder of the team’s run at Super Bowl LXI, and that could result in growing pains against contenders that turn into lessons learned later on in the postseason. Week 15: vs. New England Patriots Week 16: vs. San Francisco 49ers Week 17: at Los Angeles Week 18: vs. Las Vegas Raiders The final four-game stretch of Kansas City’s regular-season schedule features three home games and a road trip to the divisional foe currently on a path to a last-place finish this season. That could change, but overall, if the Chiefs stay in the hunt for a No. 1 seed by the time the holiday season arrives, Arrowhead Stadium could play a role in the team securing a postseason bye week and continuing to play in front of the Sea of Red.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Are the Chiefs’ offseason bets on defense paying off 4 games in?
summary: The offseason gave the Kansas City Chiefs fans plenty of reasons to ask what came next. Familiar faces departed, established defensive starters found new homes, and the Chiefs placed significant responsibility on players who had yet to take an NFL snap. Four games later, the Chiefs enter their bye week at 4-0. That makes the […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Arjoon/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images). | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The offseason gave the Kansas City Chiefs fans plenty of reasons to ask what came next. Familiar faces departed, established defensive starters found new homes, and the Chiefs placed significant responsibility on players who had yet to take an NFL snap. Four games later, the Chiefs enter their bye week at 4-0. That makes the changes easier to embrace, but an undefeated record does not automatically give every offseason decision an “A.” The better question is whether Kansas City improved the roles it needed to improve through outside additions and the development of players already on the roster — and whether the early production supports the risks Brett Veach took. We talked about the offensive changes yesterday . Let’s look on the defensive side: Secondary: A major gamble is showing encouraging returns Losing Trent McDuffie, Jaylen Watson, and Bryan Cook in the same offseason raised legitimate concerns. Kansas City responded with a combination of youth and experience: first-round cornerback Mansoor Delane, veteran safety Alohi Gilman, and the return of L’Jarius Sneed, alongside second-year cornerback Nohl Williams taking on a larger role. Delane has provided the most compelling early evidence. The sixth-overall pick intercepted Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix in the opener and has recorded 20 combined tackles and three passes defended across three appearances. His shoulder injury interrupted that debut and cost him the game against the Indianapolis Colts , making his availability part of the evaluation. His willingness to tackle is particularly encouraging. Delane recorded 10 combined tackles in each game against the Miami Dolphins and the Las Vegas Raiders . Our own Nate Christensen’s film review against the Raiders highlighted his ability to set the edge and prevent explosive runs, adding value beyond his coverage assignments. Williams belongs in that evaluation, too. Kansas City’s plan depended in part on developing a cornerback already in the building. Through four games, he has recorded 15 combined tackles, four passes defended and a sack. Those contributions deserve attention when grading how the Chiefs handled the departures of McDuffie and Watson. The offseason bet was to trust the previous year’s investment to take another step. Gilman, meanwhile, has recorded 17 combined tackles and a pass defended through four games. With Chamarri Conner making his season debut against Las Vegas, the safety rotation is still taking shape. There is enough here to feel better about the transition. There isn’t enough to declare that the Chiefs have fully replaced everything McDuffie, Watson, and Cook provided. Early grade: B Defensive front: Promising pieces, unfinished work The departures of Charles Omenihu, Mike Danna, Derrick Nnadi and Leo Chenal removed experience from several different defensive roles. Kansas City addressed the front by adding Khyiris Tonga and drafting Peter Woods and R Mason Thomas. Those moves should be evaluated together without pretending they were direct, player-for-player replacements. Chenal’s departure also put the spotlight on an in-house option: Jack Cochrane. Kansas City re-signed Cochrane in March, and he was listed as a defensive starter against Las Vegas alongside Nick Bolton and Drue Tranquill. His place in the lineup illustrates another part of the offseason plan: retaining a familiar player and trusting him at linebacker. That decision deserves its own evaluation as the season continues, including how the group handles the defensive and special-teams responsibilities Chenal left behind. Woods has recorded nine combined tackles and a pass defended through four games. Thomas has four combined tackles and one sack, which came in the season opener. Those totals do not justify calling either player a finished product. They also don’t tell the whole story. Against the Raiders, Thomas was credited with eight pressures, including five in the fourth quarter. That is meaningful evidence of disruption even though Thomas did not finish with a sack. The next step is turning those opportunities into more drive-changing plays. Woods must continue developing his influence inside, while Thomas needs to make his pressure production repeatable. The investment makes sense. The early results offer reasons for optimism, but this group still has more to prove than the backfield. Early grade: C+ An encouraging start, with more to prove My overall early offseason grade is a B+ . Walker remains my pick for the biggest addition, while finding a solid contributor at left tackle in undrafted rookie Benson represents another significant offseason win. Delane and Williams have provided encouraging returns at cornerback, and Thomas has shown why the Chiefs invested in his pass-rushing ability. On the departure side, Washington Commanders linebacker Leo Chenal is the player I believe Kansas City misses most, particularly in its base defense and on special teams. That’s why the overall grade remains a B+ : the Chiefs have made meaningful upgrades, but some of the roles left behind still need convincing answers. The remaining questions involve consistency, availability and whether the depth can handle a larger workload. The McDuffie trade also deserves patience. Kansas City received four draft picks, including the No. 29 selection used on Woods and a 2027 third-rounder. You can’t settle its full value after four games. For now, the Chiefs have won while introducing substantial change. The next stretch will reveal how much of that success their newcomers can sustain—and whether an encouraging offseason becomes the foundation for another postseason run.
author: Maurice Elston

title: The Top 5 moments of the Chiefs’ 2026 season so far
summary: The 2025 season just never felt right. The Kansas City Chiefs looked tired, undisciplined, and as if the rest of the NFL had caught up. The Chiefs lost their AFC West crown and missed the postseason for the first time since 2014. With the first four weeks of the 2026 season behind us and the […]
full_text: (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images The 2025 season just never felt right. The Kansas City Chiefs looked tired, undisciplined, and as if the rest of the NFL had caught up. The Chiefs lost their AFC West crown and missed the postseason for the first time since 2014. With the first four weeks of the 2026 season behind us and the Chiefs on bye, we can already say they’re fully back. We’ve seen special-teams blunders, division domination, an overtime win, and them playing down opponents we think they should easily beat—while still winning by two-plus scores. While the Chiefs have come out of the gate with some of the old and familiar, they’ve also evolved. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes has, for the first time in his career, the blessing of a rushing attack with the arrival of running back Kenneth Walker III. The running game threat has only helped the two-time league MVP, who’s found his deep ball again and appears no worse for wear in his return from the 2025 season-ending ACL and LCL repair. The defense has also shown flashes of speed and athleticism, which were lacking in recent seasons. Although it’s an early bye week, the Chiefs’ 4-0 start to the season has had no shortage of electric moments. In no particular order, here are the top five moments of the Chiefs’ 2026 season. Patrick Mahomes tells the world he is just fine Since Mahomes was injured last December, he has been working toward opening night of the 2026 season. Grueling months of rehab led to the Chiefs’ opening salvo against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football.” Fans were nervous; Mahomes had fully participated in training camp but hadn’t seen any live reps in the preseason. Everyone held their breath when, on the first drive of the game, Mahomes didn’t just drop back to pass in the red zone—but began to actually run with the football. Mahomes scored a rushing touchdown, not once, but twice (the first score called back due to penalty) for the first touchdown of the Chiefs’ season. Mahomes isn’t necessarily known as a running quarterback. However, when he runs with the ball, he has an uncanny ability to gain the necessary yards and be just a tick faster than the defender chasing him. After returning to the field for the first time since tearing his ACL and LCL, Mahomes looked like he hadn’t missed a beat. Kansas City’s unquestioned leader, the face of the NFL, and best player in the world—was back. Kenneth Walker III makes his KC debut There is no doubt the Chiefs made the best free agent signing of the offseason when they signed Walker, the Super Bowl LX MVP. Walker has been simply sensational for the Chiefs thus far. He is a running back weapon the Chiefs haven’t used since Jamaal Charles, and he has completely revitalized the Chiefs’ offense. After four weeks, Walker leads the NFL in rushing yards and is on pace to set the NFL record for rushing yards in a single season. Walker got off to a hot start and didn’t take long to make his presence known. In his Week 1 debut against the Broncos, Walker finished with 173 rushing yards and a touchdown, plus 3 receptions, including a receiving touchdown. It’s not just the final numbers that are impressive. It’s Walker’s fight and unwillingness to be tackled by the first defender that makes contact. Walker bullied the division rival Broncos all night—from the first possession to the final whistle. In the first series, Walker had seven rushing attempts—a statement from head coach Andy Reid and offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy that the Chiefs’ offense prioritized the run. He scored his rushing touchdown in the third quarter on a 4th-and-1 up the gut. He broke out to the outside and scampered for a 60-yard run for a touchdown. In that moment, the rest of the NFL had to wonder how they let Walker come to Kansas City. Mansoor Delane introduces himself to the NFL With cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson lost in the offseason, major question marks surrounded the Chiefs’ secondary. These questions led the Chiefs to trade up and draft cornerback Mansoor Delane with pick 6 overall out of LSU. Delane did not wait long to make an impression. On the Broncos’ first drive of the game, Delane read quarterback Bo Nix like a book, ran a route for wide receiver Courtland Sutton, and intercepted the pass. The rookie corner quickly flashed the skills the Chiefs valued in April. Unfortunately, Delane aggravated a shoulder injury on the play, which he battled throughout training camp and the preseason. He would go on to miss the rest of the Monday Night opener. Since returning to the field, Delane has continued to show amazing coverage skills and tackling ability. He should be a cornerstone for this Chiefs’ defense for years to come. The Chiefs still know how to win in clutch moments Week 2 was a 33-30 overtime thriller win over the Indianapolis Colts . The Colts have long been kryptonite for the Chiefs, and at times throughout the game it looked like it would be another disappointing outing. The game featured seven lead changes, and the overtime clock expired on kicker Harrison Butker’s game-winning 40-yard field goal. Overtime delivered drama in a classic Chiefs-Colts battle. After the Chiefs scored a field goal on their opening overtime possession, they thought they had the game in hand when wide receiver Laquon Treadwell fumbled after a deep reception. Upon replay, however, cornerback L’Jarius Sneed barely grazed Treadwell as he went to the ground. The Colts finished that drive with a field goal of their own, but the inevitable happened when the opponent gave Mahomes the ball with the game on the line. The Chiefs started the season 2-0, battle-tested, and reclaiming their clutch gene. Special teams steps up to help seal divisional win Week 4 renewed a classic AFC West rivalry as the Chiefs visited the revitalized Las Vegas Raiders. Both teams entered the game undefeated, with a chance to cement an early-season lead in the division. Late in the fourth quarter, wide receiver Tyquan Thornton who was having the game of his career, dislocated his ankle and was carted off the field. The Chiefs finished off the drive with a Walker rushing touchdown to take a 23-19 lead. On the ensuing kickoff, the much-maligned Chiefs special teams unit made a play the Chiefs needed to help seal the win. Linebacker Jeffrey Bassa punched the ball out of the returner’s hands, and the Chiefs recovered it, giving the offense the ball back near the red zone. On the next play, Walker sealed the deal with a 23-yard run to extend the lead and cement the Chiefs’ second divisional win of the season. The special teams play once again showed the Chiefs’ ability to come up big in the biggest moments and respond to adversity after their teammate’s serious injury. Agree with the list? What are some of your favorite moments from the young 2026 season? Let us know in the comments below.

title: Byron Young deserves more credit for the Rams’ elite pass rush
summary: It took an injury to Myles Garrett for Byron Young to finally get the praise that he has always deserved and not received as a pass rusher on the Los Angeles Rams. Without Garrett since Week 2, Young has been having his best season to date, including 2.5 sacks against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week […]
full_text: It took an injury to Myles Garrett for Byron Young to finally get the praise that he has always deserved and not received as a pass rusher on the Los Angeles Rams. Without Garrett since Week 2, Young has been having his best season to date, including 2.5 sacks against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 3 to place him among the leaders in the NFL. Young has never received ample credit for his success so far with the Rams, but that could change based on his early-season trajectory. Could Young be even better when Garrett is able to return from injured reserve? He’s always in someone’s shadow Young was drafted in the third round of the 2023 NFL Draft. He had as clear of a path to playing time as you can have for a mid-round pick and joined Aaron Donald for his final season. But when Young performed well as a rookie, his success was mostly credited to the attention opposing offenses paid to Donald. Then Donald retired. The Rams immediately drafted Jared Verse to replace their franchise star in the aggregate. Young stepped from one shadow to the next. This past offseason the Rams swapped Verse for Myles Garrett. Adding the best defensive player in football puts everyone else in the shadows, except for MVP quarterback Matthew Stafford. But Garrett has yet to play a healthy game in Los Angeles. Young is quietly putting together the best season of his career yet. It’s time to shine the spotlight on Byron Young. He’s an elite EDGE rusher in 2026. According to Pro Football Focus (PFF), Young ranks sixth among all EDGE defenders in total pressures with 21. He’s notched four sacks in as many games. Those in front of him are the usual suspects and good company to be in: Aidan Hutchinson – 29 pressures on 182 rushes Greg Rousseau – 29 on 140 Dallas Turner – 28 on 127 Maxx Crosby – 25 on 136 Will Anderson – 25 on 138 Byron Young – 21 on 103 Notice anything out of sorts from the above list? Young makes the top six with 24 fewer rushes than the next-lowest player on the list. He has 79 fewer rushes than pressure leader Aidan Hutchinson. Byron Young & the @rams held the Eagles to 0-12 on third downs in big road win in Philly #Ramshouse pic.twitter.com/nGuJwpoNWE — Timothy Parker (@TimothyParkertv) October 4, 2026 On a percentage basis, Young is creating pressures at the third-highest rate among EDGE rushers with at least 91 reps: Dallas Turner: 22.0% Greg Rousseau: 20.7% Byron Young: 20.4% Maxx Crosby: 18.4% Will Anderson: 18.1% PFF also has a metric called pass rush productivity that quantifies how often rushers pressure, hurry, sack, or hit opposing quarterbacks compared to frequency in opportunity. Young is also third in this metric behind Turner and Rousseau. And Young is accomplishing this level of efficiency despite a slow start. He notched only two pressures in the season opener against the 49ers. Since, he posted five pressures versus the Giants and seven against each of the Broncos and Eagles. The sacks have come in bunches. He earned one in the Giants game and three against the Eagles (PFF does not track half sacks). Players with multiple sacks in week 4: Byron Young – 2.5 Zach Sieler – 2.0 Dallas Turner – 2.0 pic.twitter.com/h6VHzLu9n2 — NFL Stats (@NFL_Stats) October 6, 2026 It’s time to give Byron Young his flowers. He belongs in the conversation as one of football’s best and most efficient pass rushers. He’s doing it without Myles Garrett. The defense—despite already being one of the NFL’s best units—should take another step forward once they are working in tandem.
author: JB Scott

title: Les Snead’s next Rams trade faces two major obstacles
summary: The NFL trade deadline is a month away but the usually-active general manager Les Snead probably can’t do much else to improve the Los Angeles Rams after an expensive offseason. It would be a stunner if the Rams were able to add any veteran players to their roster because the franchise is dead last in […]
full_text: The NFL trade deadline is a month away but the usually-active general manager Les Snead probably can’t do much else to improve the Los Angeles Rams after an expensive offseason. It would be a stunner if the Rams were able to add any veteran players to their roster because the franchise is dead last in the NFL in cap space. According to OvertheCap.com, the Rams have $1.058 million in 2026 cap space, the least amount in the league . The Carolina Panthers are the only under team with less than $3 million in cap space. Does Snead have any more tricks under his cap? How Rams could still make space The Rams have several players who have large base salaries, making it possible to maneuver around the cap with their contracts: Davante Adams makes $18 million Matthew Stafford makes $16 million A.J. Jackson makes $18.9 million Kevin Dotson makes $8 million Kyren Williams makes $5.5 million The Rams have options to restructure four of those five players. The exception is Dotson because he’s a 2027 free agent, so Snead’s only opportunity there would be a contract extension. However, do the Rams want to double-down on players like Adams, Stafford, Jackson, and Williams? I wouldn’t. And which players would be worth it? Trade rumor candidates The biggest headline-grabbing move is receiver Marvin Harrison Jr., but a) he plays with a division rival and b) he’s just not very good. Would Harrison be useful to Stafford? Possibly. But fans and the media often tend to overrate players who were simply overrated in the draft. Harrison should not have been an early first-round pick, or even a first-round pick at all. Not based on how he’s playing. Marvin Harrison Jr. on trade rumors: “I pay it no mind. I'm only focused on Detroit, helping the Cardinals win football games at the moment.” pic.twitter.com/omHCyomKrq — PHNX Cardinals (@PHNX_Cardinals) October 8, 2026 It’s the same story with Brian Thomas, Jr. He has been average since his rookie season, if not bad. Is Thomas going to expect an extension from the team that trades for him regardless of him only having 105 yards this year? We saw it with Jerry Jeudy when he was traded to the Browns. You’d be amazed at what a team would pay for an overrated first-round pick. PFF listed 15 possible trade candidates this week , including both of those receivers. And even being on rookie contracts, the Rams couldn’t afford either of them right now because they only have $1 million in cap space. They’d have to make a big cap-saving move to afford any player. PFF also mentions defensive tackle Daron Payne. It might be a position of need for the Rams, but why is Payne available—if he even is? It’s been a quiet career for Payne since his Pro Bowl season in 2022. Daron Payne is now a likely trade candidate at the deadline. The Commanders are unlikely to re-sign their premier defensive tackle, who is an upcoming free agent. Washington could net a Day 2 pick in 2027 for Payne. pic.twitter.com/SpUDN3W189 — Evan Sidery (@esidery) October 8, 2026 Plus, the Rams don’t have many picks to trade. Rams draft picks The Rams have already traded for Myles Garrett, leaving them without a first-round pick in 2027. They also gave up a second in 2028 and a third (that could become a first) in 2029. Snead also traded a third-round pick in 2027 for Trent McDuffie. And L.A. doesn’t have next year’s seventh because of Tre’Davious White. The Rams don’t have three of their original picks next year and they don’t have any compensatory picks coming to them in 2027 either, according to OTC . You think the Rams should trade for a linebacker or a receiver? With what? How do they afford him? Is that one player really going to be the difference for L.A., especially if all the acquisitions Snead already made aren’t enough? If the Rams needed help this year in an area where they are obviously deficient—maybe that’s something Snead should have addressed with his first-round pick. The help probably won’t come at the trade deadline.
author: Kenneth Arthur

title: Sean McVay has a running game tendency the Bills are built to stop
summary: Rams head coach Sean McVay has a favorite run-blocking scheme and it has delivered many of Kyren Williams’ most explosive plays this season, but on Monday night the coach faces a Buffalo Bills defense that has yet to be exploited by it. What happens when McVay’s “man” meets Jim Leonhard’s “wall”? The Rams have called […]
full_text: Rams head coach Sean McVay has a favorite run-blocking scheme and it has delivered many of Kyren Williams’ most explosive plays this season, but on Monday night the coach faces a Buffalo Bills defense that has yet to be exploited by it. What happens when McVay’s “man” meets Jim Leonhard’s “wall”? The Rams have called man-concept run-blocking calls 12.8 times per game, according to Next Gen Stats, which is the most of any offense in the NFL. That means that McVay likes his offensive linemen to have specific blocking assignments on defense and he uses pulling guards to create a running lane for Williams. As opposed to a zone-blocking scheme, in which the offensive linemen block an area — not a man — and Williams reads the blocks to pick a lane or area to run through. In other words, McVay likes to make the job as easy as possible for his running backs and it’s worked out well this season: The Rams have a 47.1% rushing success rate on man-concept runs (8th) 64% of L.A.’s explosive runs have come out of man-concept runs McVay likes to run man-blocking concepts. The concepts help the Rams offense score points and win games. That’s good. The bad? The Buffalo Bills are one of only three defenses in the NFL to not allow an explosive run (10+ yards) against a man-concept carry, among those teams that have faced at least 15 such calls. What will happen to the Rams offense if the Bills are successful at stopping L.A.’s rushing attempts out of man-concept carries? Bills underrated defensive stalwarts The big name on Buffalo’s defensive line is edge rusher Gregory Rosseau because he leads in the league in sacks with 6.5. And he is a potential problem for L.A.‘s offense. However, don’t underestimate the other guys when it comes to the run. Defensive tackle DeWayne Carter The 2024 third-round pick has been cited as an elite run-stuffer this season. You don’t know the name yet, but you probably will in a year or two. DeWayne Carter is #1 in the NFL in run stop win rate with 22 wins in 39 plays (56%) He's having quite the season — Kevin Massare (@KevinMassare) September 29, 2026 Linebacker Terrel Bernard Although he’s been called extremely slow by Bills fans, Bernard is helping Buffalo’s run defense with plays like this. Physical and willing play at the point of attack from Bradley Chubb (9), Terrel Bernard (8), and Dorian Williams (42) pic.twitter.com/TMbLJ1eJEy — Anthony Cover 1 (@Pro__Ant) October 5, 2026 One player that the Bills probably won’t have is defensive tackle Ed Oliver. He left last week’s game against the Patriots and did not return, but head coach Joe Brady doesn’t think it’s a long-term injury. Jim Leonhard’s first season The former NFL safety is in his first season as a defensive coordinator at this level. He was in that role for six years at Wisconsin and spent the last two years helping Vance Joseph’s Denver Broncos. Now he’s the DC for the Bills and he’s not off to an ideal start. The Bills rank 25th in points allowed and 27th in yards allowed. Ranking 15th in yards per carry allowed doesn’t seem that great, but considering that Buffalo’s pass defense is 27th, it could mean that teams are just reluctant to run against the Bills. Why not pass? We should see a lot of Matthew Stafford throwing to Puka Nacua and Davante Adams on Monday. But does that work as well without Williams and a solid run game? If the Rams build a lead with the passing game, can they hold it with the running game? Will McVay actually go to the run and stick to it? That’s a question that’s on the minds of both coaching staffs right now. And all I’ve got to say is … Man.
author: Kenneth Arthur

title: Rams-Bills: Recent MVPs set for prime time spotlight
summary: Monday Night Football delivers a matchup worthy of the spotlight as the Los Angeles Rams welcome the Buffalo Bills to SoFi Stadium. With two legitimate Super Bowl contenders colliding in Week 5, the game could provide an early measuring stick for two teams with championship aspirations. At the center of the stage are two quarterbacks […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 08: Matthew Stafford #9 of the Los Angeles Rams talks with Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills after the Rams defeated the Bills, 44-42, at SoFi Stadium on December 08, 2024 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images) | Getty Images Monday Night Football delivers a matchup worthy of the spotlight as the Los Angeles Rams welcome the Buffalo Bills to SoFi Stadium. With two legitimate Super Bowl contenders colliding in Week 5, the game could provide an early measuring stick for two teams with championship aspirations. At the center of the stage are two quarterbacks who have already experienced the highest individual honor in the sport. Matthew Stafford and Josh Allen bring contrasting styles, tremendous experience and the ability to take over a game when the pressure rises. But this matchup will be decided by much more than the players under center. The battle in the trenches, the collection of playmakers surrounding each quarterback, and the ability of each defense to contain explosive plays could ultimately determine which team controls the night. With both offenses capable of creating problems in multiple ways, execution in critical situations should separate these two heavyweights. QUARTERBACK Matthew Stafford simply has not been the quarterback he was in 2025. Has he been bad? No. I don’t think the 6 touchdowns to 6 interceptions tells a full story of his 2026 season. He is top 5 in the NFL in passing yards (4th, 1189 yards). The defenses he has faced so far: San Francisco (3rd), New York Giants (8th), Philadelphia (16th), and Denver (17th), in terms of points allowed per game. He’s facing stiff competition. But he has definitely missed some throws, particularly in the SF and PHI games. Josh Allen is an MVP front runner right now. If you look on ESPN , he is projected for 26 passing and 30(!) rushing touchdowns. He’s definitely playing better football right now than Matthew Stafford, but the two are the most recent NFL MVPs, so this could come down to who has the ball last. SKILL PLAYERS Puka Nacua is back for the Rams and that is a huge factor. The Rams edge over the Bills is not by much though. With Terrance Ferguson out, it looks like LA is relying on Kyren Williams, Tyler Higbee, and Davante Adams. The Bills have James Cook, DJ Moore, and an improving Keon Coleman. It’s better than what Allen has had in recent years. OFFENSIVE LINE If the Rams have an edge here its also not by much. Coleman Shelton continues to be an underrated asset for the offensive line. The Bills have two big offensive tackles that could give Josiah Stewart, Byron Young, and Wesley Bailey issues. The Bills interior line will be the question mark. Will their size win? Or will LA’s speed and explosiveness off the ball be too much? DEFENSIVE LINE Aaron Donald should return in Week 5 according to Sean McVay. That will add more firepower to the Rams defensive line featuring Kobie Turner, Poona Ford, Braden Fiske, Tyler Davis, and Ty Hamilton. The Bills have a strong interior player in Deone Walker but Ed Oliver has not evolved into the player he should have been when selected 9th overall in the 2019 NFL Draft. SECONDARY The Rams secondary has been worth every penny . Trent McDuffie and Quentin Lake have been two of the best in the NFL. Kam Curl is playing solid football and came up with a huge stop in Week 4. Kam Kinchens is flying around. There’s a lot to like about this group and it doesn’t even have Jaylen Watson fully healthy. SPECIAL TEAMS Doubt this will change all season. Rams always find a way to have one special teams blunder per game.

title: Are the Rams the best 2-2 team in the NFL?
summary: The Los Angeles Rams are a solid, but unspectacular 2-2 through the first quarter of the season, which is similar to many NFC playoff hopefuls. Not all 2-2 records are created equally, as Rams and Panthers fans likely feel much differently about the start compared to Eagles and Packers fans. Things have certainly changed for […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams are a solid, but unspectacular 2-2 through the first quarter of the season, which is similar to many NFC playoff hopefuls. Not all 2-2 records are created equally, as Rams and Panthers fans likely feel much differently about the start compared to Eagles and Packers fans. Things have certainly changed for several of these teams when I last did a panic meter for them after Week 1. Here is the panic meter for seven playoff-hopeful 2-2 NFC squads heading into Week 5. Los Angeles Rams Week 4 Result: Beat Eagles 24-20 The Rams haven’t played a complete game all year to date. That was a key issue for them around the same time last season before they went on a run. LA’s talent level is there, and has always been there. So now is the time to play like the contender they were expected to be. There are a few things to fix, including the team’s unwillingness to run the ball more and putting too much on Matthew Stafford’s plate. Defensively, the Rams played great, yet the anemic Eagles aren’t the greatest measure of anything. Right now, panic shouldn’t be on the minds of the fanbase, but simply put, Los Angeles must string together a complete game and do it soon. Panic Meter: There still isn’t much reason to panic now, especially with several injured players set to return in the coming weeks. Losing to the Bills on Monday night might change that, however. Philadelphia Eagles Week 4 Result: Lost 24-20 to Rams (so nice, I had to say it twice) Oh boy, that was a horrible loss to the Rams on Sunday. Okay, I had to say it again, but that was for the last time, I swear! The Eagles have a putrid offense and haven’t converted a third down since the first half of their game against Da Bears. Is Nick Sirianni sleeping on the job or what? They’re also set to be without several stars in this weekend’s game against the Jaguars in London. The Eagles could be without 6 starters on offense Sunday in London. DeVonta, Saquon, Dallas, Landon, Lane, Cam So Jacksonville is now a -6.5 point favorite on Sunday at 9:30 AM eastern time pic.twitter.com/7VlyD1PuVS — John Clark (@JClarkNBCS) October 6, 2026 Holy hell. Have fun with that, Jalen Hurts! Vic Fangio’s defense has its work cut out this week. Many fans have longed to see Philadelphia go down the crapper, and it would appear that they might get their wish. Panic Meter: Panic a lot, and panic often Eagles fans. You might be as the kids say, cooked. Dallas Cowboys Week 4 Result: Beat Texans 34-30 The Cowboys’ defense still hasn’t shown any improvement compared to the last time I did a panic meter post. Dallas has given up at least 30 points in two games, and nearly a third in the season opener against the Giants. If it’s any consolation, though, they might not have the worst D in Texas — sorry Houston. Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb’s chemistry remains unmatched, as evidenced by the All-Pro Lamb popping off for 189 receiving yards in Week 4. Look, the Cowboys are unlikely to get much better on defense, but if their offense manages to reach the end zone in bunches every week, it’s not going to matter in the long run. Panic Meter: Compared to Week 1, the panic has lessened quite a bit in Dallas. With the Eagles freefalling, the Cowboys can definitely take advantage and reclaim the NFC East. Carolina Panthers Week 4 Result: Beat Lions 32-26 What’s there really to panic about for the reigning NFC South champs? Yes, they’ve suffered some bad defensive injuries to begin the season. Yet, Bryce Young and second-year wideout Tetairoa McMillan showed on Sunday night that something special might be blossoming in Charlotte. The @Panthers stars showed out on SNF ⭐️ pic.twitter.com/NjAwlEN3sf — NFL (@NFL) October 5, 2026 Young’s continued growth has been a joy to see — as long as it doesn’t come at the Rams’ expense. He’s finally showing what made him so special coming out of Alabama and the best might be yet to come. Carolina will need it if it hopes to defend their division crown. Panic Meter: Like I said, there’s nothing to panic over for now. They keep up this level of play and a second straight NFC South title is in their sights. Atlanta Falcons Week 4 Result: Beat Saints 45-24 After looking like one of the worst offenses to ever grace the gridiron through the first two games, the Falcons have piled up the points in back-to-back blowout wins over the Packers and Saints in primetime. Michael Penix returning has certainly helped matters. View this post on Instagram All-Pro running back Bijan Robinson is an absolute cheat code, and the engine that keeps this team running. Anyone, and I mean anyone with a pulse can win the NFC South. Why not Atlanta? The Falcons won’t maintain this dominant pace for the rest of the season, of course, However, if their playmakers continue to perform at a high level, they can hang with anyone in the league. Panic Meter: Just copy and paste what I said about the Panthers. Atlanta is going to be just fine if Penix stays healthy. Green Bay Packers Week 4 Result: Beat Buccaneers 17-10 Green Bay returned to the win column Sunday, albeit in a painfully underwhelming win over the Baker Mayfield-less Bucs. Packers fans haven’t endured much mediocrity since winning the Super Bowl in 2010. However, this is likely their worst team in quite some time. Their defense isn’t great, and performing well against a bad Tampa Bay team isn’t going to cut it. The offense remains painfully inconsistent, even after slapping a few band-aids to fix its glaring offensive line problem. Keep in mind, this wasn’t even the guantlet of their schedule, which is set to come up. Coming out of these first few games at .500 is incredibly disappointing and shouldn’t sit right with anyone in cheesehead nation. Matt LaFleur will be fighting for his job the rest of the way. Panic Meter: The Bears being a 2.5-point favorite at FanDuel Sportsbook despite starting a backup quarterback at Lambeau Field should tell you everything you need to know. Packers fans should already be bracing for the worst yet to come. Detroit Lions Week 4 Result: Lost 32-26 to Panthers Welp, the Lions have fallen back to earth after making their long-awaited return to contention. Why is Detroit not haven’t the best season despite fielding a quality offense? Let me drop this here: The Detroit Lions defensive rankings in the NFL through Week 4: 32nd in PPG Allowed 32nd in YPG Allowed 32nd Passing YPG Allowed 32nd in 3rd Down Def (52.8%) 32nd in 4th Down Def (5/5 allowed) Most First Downs Allowed (113 – next highest 96) Changes NEED to be made. #OnePride pic.twitter.com/5lCEprkqKW — Booner (@boonersports) October 5, 2026 The offense can only do so much when the defense cannot stop a nosebleed. Plus, what happens when the offense has a bad game? Detroit’s unit isn’t good enough to account for that. It’s unrealistic to expect the Lions will be in a shootout every week, but at this rate, they might be. Panic Meter: The state of the Lions’ defense is enough reason to sound the alarms. Hope you enjoyed the ride of winning seasons the last few years, One Pride. It’s going to be a bumpy ride the rest of the way.
