title: Eagles-Jaguars Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Week 5 enemy
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles are crossing the pond to take on the Jacksonville Jaguars in London this weekend. The flight to the United Kingdom won’t be the only turbulence the Birds are experiencing with Lane Johnson retiring and Cam Jurgens getting traded. In order to preview this Week 5 matchup, I reached out to our enemies […]
full_text: METAIRIE, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 13: Liam Coen head coach of the Jacksonville Jaguars speaks to media after a joint practice at Ochsner Sports Performance Center on August 13, 2026 in Metairie, Louisiana. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles are crossing the pond to take on the Jacksonville Jaguars in London this weekend. The flight to the United Kingdom won’t be the only turbulence the Birds are experiencing with Lane Johnson retiring and Cam Jurgens getting traded. In order to preview this Week 5 matchup, I reached out to our enemies over at Big Cat Country . The gracious Gus Logue kindly took the time to answer my questions about this upcoming battle. Let’s take a look at the answers. [For my answers to Gus’s questions about the Eagles, check out BCC.] 1 – The Jags are 16-5 in the Liam Coen era. What’s he done to turn this team around since Super Bowl LII champion Doug Pederson was fired? When Coen was hired, the thought in Jacksonville was, “He seems to have the goods as a playcaller. But can he also be a culture-setter?” 18 months later, the answer is a resounding yes. Look no further than Jacksonville’s latest victory: a gritty five-point win in Cincinnati. The Bengals may not be juggernauts, but the last time the Jaguars played at their stadium (Week 2 last season), Jake Browning led a stunning second-half comeback to steal the dub. “Winning ain’t easy in this league,” Coen told the locker room after getting redemption this past week. “Do we have to clean sh*t up? Absolutely. But guess what? Our culture prevailed. Our f*cking toughness prevailed … The last time we were in this locker room, in a similar type situation, it wasn’t a great feeling, right? Talk about growth. Talk about us as a unit, us as an organization, what the f*ck we’re building. That’s what I’m proud of.” Through the first half of last season, the Coen experience was mostly encouraging, but still had its ups and downs. Then the Jaguars allowed another backup AFC quarterback to complete a second-half comeback, this time Davis Mills in Houston in Week 10. Coen had talked a whole bunch about responding to adversity, so after Jacksonville crumbled against a division opponent, everyone in town wondered how the Jaguars would respond. They rattled off 8 straight wins to clinch the division and host a playoff game. They came up just short against Josh Allen’s Bills in the Wild Card Round, but that loss must’ve left an awful taste in their mouth, because they’ve been the NFL’s second-best team (behind only the 49ers) in terms of point differential, DVOA, and ESPN’s FPI this season. We’re not wondering anymore. The relationship between Coen and Trevor Lawrence is as strong as we could’ve hoped for. They look like one of the very best playcaller/quarterback duos in the league; one that could carry a team to the playoffs. And Coen has done an outstanding job building his staff; expect defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile to become a head coach in the next year or two. But the connection between Coen and his entire football team has been better than we in Duval County ever imagined. The greatest leaders in franchise history are him and Tom Coughlin, full stop. I suppose that’s a bit of a self-own regarding Jacksonville’s poor coaching history, but you get my point. Coen isn’t just another playcalling wiz who used to work for Sean McVay. He’s one of the best all-around coaches in the NFL right now. 2 – Anthony Campanile’s defense has allowed the second-fewest points in the NFL this season. What makes that unit so good? Run defense! Everyone loooooves to talk about offenses getting in heavier personnel and under-center formations and bunched alignments and pulling guards and other schematic tweaks, all to boost efficiency against defenses with 2-high safety structures that have been molded by Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan to stop outside zone and explosive passes out of 3-WR sets. So I’m excited to talk about Jacksonville’s run defense, which Campanile has renovated into an impenetrable fortress. The Jaguars have been great against the run for years, largely thanks to their Big 4. Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker have a case as the best run-stuffing EDGE duo in the league; they contain the perimeter and funnel runs inside to nose tackle DaVon Hamilton and linebacker Foye Oluokun, who are poster children of “players who would get more love in a bigger market.” Those four players are pillars of the run defense, and other front seven defenders like Arik Armstead, Matt Dickerson, Danny Striggow, Dennis Gardeck, and Ventrell Miller have been balling out more recently as well. A few years ago, Jacksonville’s defensive motto was, “Stop the run, then we can all have fun.” If they stop the run on early downs, they can have fun on late downs by pinning their ears back and rushing the opposing quarterback. The Jaguars did have a great run defense that forced opponents into 3rd-and-long situations, but they didn’t quite have the horses to consistently get the offense off the field. Under Campanile, their defensive philosophy is “Stop the run, limit explosives, and create takeaways.” The stable is now stocked. With the collection of defenders listed above, plus an overhauled secondary that suddenly features a coverage-tilting cornerback in Travis Hunter, the Jaguars have the horses. Their defense has not allowed a single rusher to reach 75 yards on the ground in 22 games (the fourth-best streak of any team in the Super Bowl era). They rank first in interceptions (28) and tied for first in takeaways (39) since the start of last season, with a takeaway in 10 straight games. They could do a better job limiting explosive passes, but DANG, are they checking the other two boxes emphatically. While Campanile has had more talent at his disposal than previous Jaguars defensive coordinators, he deserves credit for taking the run defense from “very good” to “historically good” and especially for proving that turnovers aren’t completely dependent on luck. They actually can be manufactured with good coaching and diabolical playcalling. When opposing offenses get into 3rd-and-long situations, Campanile leans on his coaching roots by deploying Fangio-like coverage structures with Flores-like pressure packages. He has out-game-planned the vast majority of offensive coordinators he’s faced. Like Coen, he’s been as good of a playcaller AND culture-builder as we could have hoped. Remember the name. 3 – The Eagles and Jags don’t play very often. Who are some of the under-the-radar players that we should keep an eye out for? I’ll offer one name on each side of the ball. On offense, keep an eye out for rookie receiver Josh Cameron. He had an eye-popping offseason, from rookie minicamp to training camp to the preseason, and now — despite the Jaguars seemingly having a strong starting trio of wideouts — his blocking prowess and strong hands have earned him a part-time role in the regular season. The Baylor product has played 19, 10, 23, and 22 snaps through the first month. Brian Thomas Jr. is losing snaps to him. Brian Thomas Jr.! The guy we believed to be Diet Randy! But Cameron has made the most of his playing time, as he’s delivered tough blocks in the run game and crazy catches in the redzone . The guy can play some football. On defense, keep an eye out for second-year safety Rayuan Lane III. The Navy man will be thrust into action after Eric Murray (concussion) and Caleb Ransaw (knee) got banged up last week. Ransaw played 33, 7, and 19 defensive snaps through the first three weeks as Jacksonville’s No. 3 safety, so with him now on injured reserve, Lane will at least step into a role in dime personnel packages. But with Murray in jeopardy of missing Week 5 after missing practice Wednesday, Lane is probably in line to start against Philadelphia. He fell to the 200th pick last year because he isn’t a high-caliber athlete (by NFL standards), but as he showed last week when he made…

title: Eagles News: Cam Jurgens trade grades
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! The Ravens clearly have confidence that Cam Jurgens is going to be a good player for them, or else they wouldn’t have traded a 2028 second-round pick to acquire him. That’s interesting to see. Not saying they’re flawless but they’re not […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 11: Cam Jurgens #51 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on before the NFC Wild Card Playoff game against the San Francisco 49ers at Lincoln Financial Field on January 11, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! The Ravens clearly have confidence that Cam Jurgens is going to be a good player for them, or else they wouldn’t have traded a 2028 second-round pick to acquire him. That’s interesting to see. Not saying they’re flawless but they’re not dumb organization. Maybe the compensation just came to their desperation with no real viable alternatives. In any case, Howie Roseman did well to get a 2028 second-round pick for him. While I don’t think this trade signals the Eagles throwing in the towel on the 2026 season, I do think they could very well be sellers ahead of the deadline if the struggles continue. The Eagles might need something of a reset as opposed to trying to cling on to the remnants of a very successful stretch in franchise history. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … NFL trade deadline grades: Cam Jurgens to Ravens, Joey Porter Jr. to Cowboys – ESPN Ravens grade: D+ … Eagles grade: A … The Ravens are surrendering a second-round pick (plus a swap of fifth- and seventh-round picks) for the right to pay a non-premium position player market price after this season. Jurgens is due a fully guaranteed $16 million next year. He’s due $17 million (non-guaranteed) in 2028 and 2029. Jurgens’ $17 million average per year for the duration of his contract makes him the fourth-highest-paid center in the league, behind only Linderbaum, Creed Humphrey and Aaron Brewer, per OverTheCap.com. By comparison, Connor McGovern, who had better numbers than Jurgens last season, makes a little over $13 million per year. One saving grace for Baltimore is that Jurgens’ salary is cheap this season. The Eagles have already paid Jurgens’ option bonus, so the Ravens should be on the hook for only the remaining portion of his $1.2 million base salary. For the Eagles, the loss of Jurgens is the latest blow to an offensive line that is already down Dickerson and recently retired tackle Lane Johnson. Jurgens hadn’t played well at guard, but surely they saw him as their long-term center. Drew Kendall, who has played center after Jurgens’ shift, has been below average in both pass and run block win rate this season. But the Eagles seemed to believe this was a price too good to pass up. I understand that the Ravens rightfully believe they are Super Bowl contenders, probably want Ioane to stay and develop at guard and thought they needed to fill their gap at center. Making a trade before the deadline to fix that issue makes sense. But almost certainly there would have been cheaper options out there than this. And the timing is odd, considering that Jurgens is currently in concussion protocol and not expected to play Sunday. So it seems like the Eagles sensed Baltimore’s desperation and squeezed an overpay out of the Ravens. NFL trade grades: Evaluating every deal made ahead of the 2026 deadline – NFL.com EAGLES GRADE: A-. We should start with the obvious: The two-time Pro Bowler was available for a reason, especially after the same offensive line saw a future Hall of Famer Lane Johnson retire the day prior. Jurgens is currently a Pro Bowler in name only. After battling through a back injury in 2024 to help the Eagles net a Super Bowl ring, Jurgens has not been the same player. He struggled through last season and has been a liability through four games this year. His pass blocking has never been otherworldly, but it’s particularly crumbled after he was asked to move to left guard the past three weeks. Blame the previous injuries or the ill fit in the Eagles’ new blocking scheme, but Jurgens has been borderline unplayable the past few weeks. Drew Kendall played better than Jurgens at center in Sean Mannion’s scheme, so a move back wasn’t in the cards. It got so bad that Nick Sirianni was fending off questions about potentially benching the guard. Instead, Philly shipped him out of town. We know that Howie Roseman doesn’t care what year he gets his picks — famously saying a first-round pick is a first-round pick regarding the A.J. Brown trade this offseason when Philly netted a ’28 first. However, we can dock him ever so slightly for delayed satisfaction. Otherwise, getting a second-rounder for a struggling player who was not a fit is a home run. In the short term, the Eagles offensive line is in flux, with Willie Lampkin in line to take over at guard. The hope is that Landon Dickerson returns to form when he eventually comes off injured reserve. The trade is jarring coming right after Johnson’s retirement, but getting a significant draft pick back for a player who was on the verge of being benched makes sense. Philly is now loaded in the 2028 draft with two firsts and two seconds. Ravens trade for Eagles Pro Bowl center Cam Jurgens – Baltimore Beatdown Jurgens has struggled in 2026. He was playing left guard following an injury to Landon Dickerson in a struggling offense that does not fit his skill set. He did play one game at center this season where he allowed zero pressures, indicating he could show improvements in Baltimore. The Ravens are planning on moving Jurgens to his natural position, and hopefully coaching from Dwayne Ledford will help Jurgens get back to his peak. He is an excellent fit to lead Derrick Henry in Declan Doyle’s wide zone scheme. Similar to former Ravens center Tyler Linderbaum, Jurgens will need help in pass protection, but he should not struggle as much as Jovaughn Gwyn. Snapping should not be an issue, either. Is the Nick Sirianni era already over? – BGN Maybe the Eagles circle the wagons and start to turn things around. The unintentional accelerated offensive line replacement might improve the situation as the season progresses. Maybe the leaders of the team, who have previously shown the ability to bounce back, find it again. This team is trending down, but they haven’t yet sunk. There is still time to bail enough water out. Or maybe they are headed to rock bottom. The Eagles offense has been built on the line, it has fallen apart. The defense is less than the sum of its parts. A depleted roster, one that wasn’t nearly as good as originally thought, a limping defense, and a broken offense. These are all key ingredients of the end of an era. 5 Questions with Bleeding Green Nation: Do the Lane Johnson-less Eagles stand a chance? – Big Cat Country As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 5, we exchanged questions with Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation to learn more about the opposing side. NFL survivor picks, strategy: Week 5 safe, value, and trap options – SB Nation Trap pick — Jaguars (-7) over Eagles. The Eagles will be without both Saquon Barkley and Tank Bigsby. With DeVonta Smith also questionable for Sunday, it’s easy to see why people will be on the Jaguars this weekend. It’s a London game, so that raises all sorts of red flags taking the favorite. Lane Retires & Tommy Update – Iggles Blitz Lane has been a great Eagle. He helped the team get to three Super Bowls and win two of them. Him walking away early doesn’t diminish any of what he’s accomplished. I hope most people aren’t mad at him. He has to focus on himself and his family before football. I’ve told this story a few times, but it bears repeating. I watched Oklahoma play UTEP early in 2012. The announcers talked about this former QB was now playing LT. That fascinated me so I wrote his name down as a player to study. I watched him in that game and he impressed me. I followed him all season and he continued to impress. Lane went to the Combine and had one of the best workouts of all time. Would he last to pick 4 in the 2013 draft? Andy Reid did us a…

Elliott will remain on the reserve/injured list for the time being. Pittsburgh has 21 days to officially activate Elliott to the active roster or his season is over. The Steelers have relied heavily on Rayshawn Jenkins and rookie seventh-round pick Robert Spears-Jennings in Elliott’s absence, which has led to significant struggles on the back end. The Steelers signed Elliott ahead of the 2024 season to a two-year deal. In June, 2025, Pittsburgh and Elliott agreed to a two-year extension, keeping him with the Steelers through the 2027 season. He missed 12 games in 2025 and has missed the team’s first four games after being placed on IR. He has two interceptions and three forced fumbles as a Steeler. title: Steelers-Colts preview: What Indianapolis will throw at Pittsburgh
summary: The Steelers are headed into Week 5 fresh off a frustrating loss to the Cleveland Browns in which their division rival tried everything it could to give the game away. Deshaun Watson went cold in the second half, and the Browns had 14 penalties for 88 yards, but the Steelers failed to capitalize and fell […]
full_text: (Photo by Alex Pantling/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Steelers are headed into Week 5 fresh off a frustrating loss to the Cleveland Browns in which their division rival tried everything it could to give the game away. Deshaun Watson went cold in the second half, and the Browns had 14 penalties for 88 yards, but the Steelers failed to capitalize and fell to 2-2. This week, they face another 2-2 squad, the Indianapolis Colts. After dropping their first two games of the season to the Ravens and Chiefs, the Colts have pulled out ugly wins against the now 0-4 Texans and 1-3 Commanders. While Indianapolis didn’t look particularly impressive in either of those wins, they aren’t a team the Steelers should expect an easy win from. If the version of the Steelers that showed up against the Bengals emerges again, Pittsburgh should have a reasonable expectation to win. However, if the version that reared its head against the Browns or Patriots takes the field again, the Colts are a team capable enough of winning an ugly game. Let’s take a closer look at what you can expect this week when the Steelers host the Colts. What to expect from the Colts’ offense Rushing YPG: 109.5 (14th) Passing YPG: 174.8 (26th) PPG: 25.5 (14th) RP : This past Sunday, I found myself stirring awake around 6 a.m. Pacific Time. A recent role and shift change at my day job is the primary culprit behind this — though my two dogs aren’t entirely blameless, as they get antsy at the first sign of daybreak and/or morning movement from my girlfriend or me— but I found myself unable to go back to sleep. As I sat there, bleary-eyed, I remembered there was an international game in Week 4 and turned on the game to watch. There I was met with one of the ugliest displays of offense one might experience this entire NFL season. In one corner, the 1-2 Washington Commanders, who, thanks to injuries at the position, had to shift mid-first quarter to their third-string quarterback and rookie seventh-round pick Athan Kaliakmanis. In the other corner, the 1-2 Colts and Daniel Jones, the oft-injured quarterback who was one of the most fascinating stories of the 2025 season — until he tore his Achilles. While it’s admirable that Jones is back so quickly and trying to soldier through his recovery from that injury, he hasn’t looked quite right yet this season. Just look at how the game started for the Colts’ quarterback this past week. The Steelers' defense is banged up and trading away stars, but one would hope they'll be able to handle this Colts offense. Daniel Jones, I'm sorry to report, is cooked. Overcooked even. Here's how the passing game started WK 4 for Indy pic.twitter.com/NykQl13GtF — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) October 5, 2026 Indianapolis wouldn’t put points on the board until 3:23 was left in the first half. Jones completed just 12 of 22 passes, and only two of those completions traveled more than nine air yards downfield. The second half didn’t fare much better, with Jones putting together a disgusting final stat line: 19-of-34 (55.9%) for 143 yards (average 4.2 yards per completion, no touchdowns, an interception, two sacks, and an average depth of target of just 5.2 yards. So far this season, Jones’ ADOT is just 6.2, with only Cooper Rush (5.5) and Case Keenum (6.1) posting lower figures among quarterbacks with at least one start this year. Watching the reel above, it’s not hard to see what the problem is. Jones is simply not as mobile as he normally is at full health. That’s detrimental to a player whose mobility was a major part of his game. Jones wasn’t ever going to be mistaken for Lamar Jackson or Josh Allen as a runner, but he’s posted 2,366 rushing yards and 21 rushing touchdowns over his 8-year career. Even when he wasn’t rushing for yards, he was at his best when his coordinators could scheme up bootlegs and other ways to get him out of the pocket. Now, that isn’t really an option, and he’s lost his ability to evade pressure. On top of that, the Colts don’t provide Jones many threatening receiving options to work with. The team paid big money to deep threat receiver Alec Pierce this offseason — which led them to trade Michael Pittman Jr. to Pittsburgh; it’s unclear if either side has come out ahead from that deal so far — but Pierce has already been placed on injured reserve and will be out until at least late October. Thus far, slot receiver Josh Downs leads the team in receiving yards (202), with only three other players eclipsing 100 yards on the season: tight end Tyler Warren (130), 11th-year journeyman and former first-round pick Laquon Treadwell (123), and 14-year veteran Keenan Allen (100) who missed Week 4 with a groin injury. In Allen’s absence, the Colts gave a combined 49 offensive snaps to Ashton Dulin (23), 5’9 and seventh-round rookie Deion Burks (15), and Nick Westbrook-Ikhine (11). While Warren is talented — he leads the team in receptions (23) and targets (27) — he’s also not impossible to contain. Penn State fans will remember the Nittany Lions built their entire offense around the star tight end and getting him yards after the catch, but he’s been relegated to more of a possession role with these Colts. Warren had two targets in the entire first half against the Commanders, and those didn’t come until late in the second quarter. He finished the day with five receptions for 41 yards, which trailed Treadwell for the team lead on the day (42). Not exactly explosive stuff. Daniel Jones discovers the forward pass and Tyler Warren picks up a first down. #Colts #ForTheShoe #Commanders #INDvsWAS pic.twitter.com/tL3y5rSEqO — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) October 4, 2026 While he hasn’t posted big numbers this season, if there is anyone in the Colts’ passing attack that I would be worried about, it’s Downs. He has some vertical passing juice in the slot, and with how poorly the Steelers linebackers and secondary have tackled this season, bringing him down in space could be a cause for concern. First down Josh Downs! #Colts #ForTheShoe #Texans #HOUvsIND pic.twitter.com/lc2QH68yvx — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) September 27, 2026 But priority number one for the Steelers this week should be stopping All-Pro running back Jonathan Taylor. During his seven-year career, Taylor has totaled 7,951 yards on the ground with 75 touchdowns, and has added another 1,538 yards and seven touchdowns through the air. Taylor is a powerful runner, but his superpower is his ability to shift into another gear in the open field and create explosive plays with breakaway speed that seems unnatural for a person with his 226-pound frame. YOU CAN'T STOP JONATHAN TAYLOR. 83-YARD TD. ATLvsIND on @NFLNetwork Also streaming on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XiL55trl4d — NFL (@NFL) November 9, 2025 Through four weeks, Taylor is tied with Jahmyr Gibbs for the fourth-most rushing yards (353), and trails league rushing touchdown leader Derrick Henry by just one score (6). Taylor’s ability to find cutback lanes and/or bounce runs outside late in the play’s development should keep defensive coordinator Patrick Graham tossing and turning this week, especially after the abysmal display of tackling the team put on tape against Cleveland, whose offense doesn’t feature a runner with anywhere close to the amount of long-speed or short-area burst that an All-World runner like Taylor possesses. Jonathan Taylor enjoys a cup of tea after scoring pic.twitter.com/kgUcWY5cYS — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) October 4, 2026 Taylor is the engine that makes the Colts’ offense even remotely respectable. Consider that Indianapolis has the sixth-highest explosive rushing rate (runs of 10+ yards) in the NFL, but just the 31st-ranked explosive pass (passes of 20+ yards) rate. Taylor manages to create explosive runs frequently enough that the Colts rank 17th in total explosive play rate, despite their dismal passing numbers. Offensive and defensive explosive play rates: pic.twitter.com/A0SuYaZQxj — Sam Hoppen (@SamHoppen) October 6, 2026 The…

title: Seahawks fan chat: Cowboys host winless Buccaneers on ‘Thursday Night Football’
summary: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are a bad, banged up football team. They were 6-2 at the midway point last season, having beaten the Seattle Seahawks in Seattle during that stretch. Over their last 13 games they are a rancid 2-11, including 0-4 to start the 2026 season. They’re done. Finished. Cooked. It’s over for them. […]
full_text: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are a bad, banged up football team. They were 6-2 at the midway point last season, having beaten the Seattle Seahawks in Seattle during that stretch. Over their last 13 games they are a rancid 2-11, including 0-4 to start the 2026 season. They’re done. Finished. Cooked. It’s over for them. Field Gulls deputy editor John P. Gilbert will undoubtedly have his undivided attention on former Kansas star Jalon Daniels, the undrafted rookie who’s once again tasked with starting in place of the injured Baker Mayfield for the Bucs. The Dallas Cowboys don’t have a very good defense, but their offense is elite, Dak Prescott is playing some of his best football to date, and Ceedee Lamb just humiliated the Houston Texans to the point where DeMeco Ryans has resumed play-calling duties on defense. Anyway, Bucs at Cowboys isn’t competitive on paper. Dallas may be 2-2 right now but could easily be one of the toughest remaining matchups for the Seahawks toward the back-end of the season, and it’ll be interesting to see if Brian Schottenheimer’s guys can take care of an overmatched opponent. summary: The biggest name to watch as far as the Seattle Seahawks injury report for their huge Week 5 matchup with the San Francisco 49ers is Leonard Williams. Seattle’s star defensive lineman hurt his ankle in last Sunday’s win over the Los Angeles Chargers, but seemingly avoided a more serious injury. As far as his availability […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 04: Leonard Williams #99 of the Seattle Seahawks] reacts during the second quarter against the Los Angeles Chargers at Lumen Field on October 04, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The biggest name to watch as far as the Seattle Seahawks injury report for their huge Week 5 matchup with the San Francisco 49ers is Leonard Williams. Seattle’s star defensive lineman hurt his ankle in last Sunday’s win over the Los Angeles Chargers, but seemingly avoided a more serious injury . As far as his availability for this Sunday? Up in the air, and now a little cloudier. Williams practiced on a limited basis on Wednesday, an encouraging start to the week. He did not practice on Thursday and otherwise didn’t have media availability, which is often a sign that an injured player is ready to go for that weekend. Game designations come out on Friday, and by then we’ll know if Williams is going to be a question mark, a full go, or if he’ll miss a game for the first time since 2024. One thing to note is the short week for the Seahawks, who play next Thursday night at the Denver Broncos and pretty much don’t have practice for that game. There may be some extra caution as far as injury management in practice, so Williams’ DNP doesn’t automatically mean a potential setback. Seattle does have some concerns at cornerback, as rookie Julian Neal popped up on the injury report as limited with a hamstring issue. Nehemiah Pritchett, who was notably not in for the final drive against the Chargers, has been limited both days with an ankle injury. Running back George Holani is worth monitoring given he’s been limited with a rib injury from the Washington Commanders game. On the positive side, safety Ty Okada figures to be ready to play this Sunday after being a full participant for his third consecutive practice. Okada missed the first four games with a hamstring injury. Here’s the full Thursday practice report for both the 49ers and Seahawks, with wide receiver Mike Evans a notable DNP after he was limited on Wednesday. It also doesn’t look like Marques Sigle will start at safety this weekend.

title: Seahawks All-22 review: The good and bad from Seattle’s win over the Chargers
summary: After the Seattle Seahawks suffered their first loss of the season, they returned to Lumen Field needing to bounce back and, more importantly, avoid letting one setback turn into a losing streak. On the other side was a Los Angeles Chargers team that had yet to win a game this season. This was, therefore, a […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 04: Drake Thomas #32 of the Seattle Seahawks celebrates a defensive stop against the Los Angeles Chargers during the fourth quarter at Lumen Field on October 04, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images After the Seattle Seahawks suffered their first loss of the season, they returned to Lumen Field needing to bounce back and, more importantly, avoid letting one setback turn into a losing streak. On the other side was a Los Angeles Chargers team that had yet to win a game this season. This was, therefore, a game Seattle needed to take care of before heading into a much more difficult stretch of the schedule. The Seahawks did exactly that. But while the result was positive, the performance left some warning signs, and that’s where the good and the bad of this win come into play. The Good Brian Fleury is getting legitimately creative Brian Fleury’s creativity is starting to look like more than just an early-season impression. It is becoming a defining characteristic of this offense. Against the Chargers, Seattle once again found different ways to put its playmakers in favorable situations, whether by moving pieces around or using players outside of their more traditional roles. Fleury’s creativity is becoming a defining trait of Seattle’s offense. Against the Chargers, he used Shaheed out of the backfield to exploit his speed, filling a role vacated by Price’s injury. The result: 2 carries, 33 yards and a 28-yard TD. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-07T15:38:46.390Z One of the best examples was Rashid Shaheed being placed in the backfield to take advantage of his speed, something the team was missing after the injury to Jadarian Price. The WR finished the game with two carries for 33 yards, including a 28-yard TD. Excellent blocking on this toss run, allowing Shaheed to read the field like a returner and find the space for the TD. Excellent screen design. Shaheed’s motion keeps him as an option, while Wilson gets key blocks—especially from Haynes—before breaking a tackle to finish the TD. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-07T15:39:53.182Z Excellent screen design. Shaheed motions across the formation to keep him as an option, and the ball goes to Wilson, who gets good blocks (especially from Christian Haynes) and then breaks a tackle at the end for the TD. Good OC play-calling keeps defenses guessing. From the same formation and motion, Seattle runs a similar screen design but targets the TE instead. Different answer, same look—excellent game planning. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-07T15:41:03.445Z Good OC play-calling is about keeping the defense guessing. From the same formation and motion, you can call different plays. The design is very similar to what happened on Wilson’s TD, but this time the ball goes to Barner on the screen, who gets good yardage. Excellent game plan. Excellent call. Seattle shows 6 OL/2 TEs and one WR, screaming run. The Chargers bite, leaving Horton 1-on-1. With off coverage, the slant is there; press, take the fade. Quick read, easy TD. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-07T15:41:52.791Z Excellent call. Three TEs — actually, one sixth OL and two TEs — and only one WR. Everything points toward a run. The Chargers are committed to it, leaving Tory Horton one-on-one. I believe Horton should have had two options: a slant against off coverage and a fade if the defender played press. Quick pass and TD. Emanuel Wilson makes the most of his opportunity Emanuel Wilson probably had the most complete game of his NFL career: 21 carries for 81 yards and a touchdown, plus three receptions for 39 yards and another touchdown. That’s 120 yards from scrimmage and two touchdowns on an afternoon when Seattle desperately needed production from its backfield. With Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet unavailable, Wilson received a bigger opportunity and made the most of it. I don’t necessarily think he’s the ideal running back for an offense that wants to consistently attack horizontally and outside, but he found ways to produce within what the offense was asking him to do. This is the kind of rep he needs more often. The run is designed for the B-gap, but he reads Zabel’s block, cuts inside and turns it into a solid gain. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-07T15:46:29.350Z This is the kind of snap he needs to have more often. The intended gap on this run is the B-gap, but he recognizes the good block from Grey Zabel, makes the cut inside and gets a solid gain. Here, he simply puts his head down and runs. With Barner and Abe Lucas’ blocks not developing, he misses a potential cut into the A-gap. Better vision could have created more. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-07T15:48:21.406Z Here, he simply puts his head down and runs. He doesn’t look for other options, even though the blocks from Barner and Abe Lucas don’t appear to be developing. Maybe a cut into the A-gap would have been the better option. Wilson even showed that he could contribute as a blocker…BOOM! — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-07T15:48:54.004Z Wilson even showed that he could contribute as a blocker… BOOM! Drake Thomas answers back After a game that was below his usual standard against Washington, Drake Thomas showed up in a big way against the Chargers — and he did it immediately. On the opening play, Thomas reads the play-action, drops into coverage and makes the INT. Great recognition, though Herbert’s throw was poor—and Jobe likely had a shot too. Seattle wasted it with a Darnold INT on the next snap. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-07T15:48:55.913Z On the first play of the game, Thomas intercepted Justin Herbert, showing good route recognition and making a play that immediately put Seattle in a favorable position — only for Sam Darnold to throw an interception on the very next snap. Good job recognizing the play-action, dropping into coverage and coming down with a poor throw from the QB. If he doesn’t make the interception, Josh Jobe probably does. Thomas diagnoses all the misdirection on the reverse immediately. He takes the stiff arm, but his quick recognition slows the play just enough for his teammates to finish it. This is Macdonald’s defense at work. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-07T15:50:26.399Z On this play, he diagnoses all of the misdirection on the Chargers’ reverse immediately. He takes a stiff arm, but his quick diagnosis slows the play down just enough for his teammates to finish it. This is how Mike Macdonald’s defense works, as we’ve discussed before. Thomas isn’t a big linebacker, so he makes up for it with preparation. His film study shows up in reps like this, quickly diagnosing the play, anticipating the ballcarrier and putting himself in position to make the tackle. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-07T15:51:12.821Z Drake Thomas isn’t a big linebacker. He tries to compensate for that with a ton of film study. You can frequently see his quick diagnosis on plays like this, anticipating what’s coming and waiting for the RB to make the tackle. And just because he's undersized doesn't mean he can't be physical. Look at this hit on the fullback. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-07T15:51:42.737Z And just because he’s undersized doesn’t mean he can’t be physical. Look at this hit on the fullback. BOOM! The pass rush finally showed up Herbert was pressured on 55% of his dropbacks, while Seattle finished the game with four sacks — plus a fifth that was wiped out by a roughing the passer penalty. The Chargers’ offensive line had its issues and lost players during the game, so there is some context here, but Seattle did what it needed to do: it took advantage of the situation. The pressure was consistent, and it ultimately decided the game. Nwosu’s strip-sack ended the Chargers’ comeback attempt, but Love deserves credit for cutting off the passing lane and forcing Herbert to hold the ball. —…

The defense, while still being super disruptive, is missing more tackles. Otherwise, they’re still pretty nasty. That said, I am confident that Kittle, McCaffrey, and a half-healthy Evans (with a sprinkling of Deebo and Kaelon) are enough to make plays against this defense. Especially if they get the ball in space. The 49ers offensive line gets a great chance to show that their improvement is for real, especially in the run game. That’s where they really struggled in the playoff loss last year. How to solve Seahawks’ defense? 49ers’ Kyle Shanahan has admitted he’s not one to ask (paywall) “After his motions, shifts and other eye candy didn’t fool the Seahawks, Shanahan resorted to trickery to try to gain yards in the divisional playoffs. A double-reverse pass gained one yard. A 4th-and-1 option pitch from fullback Kyle Juszczyk to running back Christian McCaffrey lost three yards. “They’re never out of position,” left guard Dominick Puni said. “They always know where each other is going to be. You can see it on film. They’re always just attached.” In February, as an analyst, Shanahan explained what made Seattle’s defense so special. The Seahawks prevent explosive passing plays by playing their two safeties deep, which usually exposes a team’s run defense. However, Seattle can still stuff opponents’ rushing attacks in its nickel defense, using an extra defensive back, and with their safeties residing in Spokane.” 49ers guard Connor Colby shows speed on George Kittle’s long touchdown “I wouldn’t say I was necessarily gaining on him,” Colby said of his sprint alongside Hufanga. “I was just trying to make a block, but then I realized once I got up there, anything I did probably would have been a penalty. So I figured, I’d just let George run.” …. “The guy’s definitely an athlete,” 49ers center Jake Brendel said. “He might not look it with his hair and his style, but, I mean, there’s definitely a reason the front office and the coaches liked him. He can run. He can run wide zone. He’s a good player.” Williams rejected the label of “sneaky athletic” to describe Colby. “I wouldn’t say that,” Williams said. “I think he’s just athletic. The mullet makes it worse. But if you work closely with him and see him, you know he’s an athlete, for sure.” 49ers DE Romello Height inspired by Patrick Willis to play through broken hand (paywall) “I was going off adrenaline,” Height said of his second-half performance in the 49ers’ 35-13 win. “I felt pain, but it didn’t matter at that point. I wanted to play for my brothers, and I wanted to finish the deal.” After further evaluation postgame, doctors determined Height’s hand would require surgery. He had a procedure Sept. 22 that kept him out of the 49ers’ subsequent contest against the Cardinals, before making his return in Week 4 against the Denver Broncos, starting and playing 37 snaps. Protecting his hand was a club — a club so hard that when Height gave fellow rookie Jaden Dugger a fist bump, he questioned how Height was even playing. Beneath his club was “a lot” of protective padding, Height said, giving the cast so much bulk that it could only be compared to a boxing glove.: 49ers’ Kyle Shanahan delivers positive Mykel Williams and Nick Bosa updates “It’s been good,” Shanahan said. “It’s been his second week back, so he had a good week last week—even better this week. So, should be good to go for Sunday.” Raheem Morris, Klay Kubiak, Brock Purdy share updates ahead of 49ers-Seahawks “A technical quarterbacking question. Your non-throwing arm. What’s the role of the non-throwing arm in throwing and is that something that you’ve ever felt like you needed to adjust or tweak or anything like that? “That’s a good question. I don’t know to be honest. I think as I’ve gone throughout my life as a thrower and looking at my mechanics and things, that is something that I’ve looked at. How should the opposite arm be? Should it be tight, like you could have your thumb hold your collar of your shirt and stuff and have it tight, but then other guys are out wide. I don’t know. It’s something that I look at every once in a while, but I don’t think it drastically changes my throwing mechanics and stuff. There’s other things that I’d look at rather than that, but it is a good point. A lot of people do look at it, so it’s a good question.” John Lynch on the 49ers ahead of the trade deadline: ‘I think you’re always in active mode’ “49ers general manager John Lynch was asked about the deadline on KNBR. Lynch continued, “I always say, I think our history speaks to the fact that we will not hesitate to improve this team if we can, and we’ve done that on a number of occasions. So we’re doing our jobs, and real proud of the way our team’s playing.”

title: Cowboys-Bucs live discussion: An MVP candidate versus a rookie quarterback
summary: No Baker Mayfield last week for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. That meant rookie Jalon Daniels took the reins. The San Francisco 49ers play the Dallas Cowboys a month from now. In […]
full_text: (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images No Baker Mayfield last week for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. That meant rookie Jalon Daniels took the reins. Daniels went 9-for-27 for 148 yards, threw two interceptions, posted a 65 passer rating, and was sacked three times. It can’t get worse, right? The San Francisco 49ers play the Dallas Cowboys a month from now. In my opinion, that’s an NFC Championship preview. But the Cowboys won’t win a playoff game if their 32nd-ranked defense in EPA per play doesn’t improve. And it’s not as if teams are gashing the Cowboys, which would inflate their defensive numbers. They’re dead last in success rate, too. Something has to give on that side of the ball. There’s only one way for Daniels to go. Without Joey Porter Jr., Dallas has been more than accommodating to opposing offenses. He’s not in uniform tonight. Dak Prescott has been surgical this season. Only Brock Purdy and Lamar Jackson have generated a higher EPA. Prescott has an 8-to-1 touchdown-to-interception ratio. Historically, he’s been aggressive against the blitz. That does not bode well for a Todd Bowles defense. It could be a long night for a Tampa Bay secondary without Antoine Winfield. My gut says 31-14, Cowboys. But this is not a team that wins comfortably. Their defense won’t allow it. So I’ll go 28-24 in an exciting Thursday showdown.

title: John Lynch on the 49ers ahead of the trade deadline: ‘I think you’re always in active mode’
summary: We’re a little more than a month away from the NFL’s trade deadline. When the San Francisco 49ers have swung a deal, they’ve made deep playoff runs. Emmanuel Sanders in 2019. Christian McCaffrey in 2022. Chase Young in 2023. Two Super Bowls and an NFC Championship appearance. Looking back, it’d be nice to have the […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re a little more than a month away from the NFL’s trade deadline. When the San Francisco 49ers have swung a deal, they’ve made deep playoff runs. Emmanuel Sanders in 2019. Christian McCaffrey in 2022. Chase Young in 2023. Two Super Bowls and an NFC Championship appearance. Looking back, it’d be nice to have the 27-year-old Young. He had 10 sacks last season, and already has 3.5 this year. But hindsight is 20/20. 49ers general manager John Lynch was asked about the deadline on KNBR. He said, “I think you’re always in active mode.” Josh Sweat plays in the division, but names like Khalil Mack, Will McDonald, Danielle Hunter, Josh Uche, Kayvon Thibodeaux, and any other pass rusher with a pulse will be linked to the Niners over the next month. Lynch continued, “I always say, I think our history speaks to the fact that we will not hesitate to improve this team if we can, and we’ve done that on a number of occasions. So we’re doing our jobs, and real proud of the way our team’s playing.” That statement was a segue into how the Niners may approach the deadline, at least at edge rusher. The team is expected to get Mykel Williams back this week. Romello Height recently returned to action. The 49ers have two more weeks until the bye. It might make the most sense to give Nick Bosa that extra week. But the 49ers also would’ve placed him on the injured reserve if they felt like he’d be out after the bye, suggesting he’ll be back sooner than later. And while we’re focusing on defensive end, this is still a team that is thin at defensive tackle. Vita Vea grew up in the Bay Area, but his 2027 cap number is over $30 million. Commanders defensive tackle Daron Payne has been more productive this year and will likely be cheaper since his contract voids after this season. Lynch referenced the health of the 49ers, saying, “We’ve had a number of injuries. Hopefully, we start getting some of these guys back and stop losing people, because sometimes you can see those as acquisitions — when you start getting these players back. We’re already playing this well. Man, when these guys come back, we’re going to be hard to deal with. So looking forward ot that, and we’ll always try to improve our team in any way possible.” It sounds like the team’s health as the deadline approaches will determine how aggressive they are.

title: 3 things to watch for in 49ers-Seahawks: Kyle Shanahan vs. Mike MacDonald is the main event
