title: Inside the NFL's wild endings and why coaches need to adapt
summary: Scoring too early and kicking the ball into the end zone can be costly, as the Cowboys learned.
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts appeared positioned for exactly the kind of finish that keeps NFL stadiums packed.

 Fourth quarter. Their ball. Down one point against the Houston Texans with 1:48 remaining. On the second play of what would be their final drive in Week 3, Colts quarterback Daniel Jones ripped a pass down the middle to receiver Laquon Treadwell for a 20-yard gain. Just like that, the Colts were cooking at the Houston 45-yard line.

 What happened next left some perplexed: The Colts began to display a sudden lack of urgency.

 They ran the ball on their next play. Next, they casually allowed the clock to tick down from 40 to 29 seconds before the following play -- that's when Houston, interestingly, called a timeout. Then, another run.

 Not until the Colts faced a third-and-6 did they make a more concerted effort to achieve a first down. Receiver Keenan Allen came up inches short after a 6-yard reception, so kicker Spencer Shrader came on and booted a 53-yard game-winning field goal with 21 seconds remaining.

 Why weren't the Colts more aggressive? And when did a 53-yard field goal become a slam dunk? The situation offered a prime example of how the traditional approach to late-game situations in the NFL has necessarily evolved at a time when more and more games are being decided late.

 In some instances, the "hurry-up" offense becomes more like "hurry up ... kinda."

 

 "That is real," Colts coach Shane Steichen said. "There's no doubt. When you have an opportunity to finish the game, you want it to be the last drive."

 Just ask the Dallas Cowboys , who can attest to it after losing a Week 3 game to the Baltimore Ravens on an inexplicable seven-second scoring drive.

 If it feels like there has been more last-minute scoring in the NFL lately, it's because there has been.

 Since the latest change to the NFL kickoff process last year, with the ball positioned at the 35-yard line after touchbacks, madness has ensued in the final moments of games. The number of drives starting in the final minute of halves culminating in a touchdown or field goal attempt skyrocketed by more than 50% relative to the 10 seasons before the changes.

 Meanwhile, the increasing strength and skill level of kickers, combined with underappreciated changes to rules governing how kicking balls -- known as K-balls -- may be manipulated by teams, has spurred a 60% increase in field goal attempts of 50 yards or longer in just five seasons. Many of those attempts are coming late in games and proving decisive.

 "I think about just the other day and even last year when you think about some of the dirty-ball kicks that [former Rams kicker  Joshua Karty ] was having, and how that was an advantage for us," Los Angeles Rams coach Sean McVay said. "It's had a significant impact."

 There were an NFL-record 12 field goal conversions of 60 yards or longer last season, including Jacksonville Jaguars kicker  Cam Little 's 68-yarder, the longest in NFL history.

 Subtle changes are translating into massive impacts on the game, and the trends seem unlikely to slow anytime soon.

 "Now you're seeing, I mean, chaos out there from some teams," Jaguars coach Liam Coen said. "And it's cool to watch."

 When a touchback can cost you the game 

 Of course, it's less cool if you're on the wrong side of the outcome.

 That brings us back to the Cowboys. There are a host of reasons they lost 34-31 to the Ravens on Sept. 27 in Rio de Janeiro, among them some curious coaching decisions and poor execution by players.

 

 But not to be overlooked was the role that today's kickoff rules played in the defeat. Had the Cowboys made the exact same miscues and been subject to the same circumstances just a few years ago, they likely would have held off Baltimore and pushed the game into overtime.

 One of the biggest variables in the loss was Dallas' decision to kick into the end zone after their tying field goal. With just seven seconds remaining, kicker Brandon Aubrey was instructed to aim for a touchback. But in the past three seasons, field position after touchbacks has been overhauled. After a 2024 change, teams were awarded the ball at the 30-yard line after touchbacks. (It was previously the 25-yard line.) A year later, in 2025, the rule was amended again, placing the ball at the 35.

 Ten yards of additional field position is priceless in an environment where kickers are capable of making field goals from near midfield.

 "You get the ball at the 35," Steichen said, "and, shoot, someone hits an in-cut [route]. Next thing you know, they're at the plus-45 [yard line] and they kick a game-winning field goal."

 It's precisely what happened to Dallas, when quarterback Lamar Jackson hit receiver Zay Flowers for a 27-yard gain immediately after Dallas' kickoff. Baltimore called a timeout with one second remaining, allowing kicker Tyler Loop to convert a 56-yard field goal as time expired.

 Two-minute situations have been turned upside down by all of this.

 According to the Elias Sports Bureau, there were 49 game-winning drives that ended in the final two minutes of regulation in 2025, the most since 2000. Through four weeks of the 2026 season, there have already been 11 such drives. That puts this season on pace to match or exceed last year's total.

 "It used to be easy," said New York Giants coach John Harbaugh, who began coaching in the NFL when touchbacks translated to drive starts at the 20-yard line. "You kick a touchback and it's a gift. Good field position for your defense. They eliminated that because they want more returns, which I'm always for more."

 

 Adding to the issues is the complexity of today's dynamic kickoff process. Because the ball must land within the specified landing zone -- between the receiving team's goal line and the 20-yard line -- the possibility of a miss exists. When kickers are attempting to kick into the corners or hit kicks at specific angles to disadvantage kick returners, the odds of a miscue increase. The potential consequences are dire: The receiving team takes possession at its 40-yard line if a kick misses the landing zone or the ball goes out of bounds.

 The whole exercise is harder than it looks.

 "People don't get how hard it is for it to land just in the landing spot," San Francisco 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan said. "Not a touchback, not short and not out of bounds. It's not as easy as people think.

 "You want to kick it high in there, but you're a little amped up and [could be] a touchback and that's a big miss because it's already at the 35 now."

 Why manipulating K-balls for the kicker could be huge 

 It's a part of the game few fans concern themselves with: the origins of the footballs used on game day.

 But it's actually a huge aspect of game prep for teams, both in terms of the balls used by quarterbacks and those set aside for kicks and punts. That's why a little-discussed rule change in 2025 has seemingly played an important role in today's frenzied final minutes of games.

 The NFL years ago standardized kicking balls, putting a stop to the over-manipulation of balls by teams looking to achieve better ball flight. The balls were presented to teams by the officiating crew, fresh out of the box, 60 minutes before kickoff. Equipment managers could address the balls using water, towels and brushes, but time was limited.

 But that rule was rescinded last year. Now, teams have the freedom to address the balls to their liking throughout the week, just as they have been doing on behalf of quarterbacks for years.

 Whether it has made a tangible difference is difficult to prove. But it's hard to imagine the explosion in long field goals since last season's rule change is coincidental. Three of the seven longest field goals in NFL history have come since the start of last season.

 

 And while the accuracy rates of kickers hasn't increased substantively, the increased willingness of teams to attempt long kicks is undeniable. According to ESPN…

title: NFL Week 5 preview: Picks, predictions, schedule, betting odds, fantasy tips
summary: Bears vs. Packers? 49ers vs. Seahawks? There are 14 more games in Week 5, and we have picks, predictions and more for all of them.
full_text:
Week 5 of the 2026 NFL season is here. Can the Raiders get back on track against the Patriots after losing their first game of the season? Will the undefeated Vikings keep rolling against the Saints? Who has the edge in Bears-Packers? How will Eagles-Jaguars play out in another edition of London football? And what can we expect from the 49ers' visit to Seattle?

 We're here to get you ready for the action. First, our NFL Nation reporters take you inside the locker room with the best thing they heard this week, and ESPN Research provides a key stat to know. Then, analytics writer Seth Walder makes a bold prediction for each matchup, NFL analyst Ben Solak gives one reason to tune in to each game, fantasy analyst Eric Moody shares fantasy football intel and betting analyst Pamela Maldonado hits betting insights for each contest. We also have Football Power Index (FPI) game projections, and Maldonado, Moody and Walder all give us final score picks for every game.

 Let's get into the full Week 5 slate, which culminates with "Monday Night Football" matchup between the Bills and Rams on ESPN . (Game times are Sunday unless otherwise noted, and all odds are via DraftKings.)

 
 Jump to a matchup: 
 PHI-JAX | CHI-GB | LV-NE 
 MIN-NO | CIN-MIA | IND-PIT 
 HOU-TEN | NYG-WSH | CLE-NYJ 
 DEN-LAC | SF-SEA | DET-ARI 
 BAL-ATL | BUF-LAR 

 Thursday: TB-DAL 
 Bye: KC , CAR 

 
 

 What ESPN Analytics says ... 
 

 

 
 

 Eagles (2-2) at Jaguars (3-1)  in London 
 9:30 a.m. ET | NFL Network | JAX -7.5 (41.5 O/U) 

 What we're hearing on the Eagles: Philadelphia entered the week with significant offensive problems. The Eagles have gone three-and-out on a league-high 15 possessions and rank 25th in points per game (18.8), 29th in total yards per game (269.8) and are tied for fourth in most sacks allowed (12). Things went from bad to worse with right tackle  Lane Johnson retiring and starting offensive lineman  Cam Jurgens being traded to Baltimore . "I think it's ironic because my thing when I came in as a rookie was, 'Don't dip your toe in the water, drown in it and learn how to swim.' We're drowning right now, and we're learning how to swim," left tackle  Jordan Mailata  said. -- Tim McManus 

 What we're hearing on the Jaguars: An under-the-radar reason for the Jaguars' offensive success over the first month is how good they've been on third down. They're converting 51.1% (ranked third), and they've been especially good in third-and-short (3 yards or less), converting 10 of 13 chances (76.9%, ranked third). "The biggest reason is staying ahead of the chains and being more consistent first and second down, less penalties, less negative runs, sacks, all those things play a part in it," QB Trevor Lawrence said. -- Michael DiRocco 

 Stat to know: The Eagles have allowed the second-lowest QBR on deep passes (20-plus air yards) this season. Opponents have completed 27% of deep passes for zero touchdowns and two interceptions against Philly. -- ESPN Research 

 Bold prediction: The Jaguars will win by two touchdowns. Philadelphia is 2-2 and ranks 27th in EPA per play on offense and 25th on defense. That is rough. And in three of those games, the Eagles had the now-retired Johnson, too. We can and should think about these teams dramatically differently now than when the season began (for the Jaguars, this is a good thing!). -- Walder 

 Why you should watch this game: You can play a game called "how many Eagles players do I recognize?" as they take the field without Johnson (retired), TE Dallas Goedert  ( knee ), WR DeVonta Smith  ( hamstring ) and RB Saquon Barkley  ( hamstring ) -- and now Jurgens is a Raven! If Willie Lampkin gets the start on the now sparse offensive line, as expected, he'll be the shortest Eagles offensive lineman (5-foot-11) to start in over 60 years. -- Solak 

 

 Injuries: Eagles | Jaguars 

 Fantasy nugget: Jaguars WR Parker Washington has scored at least 13 fantasy points in three of four games this season, so I wouldn't be too concerned about his 2.0-point Week 4 performance. He also had a 39-yard reception overturned. Washington is in a good spot to bounce back against a defense that has allowed the 10th-most fantasy points per game to WRs and has struggled against slot receivers. See Week 5 rankings . -- Moody 

 Betting insight: The Eagles are 7-0 ATS (against the spread) as underdogs since 2024. Jacksonville gives up plenty of passing yards, so QB Jalen Hurts can keep drives alive with quick throws and his legs. The Jaguars can win by leaning on the run, but Philadelphia still makes passing touchdowns tough to come by. That should help the Eagles hang around and cover the spread. Read more . -- Maldonado 

 Maldonado's pick: Jaguars 24, Eagles 19 
 Moody's pick: Jaguars 30, Eagles 23 
 Walder's pick: Jaguars 31, Eagles 14 
 FPI prediction: JAX, 73.4% (by an average of 6.5 points)

 

 Matchup must-reads: How will the Eagles move forward without Johnson? ... Why Jags play 26 of next 30 regular-season games away  ... Tracking Hunter's 2026 season 

 
 

 Bears (3-1) at Packers (2-2) 
 1 p.m. ET | Fox | CHI -1.5 (45.5 O/U) 

 What we're hearing on the Bears: Coach Ben Johnson announced Tyson Bagent as the starting QB early in the week. Getting reacquainted with the silent cadence is paramount for what is expected to be a hostile environment at Lambeau Field. Bagent is no stranger to rivalry games, having gone head-to-head with Shippensburg during his years at Division II Shepherd, but being the starter for Bears-Packers carries a different weight. "This is one of the greatest rivalries in all of sports," Bagent said. "It's easy for the fans to get up for, easy for us to get up for, so it will certainly be a different feel out there." -- Courtney Cronin 

 What we're hearing on the Packers: During TE Tucker Kraft 's rehab from last season's torn ACL, he said he saw no reason he couldn't return as the same player -- or even better. Through four games, he's tied for 15th among TEs in catches (15) and tied for 17th in receiving yards (148) with only one touchdown and has also battled the drops. "Statistically, it might not look like I'm playing better," Kraft said. "Some could even say that I might've lost my stinger. ... This week, try to get back to my roots, the kind of s--- I was on my first and second year when I was playing to the echo of the whistle and being hard on the defense." -- Rob Demovsky 

 Stat to know: The Packers' 22% pass block win rate is the worst by any team through the first four games of a season since ESPN began tracking in 2017. -- ESPN Research 

 

 Bold prediction: Bears edge Dayo Odeyingbo will stay hot and record a sack for a fourth straight game. Odeyingbo looks improved, with a 22% pass rush win rate at edge that's above average for the position. And we all know the Packers' offensive line is struggling mightily. -- Walder 

 Why you should watch this game: Do you remember the past two times the Bears and Packers played? Johnson and Packers coach Matt LaFleur had handshake drama . There's a rivalry reigniting ... and you're going to miss this game? -- Solak 

 Injuries: Bears | Packers 

 Fantasy nugget: Bears RBs D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai could have big games. Green Bay ranks 25th in run stop win rate and has allowed the third-most fantasy points per game to RBs. The Bears lead the league with 35.8 rushing attempts per game, and with QB Caleb Williams ( hamstring ) unlikely to play, they should lean on the run again. See Week 5 rankings . -- Moody 

 Betting insight:  LaFleur is 11-3 ATS in his career against the Bears. Getting the ball out sooner can help Packers QB Jordan Love handle Chicago's blitz. The Bears' defense has improved against struggling offenses but still allows 5.9 yards per play. That gives Green Bay opportunities, and Bagent still has to prove he can lead Chicago to a road win and cover. Read more . -- Maldonado

full_text:
The Green Bay Packers have had their fair share of alternate uniforms throughout their distinguished history. There were the 1950s all-green look and the 1923 classic threads unveiled last year. However, no Packers combination has ever been like the ones they'll wear this week.

 

 Green Bay will debut its "Rivalries" uniforms against the Chicago Bears on Sunday. It's a look that includes a desaturated vintage green jersey with alabaster pants and a matching matte helmet. The alabaster color is reminiscent of the aged paper of historic Packers stock certificates, according to the team . With the franchise being publicly owned, fans are able to become shareholders. More than 500,000 homes in Wisconsin include framed stock certificates, which inspired the uniform design. The alabaster jersey numbers feature an engraved treatment modeled after the lettering of paper currency -- a nod to financial support for the team. "Go Pack Go" runs on the back of the helmet, while "Making History Since 1919" is inside the collar. 

 In throwback fashion, the New England Patriots are wearing their "Pat Patriot" look versus the Las Vegas Raiders . The red uniforms include tricolored shoulder stripes with white numbers. White pants and helmets complete the look with the star of the show being Pat Patriot on the lid.

title: Fantasy football last-minute pickups: Stroud, Washington among top options
summary: If injuries, bye weeks or tough matchups have you seeking lineup help, Matt Bowen lists potential options.
full_text:
At various points during the fantasy football season, injuries, bye weeks and breaking news can cause you to need reinforcements for your fantasy lineup. Every Friday throughout the 2026 NFL season, Matt Bowen will offer some late-week pickup options at each of the primary fantasy positions to help fill those holes, with an emphasis on deeper leagues. 

 Because of that, this column will focus mostly on players rostered in fewer than 50% of ESPN leagues, with occasional exceptions. 

 The Week 5 NFL schedule features some really tough matchups for fantasy football, starting with the quarterback position. However, I still have four options -- in the QB2 range -- who have some upside. There are also a handful of wide receivers below, including deeper-league fliers you can take a chance on. As always, we'll hit on the running back and tight ends, and I have two available defenses to stream this week.

 

 Quarterbacks 

   Kirk Cousins , Las Vegas Raiders (33.3% rostered; at Patriots) 

 Cousins has scored 20 or more points in three straight games, and he has thrown two or more touchdown passes in all four games this season. Now, Cousins isn't going to provide any upside as a runner. We know that. But in Klint Kubiak 's offense, one that leans on tight end usage, Cousins can play on rhythm. And the Raiders are going to throw the ball in scoring position, as Cousins' eight red zone touchdown passes are tied for second most in the league. He's a superflex starter in the road matchup versus the Patriots.

   C.J. Stroud , Houston Texans (41.1% rostered; at Titans) 

 

 Stroud benefited from the return of wide receiver Nico Collins in Week 4, producing a season-high 23.08 points in a prime matchup versus Dallas. Collins had 118 yards receiving, plus he scored two touchdowns on end zone throws. It's a much tougher matchup this week versus the Titans, but Stroud is scoring 17.1 PPG, and Collins is the difference-maker in the Houston route tree. Stroud has value here as a QB2 in superflex formats.

   Jordan Love , Green Bay Packers (48.9% rostered; vs. Bears) 

 Love averages 16.2 fantasy PPG and has thrown two touchdown passes in all four games played. And due to a subpar rushing attack in Green Bay, Love is attempting 38.5 passes per game. Yes, the Bears defense ranks in the top 12 versus quarterbacks, but I do see positive perimeter matchups here for Packers wide receivers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden . If you need a QB2 this week, Love does have some value.

   Deshaun Watson , Cleveland Browns (15.7% rostered; at Jets) 

 Watson (16.7 fantasy PPG) has scored 19 or more points in two of four games played, and he's averaging 31.8 rushing yards per game. The Jets defense ranks in the top five versus quarterbacks, so I don't love the matchup. However, if you need a QB2 with dual-threat upside Watson fits. We've seen the Browns take vertical shots in the pass game, so there is big-play potential for Watson.

 Wide receivers 

 

   Malik Washington , Miami Dolphins (33.4% rostered; vs. Bengals) 

 I really like the tape on Washington, along with his versatility in the Miami offense. Very similar to what we see with Deebo Samuel Sr . in San Francisco. Washington has scored 11 or more points in back-to-back games, and he's averaging seven targets per game (27% team target share). Plus, he's had at least two carries in two straight. I'd have him in the lineup as a WR3.

 

   Keenan Allen , Indianapolis Colts (38.5% rostered; at Steelers) 

 Allen (groin) missed the Week 4 win over the Commanders, but he is expected back for Sunday's game in Pittsburgh. In Week 3, Allen scored 18.3 points versus the Texans, catching six of nine targets for 63 yards and a score. He can still uncover and work the dirty areas of the field, which is a fit for a Colts pass game lacking a vertical element with Alec Pierce (heel) on IR. You can play Allen as a WR3.

   Darius Cooper (6.0% rostered) and  Dontayvion Wicks , Philadelphia Eagles (47.6% rostered; at Jaguars) 

 It's a tough matchup here versus the Jags defense, but with DeVonta Smith (hamstring) still out, both Cooper and Wicks are deeper-league fliers this week. Cooper saw seven targets in the Week 4 loss to the Rams, catching three passes for 33 yards and two touchdowns for 18.3 fantasy points, and Wicks has produced two games this season with 12 or more points.

   Malachi Fields , New York Giants (7.3% rostered; at Commanders) 

 Fields is a matchup play versus a Commanders defense ranking in the bottom five versus wide receivers. Fields, who scored a season-high 13.1 points in Week 4, is averaging only 3.8 targets per game, but he did catch a touchdown pass in the win over the Cardinals on a red zone throw. Fields also has the physical tools to win one-on-ones as a boundary option. He's a deeper-league flier.

   DeMario Douglas , New England Patriots (2.2% rostered; vs. Raiders) 

 With Mack Hollins (calf) expected to miss Sunday's game versus the Raiders, Douglas should see an expanded role in the Patriots' offense. Douglas' usage has been down this season (nine receptions on 17 targets for 82 yards), but he could be in a position to operate as the outlet out of the slot for Drake Maye  on Sunday.

 Running backs 

   Brian Robinson Jr ., Atlanta Falcons (44.2% rostered; vs. Ravens) 

 Robinson scored a season-high 25.7 points in the Falcons' blowout win over the Saints in Week 4, rushing for 62 yards and three touchdowns. As the No. 2 behind Bijan Robinson , Brian has seen 10 or more carries in three straight games, posting at least one rushing touchdown in two of them. Steady volume here in an offense averaging 181 rushing yards per game (second most). Brian is a deeper-league flex this week versus the Ravens.

 

   Keaton Mitchell , Los Angeles Chargers (23.5% rostered; vs. Broncos) 

 The winless Chargers moved to a three-man backfield committee in the Week 4 loss to the Seahawks, and it was Mitchell who paced the position with 15 touches, compared to Omarion Hampton 's 11 and Kimani Vidal 's seven. Mitchell rushed for only 39 yards on 10 carries, but he did catch five passes for 24 yards. Mitchell has scored 11 or more points in two straight, and he brings more receiving upside to the lineup.

   Will Shipley , Eagles (37.8% rostered; at Jaguars) 

 With both Saquon Barkley (hamstring) and Tank Bigsby (IR) down this week, Shipley is in line to see a bump in volume. However, the Eagles' No. 3 running back hasn't had more than nine touches in a game this season, and Philly is also going through major transitions on the offensive line. Plus, Dameon Pierce could also factor into the run game. Shipley should be viewed as a deeper-league option only in this matchup with Jacksonville.

   MarShawn Lloyd , RB, Packers (46.9% rostered; vs. Bears) 

 Lloyd should split touches with Kaleb Johnson this week, as Chris Brooks is dealing with an ankle injury. Lloyd's lack of rushing efficiency (2.7 YPC) remains an issue, but he does provide some value as a pass catcher. He caught five balls for 36 yards in the Week 4 win over Tampa Bay, and he has at least two receptions in three straight games, adding a touchdown grab back in Week 2.

 Tight end

 Strange scored a season-high 16.5 points in the Week 4 win over the Bengals, catching seven of eight targets for 95 yards. Strange now has 10 or more points in two of four games played, with 13 total targets over his last two. Even with a tougher matchup versus the Eagles, Strange will see opportunities on middle-of-the-field throws from Trevor Lawrence .

title: Buccaneers explode in third quarter against Cowboys to get first win
summary: Undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels and Tampa Bay held off Dallas on "Thursday Night Football."
full_text:
ARLINGTON, Texas -- The Tampa Bay Buccaneers went into halftime trailing by three points against the Dallas Cowboys  on Thursday, and then they exploded in the third quarter for 17 points to take an 11-point lead en route to a 24-16 win on the road.

 Inside linebacker Alex Anzalone picked off Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott 's pass with 1:22 to go to preserve the Bucs' first win of the season. The fact that it was Anzalone, who has struggled to assimilate into coach Todd Bowles' defense and has faced a ton of criticism for it, put a bow on things after coming into Week 5 as the only winless team in the NFC. 

 The Bucs hadn't won a Thursday night road game since beating the Philadelphia Eagles  on Oct. 14, 2021, when Tom Brady was Tampa's QB. On Thursday, undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels made his second straight start at quarterback as  Baker Mayfield recovers from a dislocated right thumb that he suffered in Week 3.

 The Bucs also ran for 241 yards, led by  Bucky Irving 's 165 on 21 carries. Irving also ran for a touchdown and caught another.

 If there were complaints for the Bucs, it would be Bowles' decision to go for it on fourth-and-goal from the 1-yard line with Sean Tucker 's run being stuffed with 8:36 left in the fourth quarter instead of kicking a field goal to go up by 17. That gave Dallas life before Anzalone's interception closed the door. The Bucs also had a staggering 14 penalties, but they capitalized on three Cowboys turnovers. 

 Here are the most important things to know from Thursday night for both teams:

 

 

 

 Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-4) 
 QB breakdown:  Remember that double mug blitz that doomed Daniels and the offensive line on the final drive last week against the Green Bay Packers ? The Cowboys showed it on third-and-4 of the Bucs' first possession, and Daniels fired a 6-yard completion to Emeka Egbuka  before finding Irving in the flat for a 5-yard touchdown. Daniels completed 19 of 25 passes for 189 passing yards and a touchdown. Daniels' arm also came alive with the deep ball -- something we've seldom seen this season from him or Mayfield -- connecting with wide receiver Tez Johnson on a corner route for a 64-yard reception.

 Biggest surprise: Heading into this game, Bucs opponents were completing 63.8% of their passes against Bowles' blitzing schemes. But on Thursday night, Prescott started out by completing 2 of 13 passes against the blitz (15.4%) through three quarters. He finished 9-of-20 (45%), but it was too little, too late. In the absence of All-Pro safety Antoine Winfield Jr ., Tykee Smith had arguably his best game, recording five quarterback pressures on seven blitzes. He also bobbled a potential interception that Yaya Diaby ultimately corralled. Cornerback Jacob Parrish had three pass breakups and allowed just one reception, while Zyon McCollum gave up just two.

 Stat to know: Irving delivered a 72-yard rush -- the longest of his career and longest by a Buccaneer since Ronald Jones II had a 98-yard run in Week 10 of the 2020 season. What was particularly impressive about the run was the offensive line finally gained some synergy in Zac Robinson's offense, gaining 64 rushing yards before contact on the play.  -- Jenna Laine 

 Next game:  vs. Pittsburgh Steelers (Oct. 18)

 

 

 

 Dallas Cowboys (2-3) 
 There are good losses, bad losses and cataclysmic losses.

 Thursday's loss to the Buccaneers is one of the worst in recent memory in part because the Buccaneers entered the game 0-4, starting an undrafted rookie quarterback and missing one of their best defenders (Winfield).

 An offense that wants to be called the "Greatest Offense There Is" was inept after the first drive. After a 70-yard touchdown drive to open the game that included five first downs, the Cowboys' next seven drives gained 152 yards (48 on one play) and seven first downs as a 10-7 lead turned into a 24-10 deficit in the third quarter.

 And the defense once again was shredded, although this time it was Daniels through the air and Irving on the ground. For the 12th straight time, dating back to last year, the Cowboys allowed 20 or more points in a game, matching a team record. They gave up a 72-yard run and a 64-yard pass, while allowing a first down on third-and-21. All in the second half.

 As good as the Cowboys could have felt after Sunday's come-from-behind win at the Houston Texans , this loss was embarrassing for a team that fancied itself a contender.

 Prescott finished the night 24-of-32 for 316 passing yards and a touchdown -- and  George Pickens had nine catches for 130 yards and a touchdown -- but the two interceptions hurt.

 Trend to watch: Daniels had a passer rating of 110.2, as the Cowboys' defense has allowed opposing quarterbacks to post a passer rating of at least 99.1 in the first five weeks. Jaxson Dart (134.2), Marcus Mariota (109.1), Jayden Daniels (99.1), Lamar Jackson (136.7) and C.J. Stroud (126.7) have had their way with the defense. Coming up next is Green Bay's Jordan Love , followed by Philadelphia's Jalen Hurts . It won't get easier.

 Most surprising performance:  For all of the defensive struggles in the first month of the season, the Cowboys' third-down defense had improved greatly during the previous two games. The Baltimore Ravens converted 3 of 9 tries in Week 3, and the Texans went 3-of-10 last week. By the end of the Buccaneers' first drive Thursday, they had four third-down conversions. And they did it with an undrafted rookie quarterback making just his second start. Tampa finished 7 of 13. Just when it seems as though the Cowboys have stopped one hole on defense, another pops up.

 Stat to know:  Through five games, Javonte Williams has six rushing touchdowns, capping the Cowboys' only first-quarter drive with a 1-yard run. Williams is the second Cowboy with at least six rushing scores in the first five games. Emmitt Smith did it twice (seven in 1994, nine in 1995), and Calvin Hill had six in 1971. Williams had a career-high 11 rushing touchdowns in his first season with the Cowboys last year.  -- Todd Archer 

 Next game:  at Green Bay Packers (Oct. 18)

title: Do the Broncos have a reliable No. 1 running back? Sorting Denver's backfield
summary: The Broncos' running game has been stuck in neutral, as J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey and Tyler Badie have struggled in the early going.
full_text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- Through four games, the Denver Broncos ' search for Mr. Right in the run game is still in progress. Or the quest for the right combination of Mr. Rights. Or the journey to discover any run game. But this isn't a new problem.

 Let's go back to Jan. 27, two days after the Broncos lost the AFC Championship Game to the New England Patriots . In his season-ending news conference, Broncos coach Sean Payton said: "When we want to run it under center and control a game, we've been able to do it a few times, but not as much as I'd like."

 Fast forward almost nine months later. After a 24-14 loss to the San Francisco 49ers dropped the Broncos to 2-2, a visibly frustrated Payton said: "I think at half we were at 30-some (rushing) yards, that's something that has to get better."

 The Broncos will enter their Week 5 matchup against the 0-4 Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday in SoFi Stadium ( 4:05 p.m. ET, CBS ) with a murky at best rotation in the backfield. That has resulted in Denver having the 29th-ranked rushing attack in the league at 81.3 rushing yards per game. At 40.3 rushing yards per game, J.K. Dobbins is the only Broncos back among the league's top 65 rushers and is below 12 quarterbacks. So, Denver hasn't been able to find that reliable back it can depend on.

 

 "Overall, just the consistency and our approach -- whether it's in the shotgun or under center -- that will continue to be a focal point for us," Payton said earlier this week. "It's always in these details."

 The struggles boiled over against San Francisco, as a frustrated Dobbins exchanged words with running backs coach Lou Ayeni on the sideline during a game in which he finished with 11 carries for 40 rushing yards. Denver running backs ended up with 20 carries for 72 rushing yards (3.6 yards per carry).

 The Broncos' backfield was set back early when fourth-round rookie Jonah Coleman suffered an ankle injury in Week 2 against the Jacksonville Jaguars and placed on injured reserve . He'll be eligible to return as soon as the Broncos' Week 7 game against the Arizona Cardinals but showed flashes of being a complement to Dobbins prior to the injury. His decisive running nature stood out, and he led the team with 39 yards on 10 carries and a second-half touchdown in the comeback victory over the Jaguars.

 That leaves Dobbins, who leads the team in carries (46) and rushing yards (161) in a current rotation with second-year man RJ Harvey (12 carries, 49 yards) and Tyler Badie (four carries, 10 yards). That group hasn't meshed smoothly. Only once has a Broncos running back had more than 11 carries in a game -- Dobbins had 17 carries for 49 yards in a Week 3 win over the Los Angeles Rams .

 Broncos offensive coordinator Davis Webb has cited a lack of assertiveness on carries -- especially from running backs not named Coleman -- as a reason why the backfield hasn't gotten on track.

 "I think we have to run with a little more conviction, for sure," Webb said. "When they can see a hole, run through it, full speed ahead. And I think our runners do that, I just think there's been some times where that can be a little bit better and I anticipate that getting better."

 Leaving yards on the field has been a problem. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, all three running backs currently on the active roster have a negative average rushing yards over expected, a metric which measures how many yards a ballcarrier gains in comparison to how well a play is blocked.

 Dobbins ranks 52nd in the NFL with minus-0.6 yards over expected per carry, and his 3.5 yards per carry is well below the 5.0 he averaged last season (153 carries for 772 yards) before getting hurt in Week 10. Harvey averages minus-0.8 yards over expected per carry, with Badie at minus-1.8 in a very small sample size. Even Coleman, at 0.1 yards over expected per carry, has essentially gotten the yardage that is blocked.

 

 By comparison, the Kansas City Chiefs ' Kenneth Walker III leads the league at 2.5 yards over expected (minimum 10 carries), with the Atlanta Falcons ' Bijan Robinson in second at 1.95 yards over expected.

 The Broncos' inability to run the ball has bled into the passing game, too. With the running backs not providing oomph on the ground, defenses have been content to sit back with two safeties deep in coverage to prevent downfield strikes in the passing game, relying on their front seven to contain the run.

 That's been successful at both levels, as the Broncos' passing game is 29th in air yards per attempt (5.9) and 20th in pass plays of 20 or more yards. Broncos quarterback Bo Nix knows how important it is to get the running backs going to make his job easier.

 "I think overall when you get 2-high zone you just want to run the football," Nix said. "And so we just got to find ways to continue to do that."

 But who will take the reins and be that consistent backfield running threat? Is it as simple as waiting for Coleman to return from injury? Payton has promised to "look at everything" to get the run game going, and facing the Chargers' 22nd-ranked run defense might help a bit.

 It's a mixed bag between Sunday and Denver's Week 10 bye, as the Broncos will face the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks (No. 11 in rushing defense), the Cardinals (No. 20), Chiefs (No. 5) and Carolina Panthers (No. 32) in Weeks 6-9.

 "It's not one thing," Payton said. " ... It's still that work in progress, with the runners, all of it, the coaches, what we're doing. We'll get there."

title: Why the Raiders' running game has struggled, and what's next for Ashton Jeanty
summary: The Raiders have made offensive strides ... except for the running game. What's next for Las Vegas and Ashton Jeanty?
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- The Las Vegas Raiders opened their Week 4 matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs with plenty of momentum. Four plays in, and they already were on the scoreboard when quarterback Kirk Cousins threw a 27-yard touchdown pass to tight end Ian Thomas .

 The Raiders tried to replicate that success on their second drive, but were unsuccessful.

 

 With 2:17 to go in the first quarter and the game tied at seven, Cousins completed a 15-yard pass to tight end Michael Mayer , then coach Klint Kubiak turned to the run game to keep the chains moving, but they didn't. Rookie running back Mike Washington Jr . was stopped for a one-yard attempt before Chiefs rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane wrapped up running back Ashton Jeanty for no gain. On third-and-9, Cousins threw an incomplete pass, which forced the Raiders to punt.

 In the Raiders' 30-27 loss to the Chiefs last Sunday, they went toe-to-toe with a team that has won nine of the past 10 AFC West titles. But the Raiders' upset attempt failed because of more than a questionable fourth-down decision from Kubiak or Dareke Young's kick return fumble. For the third straight week, Las Vegas failed to establish a consistent run game, totaling 72 yards.

 The Raiders have made significant offensive strides; they rank eighth in the league in points per game (28.7) and Cousins has thrown a league-high 11 touchdowns. However, their rushing attack has been a problem. Entering the season, the Raiders' run game was meant to be their biggest strength. Instead, their production has mirrored last year when they ranked last in nearly every rushing metric.

 Multiple factors have contributed to Las Vegas' faulty rushing attack, from playcalling to Jeanty, their top running back and 2025 first-round pick, playing through an ankle injury. Jeanty was a limited participant in Thursday's practice due to an ankle and foot injury. If the Raiders want to show their strong first month wasn't a fluke, they will need to improve their rushing numbers, starting Sunday afternoon against the New England Patriots ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ).

 "I think we've just got to be better. Simple as that," Jeanty said. "Make the plays that are out there. ... It starts with us. Starts with me. Got to break tackles and make bigger plays when they're available."

 
 

 FIXING THE RUN game was a big part of the Raiders' preparation ahead of the season. In the past three seasons, Las Vegas ranked last in rushing yards per game (82.7) and yards per attempt (3.6).

 This year was meant to be a different story. Jeanty was entering Year 2 and more experienced. Kubiak brought in a proven outside zone run scheme. The Raiders signed center Tyler Linderbaum , who is one of the better run blockers at his position. And Washington showed throughout training camp that he could be capable of being a reliable second option in the backfield.

 The Raiders didn't have issues running the rock in Week 1's victory over the Miami Dolphins . They totaled 137 rushing yards, with Jeanty recording 102 yards on 23 attempts. Since then, Las Vegas's numbers have declined.

 In the past three weeks, the team has ranked 32nd in yards per attempt (three), 28th in yards per game (80.7), 30th in rushing first downs (11) and tied for 26th in attempts for 10-plus yards (four).

 

 "Going back to that first game [against Miami], just as a whole unit, we played better," Kubiak said. "We were more efficient running the football, and that's something we got to get back to. So, it's something that we're diligent about."

 Jeanty, who was expected to make a jump in Year 2, has struggled as well. He rushed for 58 yards against the Chiefs. He has been held to under 60 rushing yards in five of his past 10 games dating back to his rookie season.

 Through four games, Jeanty has a rush success rate of 35.9% and a rush EPA of minus-23.2. Now, Jeanty's inconsistent production is not all on him. He has been playing through an ankle injury , which he suffered near the end of training camp.

 He said after the loss to Kansas City that the injury hasn't nagged him, but he expects to be 100% healthy real soon.

 "I'm going to continue to keep getting better and stronger," Jeanty said.

 Yes, Jeanty has to improve his vision and take advantage of open lanes whenever they appear. At the same time, the run blocking has to be cleaned up. Against Kansas City, Jeanty was stopped for no gain or a loss of yards on six attempts. Meanwhile, Washington had three of his nine attempts result in zero or fewer yards.

 Las Vegas is 30th in yards before first contact per attempt (1.34), and has the most carries for zero or negative yards (29).

 "You want to hit a home run every single time, but it's not going to happen," Linderbaum said. "It's how many times can we get to second-and-6 [and] second-and-5. That's the challenge. ... At the end of the day, that falls on the [offensive] line."

 
 

 AFTER THE RAIDERS' first loss of the season, Kubiak said they need to find answers for their inconsistent rushing attack. Kubiak is more than capable of finding those answers.

 When Kubiak was the offensive coordinator for the Seattle Seahawks last season, the run game started slow before finding a groove and becoming instrumental in their Super Bowl LX victory over New England.

 They averaged 3.6 rushing yards per attempt and had a success rate of 37.4% from Weeks 1-4. From Week 5 to the end of the season, the Seahawks averaged 4.3 yards per attempt, a success rate of 41.6% and recorded 14 rushing touchdowns.

 In Las Vegas, Kubiak admitted that he needs to scheme up better plays to get the run game flowing. There were times against the Chiefs when the Raiders' pre-snap motion forced a defender to move over a gap, freeing them up to stop the run.

 

 Raiders frequently face stacked boxes (eight or more defenders at the line of scrimmage), which has also been a challenge. Las Vegas has faced stacked boxes on 30.3% of its run plays -- the fourth-highest percentage.

 The reasons behind opponents loading up the box are respect for Jeanty and the Raiders utilizing heavy personnel groupings at a high volume. With Kubiak using multiple tight end and running back formations, it requires the opposing defense to bring more defenders to the line of scrimmage.

 Las Vegas has seen success in the passing game when using heavy personnel groupings. But that success hasn't translated to the run game. The Raiders are tied with the Buffalo Bills for the most carries against stacked boxes (nine per game). However, they are 14th in yards per carry (2.3) and 26th in success rate (27.8%).

 "It just becomes a little bit of the math of how many players are down inside the tight end box, and do we have angles, do we have numbers or don't we? And it changes play to play," Cousins said. "... Teams are always going to be in that cat-and-mouse game a little bit of how you're trying to defend or how you're trying to attack the defense."

 The Raiders still believe the run game can be the identity of the offense despite their early struggles to find consistency. Once they gain more momentum in their rushing attack, they will be even more dangerous on play-action plays.

 Las Vegas knows it has the right players and coaches in the building to improve its run production. As a whole, they are confident that things will turn around, and hope that shift comes against the Patriots.

 "We got a great opportunity to go out there and do great things," Jeanty said.

title: How Saints can regroup, fix slow starts ahead of matchup with unbeaten Vikings
summary: New Orleans had a tough Week 4 loss to Atlanta, which also highlighted key deficiencies the Saints need to correct.
full_text:
METAIRIE, La. -- The bitterness of the New Orleans Saints ' 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night will linger throughout a shortened week. 

 That's exactly how Saints defensive end Chase Young wants it with the 4-0  Minnesota Vikings up next on Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox ).

 "You should be upset," Young said Wednesday. "We didn't play to our standard, but the positive is seeing everybody come in today, how they're dealing with it. And that's what you want to see: dudes who have a sour taste in their mouth, dudes who are mad about it. I hope you mad. You get punched in your mouth, hopefully you ain't smiling."

 Young said he was pleased with the response of his teammates this week as they figure out how to regroup on both sides of the ball before Sunday. While Young will be facing an offense that ranks 18th in scoring, the Saints' offense will go up against the NFL's best scoring defense and top pass rush. 

 "They're undefeated, so that kind of speaks to the defense that they've had," tight end Juwan Johnson  said. "[They] bring a large amount of exotic blitzes, exotic looks. You're going to get a lot of shell looks, you're going to get a bunch of different shell looks. The biggest part is just exploiting just the gaps in their defense ... just playing our ball. We know how to play. 
 
"We just need to execute better."

 

 The Saints (1-3) will be underdogs against a Vikings squad that Saints wideout Chris Olave said is "one of the best teams in the NFL." Olave noted in an interview with French media this week that the Vikings have a lot of stunts and blitzes that can be difficult to face.

 "We're just going to have to put our best foot forward," he said. 
 
"They're 4-0, we're 1-3. On paper it's a lopsided matchup, but at the end of the day we still have to go out there and play for 60 minutes."

 Early mistakes doomed the Saints against the Falcons. The Saints allowed 205 yards on the ground after letting Bijan Robinson run 59 yards for a touchdown three plays into the game. The Saints rushed for only 50 yards as a team. 

 That rushing output and the team's slow starts have gone hand in hand. The Saints have the third-fewest first-quarter points this season (six), compared with 39 in the fourth quarter, which is tied for the most in the league with the Buffalo Bills and Denver Broncos . 

 The Saints have rushed for more than 100 yards only once this season. 

 "To be transparent, it's obvious that we've struggled running," Johnson said. "And I think we've been pretty good in the offseason just being dialed in on our keys and running the ball and it hasn't shown, but I think whenever we, and when we do well at running the ball, we're going to see an explosive amount of big plays just from our offense."

 Part of the lack of run game comes from falling behind early, which has forced the Saints to pass more. Defensively, they've given up 32 points per game, last in the league, a difficult combination for offensive balance. 

 Saints quarterback Tyler Shough has already attempted 180 passes this season, which is the second most in franchise history through four games behind Drew Brees' 191 attempts through four games in 2012. Brees had to throw often in those games (the Saints started 0-4) to try to keep pace due to a defense that still holds the record for most yards allowed in a season. 

 The current Saints know they have to eliminate mistakes they can no longer afford with such a small margin for error.

 "In the NFL, you can't live in that world where they know you're going to throw it every single time," Shough said. "And I don't have a problem doing that, but it's just tougher. 
 
"You can't have turnovers early in the game, and then we've got to be able to go down there and score. Three-and-outs, stuff like that. It's going to happen sometimes but ... limit those mistakes."

 

 So how do they fix the slow starts issue that dates to last season? Johnson said he doesn't think the Saints need to "turn practice over" or make huge adjustments. 

 "That's what people do when you have no answers, but we do have answers to the things that we do need to do. Again, we're only four games in. This is essentially this season's first quarter," Johnson said. "We know what we need to work on, and we're going to do exactly that."

 The Saints will make adjustments, though. Shough said the team put an emphasis on starting faster this week and made small changes, such as tweaking the practice schedule to try to build momentum quicker. 

 "More than anything, as players, we just have to do a better job of executing faster earlier. I think what we've done in the past and what we did last year, I think what we're going to start doing, is just have a compete period at the beginning of practice instead of the end," Shough said. "And that way you're immediately going right into it, and that's something that you can work on."

 Shough said there's no magic fix, pointing out that the team started better against the Las Vegas Raiders (the Saints scored a touchdown in the first quarter but missed the point-after attempt), then fell apart in the fourth quarter with turnovers. 

 "It's kind of a double-edged sword there," Shough said. "And more than anything, it kind of comes down to relentless execution."

title: Fantasy football buzz: Sean Payton not a cure-all for Broncos fantasy woes
summary: Sean Payton will call the plays for the Broncos' offense, but fantasy managers should temper their expectations.
full_text:
Everything that happens in the NFL has additional context when viewed from a fantasy football perspective. From position battles to injuries and so much more, the news cycle will constantly affect player values.

 Our fantasy football buzz file, with contributions from our ESPN fantasy writers and our NFL Nation reporters, aims to provide fantasy managers with the intel they need as news breaks around the league.

 

 Oct. 8: Sean Payton is not a cure-all for Broncos fantasy woes 
 By Tristan H. Cockcroft 

 It'd be understandable if fantasy managers of Denver Broncos players are giddy with excitement following the news that head coach Sean Payton is taking back playcalling duties from offensive coordinator Davis Webb.

 These Broncos, who finished 10th in yards and 14th in scoring last season, have seen those rankings dip to 27th in either category in 2026. Bo Nix is only the No. 20 quarterback in terms of fantasy scoring, and much ballyhooed offseason acquisition Jaylen Waddle is 33th among wide receivers. And don't get any of us started on Courtland Sutton or the top two running backs, J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey .

 But here's the reality of the situation: Playcalling changes don't always lend immediate, dramatic results, and this season's returns thus far might be as much of an indication of Nix's raw talent than it is the playcalling.

 

 Sure, under Webb's direction, the Broncos' offense has been more conservative, forcing Nix to rely much more on dump-offs and screens. And perhaps Payton, who coaxed decently productive seasons from the 26-year-old quarterback in 2024 and 2025, will open things up more, raising Nix's ceiling for softer matchups and getting the ball to Waddle with more space to make things happen after the catch.

 To the latter point, Waddle's average depth of target is down more than 2 yards this season, and he's on pace for 51 targets within 5 yards of, or behind, the line of scrimmage, which would be easily his most since his rookie season in 2021. I'd love to see him targeted more in the deep game, raising his ceiling into the mid-to-high range of fantasy WR2s, but it's hardly a guarantee that this coaching move will make it happen. Waddle is slightly more attractive as a trade target -- and this speaks to those of you off to slow starts in need of shaking things up with higher-upside moves -- but I'm not making rash adjustments to my valuations.

 As is, it hasn't been the easiest of schedules for Payton's Broncos (@KC, JAX, LAR, @SF), and things do ease up with matchups against the  Los Angeles Chargers (Week 5) and Arizona Cardinals (Week 7) upcoming. Denver's second-half schedule is better than the first as well. That's as much of an actionable on the trade front for Broncos players, but it's also not something that should dramatically swing the arrow upward.

 Oct. 8: Week 5 stats to know 
 by Michael F. Florio

 

 
 David Montgomery has posted career lows in yards per carry, forced missed tackles rate, explosive run rate, yards before and after contact per carry, average speed and success rate. Simply put, outside of the three TDs in Week 1, it's been rough for Monty. Wait for his next big game, which could be this week against the Tennessee Titans , and then look to trade him. 
 Carnell Tate 's target share has climbed every week, reaching 43% in Week 4. He is being used downfield more. It seems like the Titans are unlocking him. On the season, 26 of his 32 targets have come against zone coverage, which the Houston Texans play 83% of the time. 
 Every QB who faced the Detroit Lions has scored at least 21 fantasy points. They have weekly finishes of QB8, QB1, QB3 and QB6. Start Jacoby Brissett this week. 
 Three of four QBs to face the Washington Commanders have topped 23 fantasy points. Jameis Winston is in play as a streaming option this week. 
 The Lions have allowed the most yards before contact per carry (2.0) and the second-highest explosive run rate (15%) to RBs. Jeremiyah Love is poised for a bounce-back performance. 
 Quinshon Judkins saw a career-high seven targets last week and his touches have increased every game, reaching 23 in Week 4. The New York Jets have allowed the fourth-most rushing yards per game to RBs. 
 Garrett Wilson has a 50% target share against man coverage, which is tied for the highest in the NFL ( Amon-Ra St. Brown ). The Cleveland Browns play man coverage at the highest rate in the NFL (50%). 
 DK Metcalf is tied for the league lead with 10 deep targets. This week he faces the Indianapolis Colts , who have allowed the most yards on deep passes. 
 Isaiah Likely has a 33% target share with Winston at QB. He faces the Commanders, who are in the top five in terms of most touchdowns and fantasy PPG allowed to tight ends. 
 Dalton Kincaid , who has just five targets and 45 yards in his last two games combined, faces the Los Angeles Rams who have allowed a league-low 85 yards to tight ends this season and just one touchdown. 
 

 Oct. 7: Trade for or trade away? SOS says make these six moves today 
 

 By Tristan H. Cockcroft 

 We're at that time of season where the fantasy football trade market is either heating up or is already at peak temperature.

 There's inevitably a 0-4 team in your league, grasping to hopes of a miracle comeback. And it can be done, especially if I remind you that all you probably need is a 7-3 hot streak to make the playoffs as an I-sure-don't-want-to-face-them No. 4 seed. Trades -- especially bigger, badder and bolder ones -- are the best way to turn around a slow start.

 One way to unearth the highest-ceiling trades is to lean heavily upon the upcoming schedule. Mix and match your way into the playoffs and be that maddening team to face! This week, Mike Clay has released his initial version of the rest-of-season schedule rankings at each position -- kickers and defenses, too!

 It's a great tool for determining how fluky your player's extreme hot-or-cold start to the season might have been, as well as which players are in the best positions to thrive over the remaining 13 weeks of the fantasy season.

 Here are six trade-related takeaways to consider as you start offering deals:

 
 Bryce Young has been an unexpected early breakthrough , going from a No. 186 overall ADP and 11.1% opening-week roster rate to scoring the third-most fantasy points among quarterbacks through four weeks. He has certainly capitalized upon a soft schedule, the seventh-best at the position thus far. Young and his Carolina Panthers are on bye, but they have the position's third toughest the rest of the year. Young might be a tough player to trade based upon his past history, but considering his schedule and how bruised and battered the quarterback position on the whole, he's a name worth floating if you're confident in your QB1. 
 He might seem like an unappealing fantasy RB2 , but Aaron Jones Sr . could be one of the sneakiest running back values amongst that valuation tier, particularly over the next six weeks. Since Jordan Mason landed on IR , Jones' 78% snap and 73% rushing shares both rank fourth, and his 41.5 fantasy points are 14th, among running backs. Jones and the Minnesota Vikings also face the third most-favorable remaining schedule at the position, including nothing but upper-half matchups (aside from a Week 6 bye) the next seven weeks (@NO, bye, IND, @DET, BUF, @GB, @SF). 
 Colston Loveland 's fantasy managers are surely displeased after the No. 37 overall pick in terms of ADP has placed just 19th in target share (14.9%) and 31st in fantasy points (20.1) among tight ends through four weeks. His  Chicago Bears ' remaining schedule offers some hope of recovering TE1 value, as theirs has been the third toughest at the position thus far but the third most- favorable the rest of the year.
